mc.stem: Axolotls—salamanders that can regrow lost limbs, damaged heart tissue, and even parts of the ______ survive in the wild mainly in the canals of Xochimilco, near Mexico City, where their numbers have fallen sharply since the 1990s. Many of the axolotls that researchers study today descend from animals shipped to laboratories in Europe in the 1860s.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
(A) brain,
(B) brain—
(C) brain;
(D) brain
parts.a: (B). The dash after "Axolotls" opens a nonessential element ("salamanders that can regrow ... parts of the brain"), and the sentence's verb, "survive," comes only after that element ends. A nonessential element must close with the same mark that opened it, so a second dash belongs after "brain." (A) closes a dash-opened element with a comma; the commas inside the list make a comma feel natural, but those commas separate the list items inside the dashes and cannot also close the dash. (C) puts a semicolon between the subject "Axolotls" and its verb "survive"; a semicolon needs a complete sentence on each side, and neither side is one. (D) leaves the dash unclosed, so the interruption runs straight into the main verb.
parts.n: Type: Boundaries (closing a nonessential element). Rule or move: find where the interruption opened and close it with the same mark: dash with dash, comma with comma, parenthesis with parenthesis. Trap: (A), because the commas in the list inside the dashes make a comma look like the natural mark to end on.

mc.stem: In 1995, astronomers announced the discovery of 51 Pegasi b, the first planet found orbiting a Sun-like star. Since then, the number of known planets beyond our solar system ______ to more than 5,000, a milestone NASA announced in 2022, and the count keeps rising as new telescopes come online.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
(A) have climbed
(B) were climbing
(C) climb
(D) has climbed
parts.a: (D). The subject of the clause is "the number," which is singular; "of known planets beyond our solar system" is a prepositional phrase that describes it. A singular subject needs a singular verb, and "Since then" (a span running from 1995 to the present) calls for the present perfect: "the number ... has climbed." (A) is plural: it agrees with "planets," the object of the preposition "of," rather than with the subject. (B) is plural and also in the past progressive, which clashes with "Since then." (C) is a plural present-tense verb and also ignores the time span that "Since then" sets up.
parts.n: Type: Form, structure, and sense (subject-verb agreement). Rule or move: "the number of X" is singular ("has"), while "a number of X" is plural ("have"); cross out the prepositional phrase to find the true subject. Trap: (A), which agrees with "planets," the plural noun inside the phrase that separates the subject from its verb.

mc.stem: Most meteorites that reach the ground are stony, and many look so much like ordinary rocks that they are never noticed. Iron meteorites make up only about 5 percent of the meteorites seen to ______ account for a far larger share of those found by chance long after landing, since their weight and metallic sheen make them hard to overlook.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
(A) fall, they, however,
(B) fall however; they
(C) fall; they, however,
(D) fall, however, they
parts.a: (C). "Iron meteorites make up only about 5 percent of the meteorites seen to fall" and "they account for a far larger share..." are both independent clauses, so they must be joined by a semicolon (or split by a period), not by commas. The contrast belongs to the second clause (a small share of falls versus a large share of finds), so "however" sits inside that clause, set off by commas: "; they, however, account." (A) joins the two independent clauses with only a comma, a comma splice. (D) is also a comma splice: "however" is not a conjunction, so putting it between the clauses with commas does not join them. (B) uses a semicolon but attaches "however" to the first clause with no comma before it, and that clause does not contrast with anything before it: the first sentence already said most meteorites are stony.
parts.n: Type: Boundaries (conjunctive adverbs). Rule or move: however, therefore, moreover and their kin cannot join two sentences; put a semicolon or period between the clauses and set the adverb off with commas inside the clause it belongs to. Trap: (D), which puts "however" between the clauses with a comma on each side, the comma splice strong writers most often miss.

mc.stem: Beneath nearly four kilometers of Antarctic ice ______ Lake Vostok, a body of liquid water about 250 kilometers long that has been cut off from the atmosphere for what may be millions of years. Researchers study the lake partly as a model for the ice-covered oceans thought to exist on Jupiter's moon Europa.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
(A) lies
(B) lie
(C) have lain
(D) are lying
parts.a: (A). This sentence is inverted: it opens with a prepositional phrase ("Beneath nearly four kilometers of Antarctic ice"), and its subject, "Lake Vostok," comes after the verb. "Lake Vostok" is singular, so the verb must be the singular "lies." (B), (C), and (D) are all plural forms ("lie," "have lain," "are lying"), which would agree only with "kilometers," the object of the preposition "of," not the subject. Tense does not rescue any of them: whatever the tense, a plural verb cannot agree with a singular subject.
parts.n: Type: Form, structure, and sense (subject-verb agreement, inverted order). Rule or move: when a sentence begins with a place phrase and the verb comes first, look after the verb for the subject and make the verb agree with it. Trap: (B), which agrees with "kilometers," the plural noun right before the blank.

mc.stem: Each year the Moon moves slightly farther from ______ drift of about 3.8 centimeters that scientists measure by timing laser pulses bounced off reflectors that Apollo astronauts left on the lunar surface. The cause is the tides: the bulge that the Moon's gravity raises in Earth's oceans pulls the Moon forward in its orbit, lifting it gradually outward.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
(A) Earth; a
(B) Earth. A
(C) Earth a
(D) Earth, a
parts.a: (D). "A drift of about 3.8 centimeters that scientists measure by timing laser pulses..." is a noun phrase that renames the Moon's yearly movement; its only verbs ("measure," "left") sit inside the relative clauses "that scientists measure" and "that Apollo astronauts left," so the phrase has no verb of its own and cannot stand alone. It attaches to the main clause with a comma. (A) puts a semicolon before it, but a semicolon must be followed by an independent clause. (B) makes "A drift of about 3.8 centimeters..." a separate sentence, which is a fragment. (C) runs "Earth" straight into "a drift" with no punctuation, so the phrase seems to continue the prepositional phrase "from Earth."
parts.n: Type: Boundaries (clause or phrase?). Rule or move: before choosing a semicolon or period, find the subject and verb of what follows; a verb that sits inside a "that" or "which" clause does not make the phrase a sentence. Trap: (A), because "that scientists measure" looks like a subject and verb, so the phrase feels like a clause.

mc.stem: Saturn's main rings, which are made mostly of chunks of water ice ranging from dust grains to boulders, span roughly 280,000 kilometers from edge to edge, more than twice the width of the planet itself. Yet in most places ______ thickness is only about 10 meters, making them, in proportion, far thinner than a sheet of paper.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
(A) its
(B) it's
(C) their
(D) they're
parts.a: (C). The thickness being described belongs to the rings: they span 280,000 kilometers, yet they are only about 10 meters thick, and "making them" later in the sentence confirms the plural. The antecedent "Saturn's main rings" is plural, so the plural possessive "their" is correct. (A) is singular; it would refer to Saturn or to "the planet itself," the nearest singular noun, but the planet is not 10 meters thick. (B) is the contraction of "it is," which makes no sense before "thickness." (D) is the contraction of "they are," not a possessive.
parts.n: Type: Form, structure, and sense (pronoun-antecedent agreement). Rule or move: ask whose thickness, width or share the sentence means, then match the possessive to that noun, not to the nearest noun. Trap: (A), because "the planet itself" is the last noun before the blank and "its" sounds natural after it.

mc.stem: In January 1610, Italian ______ turned a telescope of his own making toward Jupiter and noticed three small points of light lined up near the planet. Over the following nights their positions shifted, and after spotting a fourth, he concluded that all four were moons circling Jupiter, a direct challenge to the view that everything in the heavens revolved around Earth.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
(A) astronomer, Galileo Galilei,
(B) astronomer Galileo Galilei
(C) astronomer Galileo Galilei,
(D) astronomer, Galileo Galilei
parts.a: (B). "Italian astronomer" is a descriptive title placed directly before the name, with no article; the name is essential to identify which Italian astronomer is meant, so no punctuation separates the title from the name, and none separates the name (the subject) from its verb, "turned." (A) sets the name off as if it could be removed, but "In January 1610, Italian astronomer turned a telescope..." is not a sentence. (C) puts a comma between the subject and its verb. (D) separates the title from the name and then runs the name into the verb, so the comma opens an interruption that never closes.
parts.n: Type: Boundaries (restrictive appositive). Rule or move: a title or description used like a label before a name ("physicist Marie Curie," "the novelist Toni Morrison") takes no commas; commas go around a name only when the sentence would be complete without it. Trap: (A), because a name following a description looks like the classic nonessential appositive.

mc.stem: Soil scientist Lena Marsh studies how forests recover after fire. In burned plots in California's Sierra Nevada, she has found that the charcoal left behind by a low-intensity fire, along with the fine ash that settles into the gaps between soil particles, ______ the soil's capacity to hold water for several years after the burn.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
(A) improve
(B) have improved
(C) are improving
(D) improves
parts.a: (D). The subject of the "that" clause is "the charcoal," which is singular. "Along with the fine ash that settles into the gaps between soil particles" is an interrupting phrase set off by commas; unlike "and," "along with" does not join two nouns into a plural subject. A singular subject takes the singular verb "improves." (A), (B), and (C) are all plural ("improve," "have improved," "are improving"); they treat the charcoal and the ash as a compound subject, or agree with "particles," the plural noun just before the blank.
parts.n: Type: Form, structure, and sense (subject-verb agreement). Rule or move: along with, as well as, together with and in addition to add information but not subjects; only "and" makes a compound subject. Trap: (A), because two substances are named and "particles" sits right before the blank.

mc.stem: Before 1883, most American towns set their clocks by the Sun, so noon in Boston came about twelve minutes earlier than noon in New York. The confusion that dozens of different local times created for railroads trying to publish reliable ______ the major lines to adopt four standard time zones across the country on November 18, 1883, a system that Congress did not write into law until 1918.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
(A) timetables prompted
(B) timetables, prompted
(C) timetables—prompted
(D) timetables; prompted
parts.a: (A). The second sentence has one long subject, "The confusion that dozens of different local times created for railroads trying to publish reliable timetables," and its verb is "prompted." Nothing separates a subject from its verb, however long the subject is, so no punctuation belongs between "timetables" and "prompted." (B) puts a single comma between subject and verb; the comma is tempting because a reader naturally pauses after a long subject, but a pause is not a boundary. (C) inserts a dash, which would have to open or close an interruption, and there is none. (D) uses a semicolon, which needs a complete sentence on each side; "prompted the major lines to adopt..." has no subject.
parts.n: Type: Boundaries (subject and verb). Rule or move: however long the subject, no single mark goes between it and its verb; find the verb, then check that nothing splits it from its subject. Trap: (B), because the subject is so long that a comma where you would pause sounds right.

mc.stem: The Great Oxidation Event, a rise in atmospheric oxygen that began roughly 2.4 billion years ago as photosynthesizing cyanobacteria released oxygen faster than volcanic gases and exposed minerals could absorb it, ______ the chemistry of Earth's oceans and land surface permanently.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
(A) altering
(B) altered
(C) having altered
(D) to alter
parts.a: (B). The sentence's subject is "The Great Oxidation Event," and everything from "a rise" to "absorb it" is an appositive that renames it. The verbs in that appositive ("began," "released," "could absorb") belong to its own clauses, so the sentence still needs a main verb for its subject. Only "altered" is a finite verb that can do that job. (A) "altering" and (C) "having altered" are participles, and (D) "to alter" is an infinitive; none of them can serve as the main verb of a sentence, so each leaves the subject without a predicate and the sentence a fragment.
parts.n: Type: Form, structure, and sense (finite and nonfinite verbs). Rule or move: after a long appositive, go back to the subject and check that it has a main verb of its own; -ing forms, having + participle, and to + verb cannot be that verb. Trap: (A), because the long appositive already contains verbs, so the sentence feels complete and "altering" reads like an add-on.

mc.stem: Ecologist Ruth Okafor and her team spent two summers recording every insect and bird that visited alpine sunflowers on a single slope in the Colorado Rockies. Three visitors surprised them: the white-lined sphinx moth, which often feeds at ______ the rufous hummingbird, a species more often seen at red, tubular flowers; and a small beetle that had never before been recorded at such a high elevation.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
(A) dusk,
(B) dusk:
(C) dusk;
(D) dusk
parts.a: (C). The colon introduces a list of three visitors, and the items themselves contain commas ("the white-lined sphinx moth, which often feeds at dusk"; "the rufous hummingbird, a species..."). When list items contain commas, semicolons separate the items, as the "; and" before the third item shows. A semicolon therefore belongs after "dusk," the end of the first item. (A) uses a comma, which would make the reader think "the rufous hummingbird" is another piece of the first item and would clash with the semicolon that separates the second and third items. (B) uses a second colon inside a list that a colon has already introduced. (D) runs the first item into the second with no punctuation.
parts.n: Type: Boundaries (complex series). Rule or move: when any item in a list contains a comma, separate all the items with semicolons, and look ahead in the sentence for the "; and" that confirms the pattern. Trap: (A), because a comma is the normal list separator and the reader stops looking before the "; and" near the end.

mc.stem: Of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, only one still stands, and it is also the oldest. Built for the pharaoh Khufu around 2560 BCE from an estimated 2.3 million blocks of stone, ______

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
(A) the Great Pyramid of Giza originally stood about 146 meters tall, a height no human-made structure would exceed for more than 3,800 years.
(B) about 146 meters was the original height of the Great Pyramid of Giza, a height no human-made structure would exceed for more than 3,800 years.
(C) Khufu's builders raised the Great Pyramid of Giza to a height of about 146 meters, which no human-made structure would exceed for more than 3,800 years.
(D) the Great Pyramid of Giza's original height of about 146 meters would not be exceeded by any human-made structure for more than 3,800 years.
parts.a: (A). The introductory phrase "Built for the pharaoh Khufu around 2560 BCE from an estimated 2.3 million blocks of stone" describes a structure, so the subject that follows the comma must name that structure: the Great Pyramid of Giza. Only (A) makes "the Great Pyramid of Giza" the subject. (B) makes "about 146 meters" the subject, as if a measurement had been built from stone blocks. (C) makes "Khufu's builders" the subject; the builders did the building, but they were not built for Khufu from blocks of stone. (D) is the closest trap: "the Great Pyramid of Giza's" is a possessive that modifies the real subject, "height," and a height is not built from stone.
parts.n: Type: Form, structure, and sense (dangling modifier). Rule or move: the noun right after an introductory modifier's comma must be the thing the modifier describes, and a possessive such as "the Pyramid's" is not that noun; the noun it modifies is. Trap: (D), which puts "the Great Pyramid of Giza's" first, so the right words appear in the right place while the subject is actually "height."

mc.stem: Most fish are the same temperature as the water around them, but the Atlantic bluefin tuna can keep its swimming muscles more than 10 °C warmer than the surrounding sea. The heat is generated by the muscles themselves and is retained by a dense network of blood vessels called the rete ______ transfers heat from warm blood leaving the muscles to cold blood arriving from the gills.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
(A) mirabile; which
(B) mirabile, it
(C) mirabile, and which
(D) mirabile, which
parts.a: (D). "Which transfers heat from warm blood ... to cold blood arriving from the gills" is a nonessential relative clause describing the rete mirabile; it attaches to the main clause with a comma. (A) puts a semicolon before a "which" clause, but what follows a semicolon must be an independent clause, and a "which" clause is dependent. (B) makes "it transfers heat..." an independent clause and joins it to the first with only a comma, a comma splice. (C) "and which" would need an earlier "which" clause for the second one to pair with; with none, the "and" leaves the clause stranded.
parts.n: Type: Boundaries (relative clause). Rule or move: "which" turns a clause dependent, so it attaches with a comma; swapping "which" for "it" makes a new sentence that needs a semicolon or period. Trap: (B), because "it transfers" reads smoothly and the comma splice is easy to miss.

mc.stem: When Charles Darwin collected birds in the Galápagos Islands in 1835, he did not recognize many of them as finches; the ornithologist John Gould made that identification after the specimens reached London. Biologists now recognize more than a dozen finch species on the islands, and differences in the ______ correspond closely to differences in what each species eats, from hard seeds to insects to cactus nectar.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
(A) specie's beaks
(B) species' beaks
(C) species beak's
(D) species beaks'
parts.a: (B). The sentence compares the beaks belonging to the many finch species, so "species" (the same form in the singular and the plural) must be a plural possessive, "species'," and "beaks" must be a plain plural, since the beaks own nothing here. (A) invents a singular "specie" (a word that actually means coins) and makes it possessive. (C) leaves "species" without a possessive and makes "beak's" possessive, though the beaks own nothing. (D) likewise makes the beaks, rather than the species, the owners.
parts.n: Type: Form, structure, and sense (plurals and possessives). Rule or move: decide which noun owns something (it gets the apostrophe) and which is simply plural (no apostrophe); a plural ending in s takes the apostrophe after the s. Trap: (A), because "specie" looks like the singular of "species" and "specie's" looks like a correct possessive.

mc.stem: Cecilia Payne, whose 1925 doctoral thesis used the spectra of stars to show that they are made overwhelmingly of hydrogen and ______ persuaded by a senior astronomer to describe that result as probably spurious. Within a few years, other researchers had reached the same conclusion, and her finding is now a foundation of astrophysics.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
(A) helium was
(B) helium; was
(C) helium, was
(D) helium—was
parts.a: (C). The comma after "Payne" opens a nonessential clause ("whose 1925 doctoral thesis ... hydrogen and helium") that sits between the subject, "Cecilia Payne," and its verb, "was persuaded." That clause must close with a matching comma before the verb. (A) never closes it, so "hydrogen and helium was persuaded" reads as if helium were the thing persuaded. (B) puts a semicolon between the subject and its verb; neither side is an independent clause. (D) closes a comma-opened clause with a dash; the marks around an interruption must match.
parts.n: Type: Boundaries (closing a nonessential clause). Rule or move: when a comma opens a "who," "whose" or "which" clause between a subject and its verb, a second comma must close it right before the verb, however long the clause runs. Trap: (A), because the clause ends with a noun, "helium," that looks like the subject of "was."

mc.stem: On January 17, 1912, Robert Falcon Scott and four companions reached the South Pole after a march of more than two months. The next day, nearby, they found a tent flying the Norwegian flag. Roald Amundsen's team ______ there on December 14, 1911, more than a month before them.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
(A) had arrived
(B) arrives
(C) has arrived
(D) will have arrived
parts.a: (A). The passage narrates Scott's arrival in the past tense ("reached," "found"), and Amundsen's arrival happened before it, on December 14, 1911. An action completed before another past action takes the past perfect, "had arrived." (B) is the present tense, which clashes with a passage set entirely in 1911 and 1912. (C), the present perfect, ties a past action to the present and cannot be used with a specific past date such as "on December 14, 1911." (D) is the future perfect, which describes an action that will be complete at some future time.
parts.n: Type: Form, structure, and sense (verb tense). Rule or move: in a past-tense narrative, an event that happened before the main events takes had + past participle; the present perfect never goes with a specific past date. Trap: (C), because "has arrived" sounds like completion and the student forgets that the story is set in the past.

mc.stem: Venom is common among snakes, spiders, and jellyfish but rare among mammals: of the more than 6,000 known mammal species, only a small number are venomous. These ______ the platypus, several species of shrew, the solenodons of Cuba and Hispaniola, and the slow lorises of South and Southeast Asia.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
(A) include:
(B) include—
(C) include;
(D) include
parts.a: (D). "These include" is a subject and a verb whose object is the list that follows; a verb and its object are never separated by punctuation. (A) is the trap: a colon can introduce a list, but only after an independent clause, and "These include" is not complete until its object arrives. (B) a dash between the verb and its object splits the clause in the same way. (C) a semicolon needs an independent clause on each side, and neither "These include" nor the list is one.
parts.n: Type: Boundaries (colon use). Rule or move: a colon must follow a complete sentence; if the words before it end in a verb or a preposition ("include," "are," "such as"), no colon. Trap: (A), because "a colon introduces a list" is only half the rule.

mc.stem: Gray wolves were reintroduced to Yellowstone National Park in 1995 and 1996, roughly seventy years after the park's last native wolves were killed. Since then, ecologists ______ whether the wolves' return set off a chain of effects, from fewer elk browsing along streams to the recovery of willow and aspen, or whether other factors, such as drought and a rise in the number of bears, explain much of that change.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
(A) debated
(B) had debated
(C) have debated
(D) will debate
parts.a: (C). "Since then" marks a span of time that begins with the reintroduction and runs to the present, and the rest of the sentence treats the question as still open ("explain" is present tense). An action that began in the past and continues now takes the present perfect, "have debated." (A), the simple past, presents the debate as finished at some past moment, which clashes with "Since then." (B), the past perfect, needs a later past event to precede, and there is none. (D), the future tense, contradicts "Since then": the debate has already been going on.
parts.n: Type: Form, structure, and sense (verb tense). Rule or move: "since" plus a past time (since then, since 1995) calls for has or have + past participle, because the span reaches the present. Trap: (A), because the reintroduction sentence is in the simple past and "debated" seems to match it.

mc.stem: Although the side of the Moon that never faces Earth is often called its "dark side," a nickname suggesting endless ______ receives just as much sunlight as the near side does. The name reflects what was once unknown, not what is unlit: no one saw the far side until the Soviet probe Luna 3 photographed it in 1959.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
(A) night; it
(B) night, it
(C) night. It
(D) night: it
parts.a: (B). The sentence opens with "Although," so everything up to "night" (the "Although" clause and the appositive "a nickname suggesting endless night" that renames "dark side") is dependent. The independent clause is "it receives just as much sunlight as the near side does." A dependent clause that comes first joins the main clause with a comma. (A) uses a semicolon, which needs an independent clause before it as well as after. (C) turns "Although ... night." into a fragment. (D) uses a colon, which also must follow an independent clause.
parts.n: Type: Boundaries (dependent and independent clauses). Rule or move: check the first word of the sentence; a clause that begins with although, because, when or if is dependent, however long it runs, and joins the main clause with a comma. Trap: (A), because the appositive in the middle makes the reader forget the "Although" that began the sentence, so the first half feels complete.

mc.stem: In 1920, astronomers Harlow Shapley and Heber Curtis publicly debated whether the spiral nebulae were clouds of gas within the Milky Way or separate galaxies far beyond it. The question was settled not by argument but by ______ Hubble found pulsating stars called Cepheid variables in the Andromeda nebula, and their periods revealed that it lay far too distant to be part of our galaxy.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
(A) measurement. Edwin
(B) measurement, Edwin
(C) measurement Edwin
(D) measurement, however, Edwin
parts.a: (A). "The question was settled not by argument but by measurement" is an independent clause, and so is "Edwin Hubble found pulsating stars ... in the Andromeda nebula" (it has its own subject and verb and continues with "and their periods revealed..."). Two independent clauses need a period (or a semicolon or colon), so the period is correct. (B) joins them with only a comma, a comma splice. (C) fuses them with no punctuation at all. (D) is also a comma splice, since "however" is an adverb, not a conjunction, and the contrast it signals is wrong: the second sentence explains the measurement rather than opposing it.
parts.n: Type: Boundaries (sentence boundaries). Rule or move: if the words after the blank have their own subject and verb, and the words before do too, you need a period, semicolon or colon, never a lone comma. Trap: (B), because "by measurement, Edwin Hubble found" can be misread as an introductory phrase leading into Hubble's discovery.

mc.stem:
The following text is from Jane Austen's 1813 novel Pride and Prejudice.

Mr. Bennet was so odd a mixture of quick parts, sarcastic humour, reserve, and caprice, that the experience of three-and-twenty years had been insufficient to make his wife understand his character. Her mind was less difficult to develop. She was a woman of mean understanding, little information, and uncertain temper.

parts.q:
As used in the text, what does the word "develop" most nearly mean?
(A) cultivate
(B) figure out
(C) expand
(D) bring into being
parts.a: (B). "Develop" is used in its older sense of unfolding or laying open something so that it can be understood. The sentence answers the one before it: twenty-three years of marriage had not been enough for Mrs. Bennet to understand her husband's character, whereas her own mind is easy to figure out, and the next sentence proves it by summing her up in one line ("mean understanding, little information, and uncertain temper"). (A) is wrong: "cultivate" is the modern sense of developing a mind, but the passage contrasts how hard each spouse is to understand, not how easy each is to educate. (C) is wrong for the same reason: nothing in the text is about enlarging her mind, and the next sentence stresses how small it is. (D) is wrong: her mind already exists; no one in the text is creating it.
parts.n: Type: Words in context (older sense of a common word). Rule or move: When a familiar word seems to fit in its modern sense, test it against the sentence it answers: "less difficult" answers "insufficient to make his wife understand," so "develop" must be about understanding. Trap: (A) cultivate, the modern sense a strong reader supplies from habit rather than from the sentence.

mc.stem: In 1966, economists William J. Baumol and William G. Bowen observed that performing a string quartet takes as many musicians, and as much time, as it did when the music was written. Since musicians' wages must still rise along with wages in industries whose output per worker has soared, the cost of live performance climbs faster than the cost of most manufactured goods. Baumol and Bowen used this idea, now called "cost disease," to explain the finances of orchestras and theaters, but the pattern is hardly ______ the performing arts: the same logic applies to any labor-intensive service, such as teaching or nursing, whose output per worker resists increase.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
(A) detrimental to
(B) indebted to
(C) peculiar to
(D) foreign to
parts.a: (C). "Peculiar to" means belonging only to, or exclusive to. The sentence contrasts where Baumol and Bowen first applied the idea (orchestras and theaters) with where it actually operates, and the colon explains the contrast: the same logic applies to teaching, nursing and any labor-intensive service. So the pattern is hardly exclusive to the performing arts. (A) is wrong: rising costs plainly do harm the arts' finances, so "hardly detrimental" contradicts the text, and the colon's point about other services has nothing to do with harm. (B) is wrong: "indebted to" means owing something to, and a pattern of rising costs owes nothing to the arts. (D) is wrong: "hardly foreign to the performing arts" would stress that the pattern belongs in the arts, which is no contrast with its having been used to explain orchestras and theaters, so the "but" makes no sense; the colon also points outward, to other services, not back to the arts.
parts.n: Type: Words in context (common word, uncommon sense). Rule or move: Let the colon choose the word: what follows a colon explains or proves the claim before it, so "applies to any labor-intensive service" demands a phrase meaning "exclusive to." Trap: (A) detrimental to, because the word "disease" primes a choice about harm.

mc.stem: The loose, unfinished-looking brushwork at the edges of the painter Clara Voss's canvases has often been taken as a sign of haste. Art historian Leila Haddad argues that this apparent carelessness is ______: X-ray images show that beneath the rough strokes lie carefully finished passages, which Voss painted over to achieve a sketchier effect.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
(A) studied
(B) incidental
(C) conspicuous
(D) excessive
parts.a: (A). In this sense "studied" means deliberate or carefully contrived, as in "a studied casualness." Haddad disputes the usual reading of the rough edges as haste, and the X-ray evidence after the colon shows that Voss first finished those areas and then painted over them to look sketchy: the carelessness is a calculated effect. (B) is wrong: "incidental" (happening by chance, as a side effect) is the very view Haddad argues against. (C) is wrong: the brushwork is certainly visible, but the X-ray evidence addresses whether the roughness was intended, not how noticeable it is. (D) is wrong: nothing in the text says Voss overused the effect; the evidence concerns how she produced it, not how much of it there is.
parts.n: Type: Words in context (uncommon sense of a common word). Rule or move: "Apparent X is ___" followed by evidence that X was planned calls for a word meaning deliberate; "studied" in this sense means carefully contrived. Trap: (C) conspicuous, which describes the brushwork accurately but is not what the X-ray evidence proves.

mc.stem: Architectural historian Paulo Mendes contends that a small brick chapel, long dismissed as a minor early commission of the architect Ruth Adair, is in fact ______ her mature style. Built a decade before any of her celebrated civic buildings, the chapel already has, in compact form, nearly every feature for which those buildings are admired: the recessed entrances, the high bands of clerestory windows, the absence of applied ornament.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
(A) a culmination of
(B) an aberration from
(C) a concession to
(D) a harbinger of
parts.a: (D). A harbinger is something that comes before and signals what is to follow. Mendes rejects the view of the chapel as minor, and his evidence is chronological: it was built ten years before the civic buildings, yet it already shows their defining features, so it announces the mature style in advance. (A) is tempting because the chapel already has "nearly every feature" of the mature style, but a culmination is the final, highest point of a development; the chapel was built a decade before the civic buildings, so it begins the style rather than crowning it. (B) is wrong: an aberration is a departure from the norm, which would support the old view that the chapel is unrepresentative, whereas Mendes stresses how much it shares with the later work. (C) is wrong: "a concession to" would mean the chapel yields to or accommodates the mature style, and nothing in the text suggests a compromise between two styles.
parts.n: Type: Words in context (precise sophisticated word). Rule or move: Check close choices against every fact in the text, especially time order: "built a decade before" rules out any word that places the chapel at the end of the development. Trap: (A) a culmination of, which matches "nearly every feature" but reverses the chronology.

mc.stem: In a study of how people value what they own, economist Ines Park and colleagues found evidence consistent with the endowment effect: participants given a coffee mug demanded more to sell it than other participants were willing to pay for the same mug. Park is careful, however, to ______ the finding. The gap between selling and buying prices appeared only among participants who had held the mug for more than a few minutes, and it vanished entirely when the mug was described as having been bought for resale.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
(A) corroborate
(B) qualify
(C) generalize
(D) disavow
parts.a: (B). To qualify a claim is to limit it or attach conditions to it. "However" signals that Park is doing something other than simply reporting the effect, and the next sentence supplies two conditions: the effect appeared only after participants had held the mug for a few minutes, and it vanished when the mug was framed as bought for resale. (A) is wrong: corroborating means confirming with further evidence, but what follows restricts the finding rather than strengthening it, and "however" marks a turn away from simple support. (C) is wrong: generalizing would extend the finding to more cases, the opposite of stating where it fails. (D) is wrong: to disavow is to reject outright, yet Park's own data show the effect under some conditions; she narrows the claim rather than abandoning it.
parts.n: Type: Words in context (common word, specialized sense). Rule or move: When a text reports a finding and then lists the conditions under which it holds or fails, the verb it wants is "qualify": to limit, not to reject. Trap: (D) disavow, which overreads "vanished entirely" and ignores that the effect did appear under the first condition.

mc.stem: The Danish painter Vilhelm Hammershøi (1864–1916) is best known for his quiet gray interiors, many of them showing rooms of his own Copenhagen apartment, often with a single figure, usually his wife, Ida, seen from behind. Critics have frequently treated these near-empty rooms as confessions of loneliness. Art historian Anna Lund finds such readings ______: nothing in Hammershøi's letters or recorded remarks mentions loneliness, and the same bare rooms, she notes, can just as plausibly be seen as an exercise in balancing light, line, and empty space.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
(A) anachronistic
(B) derivative
(C) speculative
(D) unassailable
parts.a: (C). "Speculative" means based on conjecture rather than evidence. Lund's two points after the colon are that no documentary evidence (letters or recorded remarks) supports the loneliness reading and that another reading fits the paintings equally well; together they show that the loneliness interpretation is a guess. (A) is wrong: "anachronistic" would mean the readings project a later era's ideas onto the paintings, and Lund's evidence says nothing about the time period of the ideas. (B) is wrong: "derivative" (copied from earlier work) would require evidence that critics borrowed the idea from one another, and the text offers none. (D) is wrong: "unassailable" (impossible to challenge) is the opposite of Lund's position, since she is challenging the readings.
parts.n: Type: Words in context (precise sophisticated word). Rule or move: Match the word to the kind of evidence offered: "no documentary support" plus "an equally plausible alternative" is the standard case against a claim as speculative. Trap: (B) derivative, which sounds like critical disapproval but needs evidence of copying that the text never gives.

mc.stem:
The following text is adapted from Jane Austen's 1817 novel Persuasion. Years earlier, Anne Elliot had been persuaded to break off her engagement to a young naval officer whose prospects seemed uncertain.

How eloquent could Anne Elliot have been! how eloquent, at least, were her wishes on the side of early warm attachment, and a cheerful confidence in futurity, against that over-anxious caution which seems to insult exertion and distrust Providence! She had been forced into prudence in her youth, she learned romance as she grew older: the natural sequel of an unnatural beginning.

parts.q:
As used in the text, what does the word "sequel" most nearly mean?
(A) consequence
(B) installment
(C) repetition
(D) justification
parts.a: (A). The last sentence describes the order of Anne's life: prudence was forced on her when she was young, and romance came afterward. Austen calls the later romance the "natural sequel," that is, the natural consequence or result, of that unnatural (forced) beginning. (B) is wrong: "installment" is the modern sense of a sequel as the next part of a book or film, but no story is being continued here, only a development in Anne's character. (C) is wrong: romance does not repeat the early prudence; it is its opposite. (D) is wrong: the text does not say the later romance justifies the early caution; the passage, if anything, regrets that caution.
parts.n: Type: Words in context (literary, older sense). Rule or move: Substitute each choice into the phrase and test it against the whole sentence: "the natural ___ of an unnatural beginning" needs a word for what follows as a result. Trap: (B) installment, the modern entertainment meaning of the word.

mc.stem:
The following text is Walt Whitman's poem "When I Heard the Learn'd Astronomer," first published in 1865.

When I heard the learn'd astronomer,
When the proofs, the figures, were ranged in columns before me,
When I was shown the charts and diagrams, to add, divide, and measure them,
When I sitting heard the astronomer where he lectured with much applause in the lecture-room,
How soon unaccountable I became tired and sick,
Till rising and gliding out I wander'd off by myself,
In the mystical moist night-air, and from time to time,
Look'd up in perfect silence at the stars.

parts.q:
Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
(A) A series of scientific claims is presented and then disproved by the speaker's own observation of the night sky.
(B) A lecture that the speaker at first admires is described, followed by an explanation of why his admiration faded.
(C) A comparison between the astronomer and his applauding audience leads the speaker to side with the audience.
(D) An account of a formal lecture about the stars gives way to an account of the speaker's solitary, wordless view of them.
parts.a: (D). The four "When" lines build up the lecture (proofs, figures, charts, diagrams, the lecture-room); the turn comes at "How soon unaccountable I became tired and sick," after which the speaker walks out alone and looks at the stars "in perfect silence." The poem moves from a formal presentation about the stars to a private, wordless experience of them. (A) is wrong: the speaker never disputes the astronomer's proofs; he leaves, he does not refute. (B) is wrong on both halves: the "much applause" belongs to the audience, not to the speaker, and "unaccountable" means he cannot account for his reaction, so the poem offers no explanation of it. (C) is wrong: the audience applauds the astronomer, and the speaker walks away from both.
parts.n: Type: Text structure (overall structure of a poem). Rule or move: Find the turn (here "How soon unaccountable I became tired and sick") and describe each half in neutral terms; reject any choice that adds an action the speaker never takes, such as refuting or explaining. Trap: (B), which reads the audience's applause as the speaker's admiration and misses that "unaccountable" means he cannot explain his reaction.

mc.stem:
The following text is Christina Rossetti's sonnet "Remember," first published in 1862.

Remember me when I am gone away,
Gone far away into the silent land;
When you can no more hold me by the hand,
Nor I half turn to go yet turning stay.
Remember me when no more day by day
You tell me of our future that you planned:
Only remember me; you understand
It will be late to counsel then or pray.
Yet if you should forget me for a while
And afterwards remember, do not grieve:
For if the darkness and corruption leave
A vestige of the thoughts that once I had,
Better by far you should forget and smile
Than that you should remember and be sad.

parts.q:
Which choice best describes how the last six lines of the text relate to the first eight lines?
(A) They restate the opening request but support it with a new and more urgent reason.
(B) They qualify the opening request by placing the listener's happiness above being remembered.
(C) They withdraw the opening request because the speaker has come to doubt the listener's devotion.
(D) They predict that the listener's grief will fade as the speaker's absence grows longer.
parts.a: (B). The first eight lines repeat one request: "Remember me." At "Yet" the speaker limits it: if the listener forgets for a while, the listener should not grieve, because it is "better by far" to forget and smile than to remember and be sad. The request still stands, but it now yields to the listener's happiness, which is a qualification. (A) is wrong: the last six lines do not repeat the request; they soften it. (C) is wrong: the speaker does not take the request back (forgetting is only "for a while," followed by remembering), and the poem gives no hint that she doubts the listener's devotion. (D) is wrong: the lines are conditional ("if you should forget"), not a prediction, and they concern whether the listener should grieve, not how grief changes over time.
parts.n: Type: Text structure (relationship between parts of a poem). Rule or move: A "Yet" at the turn of a sonnet often limits the first idea rather than reversing it; ask whether the speaker drops the opening claim or places a condition on it. Trap: (C), which treats the limit as a withdrawal and invents a motive (doubt) that the poem never states.

mc.stem: When asked to estimate a quantity, people tend to stay close to any number they have just seen, even an arbitrary one, a bias known as anchoring. Psychologist Dana Whitfield wondered whether experts are immune. She asked professional art appraisers to estimate the value of a painting after showing them a catalog page on which a lot number was printed; half saw a low number and half a high one. The appraisers' estimates rose with the lot number, yet every appraiser, when asked afterward, insisted that the number had played no part in the judgment. The finding suggests that expertise may make a bias harder to detect in oneself without making it any less powerful.

parts.q:
Which choice best describes the function of the fourth sentence ("The appraisers' estimates rose...") in the text as a whole?
(A) It presents a result that contradicts Whitfield's hypothesis, which the final sentence then tries to explain away.
(B) It describes a flaw in the study's method that the final sentence acknowledges as a limitation of the finding.
(C) It reports a pair of observations that together form the basis for the conclusion drawn in the final sentence.
(D) It offers an example of anchoring among nonexperts for comparison with the appraisers' behavior.
parts.a: (C). The fourth sentence reports two things: the appraisers' estimates tracked the arbitrary lot number, and the appraisers denied that the number affected them. The final sentence draws its conclusion from exactly that pair: expertise may make the bias "harder to detect in oneself" (the denial) "without making it any less powerful" (the estimates still moved). (A) is wrong: Whitfield only "wondered whether" experts are immune, which is a question, not a hypothesis that they are, and the final sentence interprets the result rather than explaining it away. (B) is wrong: the sentence reports findings, not a methodological flaw, and the final sentence states no limitation. (D) is wrong: the appraisers are the experts; no nonexpert group is described.
parts.n: Type: Text structure (function of a sentence). Rule or move: Define a sentence by its job relative to its neighbors: here it supplies the two facts that the next sentence turns into a two-part conclusion. Trap: (A), which mistakes "wondered whether experts are immune" for a hypothesis that experts are immune.

mc.stem: In 1940 and 1941, Jacob Lawrence painted sixty small panels depicting the Great Migration, the movement of Black Americans from the rural South to cities in the North. Rather than finishing one panel before starting the next, Lawrence laid out all sixty together and applied a single color at a time to every panel that needed it, working through his palette color by color. The method kept his colors consistent from panel to panel, but it also shaped how the series is experienced: because no panel was completed in isolation, the work reads less as a sequence of separate pictures than as one continuous composition.

parts.q:
Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
(A) To describe a painter's working method and suggest how it affects the way his series is perceived
(B) To explain why a painter chose the Great Migration as the subject of an ambitious series
(C) To argue that a series of paintings ought to be exhibited as a single work rather than as separate panels
(D) To contrast a painter's method of working with the methods used by other painters of his time
parts.a: (A). The text spends its middle sentence on Lawrence's method (all sixty panels at once, one color at a time) and its last sentence on two effects of that method: consistent color and a series that "reads" as one continuous composition. So it describes a method and suggests how the method shapes perception of the work. (B) is wrong: the text names the subject but never explains why Lawrence chose it. (C) is wrong: saying the series reads as one composition is an observation about how it is experienced, not a recommendation about how it should be exhibited. (D) is wrong: no other painters are mentioned.
parts.n: Type: Text structure and purpose (main purpose). Rule or move: A purpose choice must cover the whole text and claim no more than the text does; "describes and interprets" is not "recommends." Trap: (C), which turns the author's observation about how the series reads into a prescription the text never makes.

mc.stem: Most words bear no natural relationship to what they mean: nothing about the sound of "tree" suggests a tree, and other languages use entirely different sounds for the same thing. Yet the arbitrariness is not total. In surveys covering thousands of languages, words meaning "small" contain the vowel sound heard in "teeny" more often than chance would predict. Such a pattern is too widespread to be explained by shared ancestry or by borrowing between languages. It suggests instead that some links between sound and meaning may be rooted in the way human beings perceive the world.

parts.q:
Which choice best describes the function of the fourth sentence ("Such a pattern is too widespread...") in the text as a whole?
(A) It concedes that the pattern described in the third sentence is less widespread than the text at first suggests.
(B) It identifies shared ancestry and borrowing as the likely sources of the pattern described in the third sentence.
(C) It explains why the generalization in the first sentence has come to be so widely accepted by linguists.
(D) It sets aside two possible explanations of a pattern before the final sentence proposes a different one.
parts.a: (D). The fourth sentence names two ordinary ways a sound pattern can spread across languages (inheritance from a common ancestor and borrowing) and dismisses both: the pattern is "too widespread to be explained by" them. That clears the ground for the final sentence, which offers another explanation ("instead"): a basis in human perception. (A) is wrong: the sentence insists the pattern is very widespread; it concedes nothing. (B) is wrong: it names ancestry and borrowing only to rule them out, as the word "instead" in the next sentence confirms. (C) is wrong: the sentence is about the pattern in the third sentence, not about why the first sentence's generalization is accepted.
parts.n: Type: Text structure (function of a sentence). Rule or move: A sentence that names possible causes may be eliminating them rather than endorsing them; check for words like "too ... to be explained by" and a following "instead." Trap: (B), which notices the two named sources but misses that the sentence dismisses them.

mc.stem:
The following text is adapted from Edith Wharton's 1920 novel The Age of Innocence.

On a January evening of the early seventies, Christine Nilsson was singing in Faust at the Academy of Music in New York.

Though there was already talk of the erection, in remote metropolitan distances "above the Forties," of a new Opera House which should compete in costliness and splendour with those of the great European capitals, the world of fashion was still content to reassemble every winter in the shabby red and gold boxes of the sociable old Academy. Conservatives cherished it for being small and inconvenient, and thus keeping out the "new people" whom New York was beginning to dread and yet be drawn to; and the sentimental clung to it for its historic associations, and the musical for its excellent acoustics, always so problematic a quality in halls built for the hearing of music.

parts.q:
Which choice best describes the function of the final sentence in the text as a whole?
(A) It suggests that the new opera house mentioned in the previous sentence is unlikely ever to be built.
(B) It accounts for the attachment described in the previous sentence by listing the differing reasons of different groups.
(C) It shifts attention away from the building and toward the performance of Faust mentioned in the first sentence.
(D) It reveals the narrator's own preference for the old Academy over the proposed new opera house.
parts.a: (B). The previous sentence says fashionable New York was "still content" to gather in the "shabby" old Academy despite talk of a grander house. The final sentence explains that contentment group by group: conservatives valued the Academy for keeping out "new people," the sentimental for its history, and the musical for its acoustics. (A) is wrong: the sentence makes no prediction about the new opera house. (C) is wrong: the sentence stays with the building and its patrons; Faust is not mentioned again. (D) is wrong: the reasons are attributed to "Conservatives," "the sentimental," and "the musical," not to the narrator, whose aside about acoustics being "problematic" in concert halls is a general, ironic observation rather than a statement of preference.
parts.n: Type: Text structure (function of a sentence in fiction). Rule or move: Ask whose views a sentence reports; a narrator who lists what different groups believe is explaining a situation, not voicing an opinion. Trap: (D), which mistakes the narrator's ironic report of other people's reasons for the narrator's own preference.

mc.stem: Music historians have often described the rise of the solo piano recital in the nineteenth century as the triumph of a new ideal: the performer as a faithful interpreter of a composer's finished work. Musicologist Hana Sato examined more than 1,200 printed recital programs from London, Paris, and Vienna. Until the 1870s, she found, most so-called solo recitals also featured songs or chamber pieces performed by other musicians, and nearly half ended with the pianist improvising on themes suggested by the audience. The program of composed works performed by a single pianist, Sato concludes, became standard decades later than the usual account implies.

parts.q:
Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
(A) It describes a traditional account, presents evidence that the account misidentifies what nineteenth-century recitals celebrated, and proposes an alternative ideal.
(B) It describes a traditional account, presents evidence that supports it, and extends the account to cities that it had previously overlooked.
(C) It describes a traditional account, presents evidence bearing on its chronology, and concludes that a development it describes came later than it implies.
(D) It describes a scholarly debate, presents evidence on both sides, and concludes that the debate cannot yet be resolved.
parts.a: (C). The text opens with the usual account (the solo recital as the triumph of the faithful-interpreter ideal), then gives Sato's evidence from the programs (mixed performers and improvisation lasting until the 1870s), and closes with her conclusion, which is about timing: the all-solo program of composed works "became standard decades later" than the account implies. (A) is wrong: Sato's evidence might seem to challenge the ideal, but her conclusion concerns when the program became standard, and she proposes no alternative ideal. (B) is wrong: the evidence complicates the account rather than supporting it, and the three cities are simply her sample. (D) is wrong: there is one account, not two sides of a debate, and Sato reaches a definite conclusion.
parts.n: Type: Text structure (overall structure). Rule or move: Pin the conclusion down exactly before matching a structure choice: here it is a claim about timing, so any choice that has the text replacing the ideal itself overreaches. Trap: (A), which follows the evidence (songs, improvisation) to a conclusion the author never draws.

mc.stem:
Text 1
Some art historians argue that Johannes Vermeer (1632–1675) painted with the help of a camera obscura, a darkened box or room in which a lens projects an image of a scene onto a flat surface. Art historian Rolf Brink points to the glinting, slightly blurred highlights in Vermeer's pictures, on crusts of bread, metal jugs, and pearls, which resemble the soft disks of light an unfocused lens produces. For Brink, these highlights are the fingerprints of an optical device used in making the paintings.

Text 2
Art historian Maria Voorn grants that Vermeer's highlights look much like the blur a lens produces. But a resemblance, she argues, shows only that Vermeer knew what such images look like. A painter who had merely looked into a camera obscura, or at reflections in a curved mirror, could have learned the effect and then reproduced it freehand, choosing where to place each highlight for the sake of the composition. The highlights, in other words, may just as well be the fingerprints of an observant eye.

parts.q:
Based on the texts, how would Voorn (Text 2) most likely respond to Brink's conclusion about the highlights in Vermeer's paintings?
(A) She would argue that the highlights Brink describes do not in fact resemble the effects that a lens produces.
(B) She would accept his conclusion but argue that Vermeer used a curved mirror rather than a camera obscura.
(C) She would argue that Vermeer's familiarity with optical effects proves that he never used a camera obscura.
(D) She would argue that the highlights can be explained without supposing that an optical device was used in painting.
parts.a: (D). Brink concludes that the highlights are "fingerprints of an optical device used in making the paintings." Voorn's reply is that the resemblance is equally well explained by a painter who had seen such effects and then painted them freehand; the highlights may be "the fingerprints of an observant eye." She therefore holds that the evidence does not require a device to have been used in painting. (A) is wrong: Voorn "grants" the resemblance. (B) is wrong: she mentions a curved mirror only as one place a painter might have seen the effect, not as a tool Vermeer painted with, and she does not accept Brink's conclusion. (C) is wrong: she says the evidence does not prove use of the device; she does not claim it proves the opposite.
parts.n: Type: Cross-text connections (response to a claim). Rule or move: Distinguish "the evidence does not establish X" from "the evidence establishes not-X"; most Text 2 critics make the first, weaker claim. Trap: (C), which turns Voorn's alternative explanation into a proof that the device was never used.

mc.stem:
Text 1
In a widely publicized 1993 study, college students who listened to ten minutes of a Mozart sonata before taking a test of spatial reasoning outscored students who had first sat in silence or listened to relaxation instructions. The improvement faded within about fifteen minutes, but the "Mozart effect," as it came to be called, inspired a popular belief that listening to classical music makes people smarter.

Text 2
Later experiments complicated the picture. Listening to Mozart before a spatial test did raise scores in several studies, but so did listening to an upbeat piece by another composer and, for listeners who enjoyed it, hearing a story read aloud. A slow, somber piece of classical music produced no benefit, and when researchers measured listeners' mood and alertness, differences in those measures accounted for the differences in test scores.

parts.q:
Based on the texts, how would the researchers who conducted the experiments described in Text 2 most likely explain the result of the 1993 study described in Text 1?
(A) The students who heard the sonata probably began the test in a more positive and alert state than the other students.
(B) Mozart's music probably has structural features that resemble the mental operations used in spatial reasoning tasks.
(C) The result was probably a statistical accident, since later experiments found no rise in scores after listeners heard Mozart.
(D) The students who sat in silence were probably distracted by the unfamiliar setting in which the test was given to them.
parts.a: (A). Text 2 reports that the benefit appeared with any enjoyable, energizing input and that mood and alertness "accounted for the differences in test scores." Applied to the 1993 study, that points to the sonata leaving students more positive and alert than silence or relaxation instructions did. (B) is wrong: Text 2's findings (a story helped; a somber classical piece did not) argue against anything special in Mozart's musical structure. (C) is wrong: Text 2 says listening to Mozart "did raise scores in several studies," so the original result was reproduced, not an accident. (D) is wrong: nothing in either text concerns distraction or the testing environment; the explanation Text 2 supports concerns the listeners' state, not a flaw in the silent condition.
parts.n: Type: Cross-text connections (applying one text's explanation to the other's finding). Rule or move: Take Text 2's mechanism (here mood and alertness) and apply it to the conditions in Text 1: silence and relaxation instructions are exactly the low-arousal conditions. Trap: (C), which confuses "the effect is not about Mozart" with "the effect did not occur."

mc.stem:
Text 1
When one company changed its retirement plan so that new employees were enrolled automatically unless they chose to opt out, participation among new hires jumped from under half to nearly nine in ten. Economist Theo Marsh sees in such results a strong case for deliberate "choice architecture." Because people tend to stick with whatever option is presented as the default, he argues, carefully chosen defaults can steer people toward decisions that serve their own long-term interests, without taking away anyone's freedom to choose otherwise.

Text 2
Economist Rosa Iqbal points to a less celebrated feature of such results. Most automatically enrolled workers also stayed at the plan's default contribution rate, which was low, lower in many cases than the rate that workers who had enrolled on their own tended to choose. For Iqbal, the same inertia that makes a default effective also makes it risky: a default serves people well only if whoever sets it chooses well.

parts.q:
Based on the texts, how would Iqbal (Text 2) most likely respond to Marsh's claim that carefully chosen defaults can steer people toward decisions that serve their long-term interests?
(A) She would reject the claim, arguing that automatic enrollment reduces the share of workers who save for retirement.
(B) She would dismiss the claim on the grounds that defaults restrict employees' freedom to choose for themselves.
(C) She would accept it in principle but warn that the inertia it relies on can also hold people to a poorly chosen default.
(D) She would accept the claim but argue that defaults influence only newly hired employees, whose habits are not yet formed.
parts.a: (C). Marsh's claim is conditional ("carefully chosen defaults"), and Iqbal's conclusion shares that condition: a default "serves people well only if whoever sets it chooses well." She does not deny that defaults work; her point is that the same inertia that makes people accept a good default makes them accept a bad one, as the workers stuck at a low contribution rate did. (A) is wrong: participation rose; Iqbal's concern is the contribution rate, not the number of savers. (B) is wrong: freedom to choose is Marsh's topic, and Iqbal never raises it. (D) is wrong: both texts discuss new hires because that is where the plan changed, but Iqbal never claims that defaults affect only them.
parts.n: Type: Cross-text connections (agreement with a qualification). Rule or move: When Text 2's conclusion contains the same condition as Text 1's claim, the relationship is usually "accepts, but stresses a risk," not rejection. Trap: (A), which assumes a "less celebrated feature" must undercut the headline result.

mc.stem:
Text 1
Translators of poetry face a familiar dilemma: preserve the literal sense of each line, or recreate the poem's rhyme and meter in the new language. Translator Nadia Ferrante argues for the second course. A poem's music, she contends, is not decoration laid over its meaning but part of what the poem means; a literal version that abandons the music preserves the words while losing the poem.

Text 2
Scholar Owen Pryce is wary of translations that reproduce a poem's rhyme scheme. Because rhymes seldom fall on the same words in two languages, a translator who insists on them must pick words for their sound, and the substitutions accumulate: images appear that the original never contained, and others vanish. Pryce does not deny that sound matters in poetry. But he holds that a translator's first duty is to the images and statements the poet actually wrote, and that readers who want the music should read the original alongside the translation.

parts.q:
Based on the texts, how would Pryce (Text 2) most likely respond to Ferrante's claim that a literal translation "preserves the words while losing the poem"?
(A) He would argue that a poem's sound is irrelevant to its meaning and should be ignored by translators.
(B) He would grant that sound matters in poetry but argue that forcing rhymes distorts what the poem actually says.
(C) He would agree that literal translations fail and recommend that translators abandon both rhyme and literal sense.
(D) He would argue that literal translations in fact preserve more of a poem's music than Ferrante assumes.
parts.a: (B). Pryce concedes Ferrante's premise in part ("does not deny that sound matters") but argues that the price of reproducing rhyme is too high: words chosen for sound add images the poet never wrote and drop others. He therefore answers her charge against literal translation by pointing to what rhymed translation loses, and he supplies the music by another route (reading the original alongside). (A) is wrong: he explicitly does not deny that sound matters. (C) is wrong: he defends literal fidelity ("first duty is to the images and statements the poet actually wrote"); he does not agree that literal translations fail. (D) is wrong: he never claims literal translations keep the music; he sends readers to the original for it.
parts.n: Type: Cross-text connections (response to a claim). Rule or move: Look for Text 2's concession ("does not deny") and its counterweight ("but"); the right answer usually contains both halves. Trap: (A), which ignores the concession and makes Pryce more extreme than he is.

mc.stem:
Text 1
In his essay "Ornament and Crime," the Austrian architect Adolf Loos (1870–1933) condemned applied ornament as a waste of labor, money, and material, a habit that modern society had outgrown. His argument helped inspire the plain, unornamented surfaces that came to dominate much twentieth-century architecture.

Text 2
Environmental psychologist Lena Okoro has studied how pedestrians respond to building facades. In her observations, people walking past long, blank facades walked faster, looked around less, and later recalled less about the street than did people walking past facades broken up by windows, doors, and decorative detail. Okoro argues that such detail gives the eye places to rest and the mind landmarks to remember, functions that a purely economic accounting of a building's cost tends to overlook.

parts.q:
Based on the texts, how would Okoro (Text 2) most likely respond to Loos's view of ornament?
(A) She would agree that ornament serves no practical purpose but argue that its beauty justifies its cost.
(B) She would argue that the labor and material that ornament requires are less costly than Loos claimed.
(C) She would argue that ornament is justified only when it helps people find their way inside a building.
(D) She would argue that the view overlooks effects that detail has on people passing a building, which a tally of costs misses.
parts.a: (D). Loos judges ornament by its cost in labor, money and material. Okoro reports effects of detail on pedestrians (they slow down, look around and remember more) and says these functions are what "a purely economic accounting of a building's cost tends to overlook." She would say Loos's accounting leaves out those effects. (A) is wrong: Okoro describes practical, psychological functions of detail, so she would not grant that it serves no purpose, and she never argues from beauty. (B) is wrong: she does not dispute the costs; she says the accounting omits benefits. (C) is wrong: her evidence concerns pedestrians on the street, and "landmarks to remember" refers to the street, not to finding one's way inside a building.
parts.n: Type: Cross-text connections (response to a view). Rule or move: Identify the measure each text uses (Loos: cost; Okoro: effects on people) and choose the answer that says one measure leaves out what the other counts. Trap: (A), which assumes any defense of ornament must be an aesthetic one.

mc.stem:
Text 1
Russian has two basic color words for what English speakers call blue: "goluboy" for lighter blues and "siniy" for darker ones. In experiments, Russian speakers told two shades of blue apart faster when the shades fell on opposite sides of this boundary than when they fell on the same side; English speakers showed no such advantage. Linguist Irina Volkova takes such results as evidence that the language a person speaks shapes how that person perceives color.

Text 2
Psychologist Marcus Hale notes that in experiments of this kind, the Russian speakers' advantage disappeared when they were asked to silently rehearse a string of digits while comparing the colors, a task that ties up the mental resources used for words. A nonverbal task of similar difficulty did not erase the advantage. For Hale, the pattern indicates that the Russian speakers were drawing on their color words at the moment of each comparison.

parts.q:
Based on the texts, how would Hale (Text 2) most likely respond to Volkova's interpretation of the results described in Text 1?
(A) He would argue that the results reflect the speakers' use of color words during the task, not a lasting change in perception.
(B) He would argue that the results show that the language people speak has no influence of any kind on how they judge colors.
(C) He would accept her interpretation and add that the effect grows stronger when speakers' verbal memory is occupied by another task.
(D) He would argue that the gap between the groups reflects a general advantage in verbal memory rather than any effect of color words.
parts.a: (A). Volkova reads the results as language shaping perception itself. Hale's evidence is that the advantage vanishes when verbal resources are tied up but survives an equally hard nonverbal task, so it depends on words being used during the comparison; he concludes that the speakers were "drawing on their color words at the moment of each comparison." That is an influence of language on the judgment as it is made, not evidence of a lasting change in how colors look. (B) is wrong: Hale's own explanation is an effect of language (color words in use), just a different kind than Volkova claims. (C) is wrong: the advantage disappeared when verbal memory was occupied. (D) is wrong: the advantage appeared only across the goluboy/siniy boundary, which ties it to color words, not to a general memory difference, and Hale attributes it to color words.
parts.n: Type: Cross-text connections (competing interpretations of one result). Rule or move: When Text 2 narrows how an effect works, the answer is usually "a different mechanism," not "no effect at all." Trap: (B), which turns "not a change in perception" into "no influence of language whatsoever."

mc.stem: For much of the nineteenth century, many geologists explained the huge boulders scattered across northern Europe, often far from any bedrock of the same kind, as debris swept there by an ancient flood or dropped by icebergs drifting across a sea that once covered the land. In 1837, naturalist Louis Agassiz rejected both explanations. The boulders, he argued, had not been carried by water at all. ______ they had been pushed and dragged there by vast sheets of ice that once covered much of the continent.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
(A) Moreover,
(B) Instead,
(C) Thus,
(D) Similarly,
parts.a: (B). The sentence before the blank denies one account ("had not been carried by water at all"), and the sentence after supplies the account Agassiz put in its place (sheets of ice). "Instead" signals exactly that: an alternative replacing what was just ruled out. (A) "Moreover" would add a second, independent claim of the same kind, but the ice sentence does not add to the denial; it replaces the rejected explanation. (C) "Thus" would present the ice as a conclusion drawn from the denial, but ruling out water does not by itself establish ice; the two claims are alternatives, not premise and conclusion. (D) "Similarly" would mean the ice claim resembles the water claim, when it is its opposite.
parts.n: Type: Transitions (replacement). Rule or move: after a sentence that says what something is not, look for instead or rather to introduce what it is. Trap: (C), because Agassiz's argument feels like a chain of reasoning and "Thus" sounds like its conclusion.

mc.stem: When the Hubble Space Telescope began returning images after its launch in 1990, astronomers were dismayed to find them blurry: the telescope's 2.4-meter primary mirror had been ground to a slightly wrong shape. Replacing the mirror in orbit was impossible. ______ the flaw could be corrected. In 1993, astronauts installed new instruments whose optics were designed to cancel out the mirror's error, and Hubble's images became as sharp as originally intended.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
(A) Still,
(B) Therefore,
(C) Likewise,
(D) Indeed,
parts.a: (A). The sentence before the blank states a limitation (the mirror could not be replaced), and the sentence after says that the problem could be fixed anyway. "Still" signals a point that holds true despite what was just said. (B) "Therefore" would claim that the flaw could be corrected because the mirror could not be replaced, which reverses the logic. (C) "Likewise" would mean the second statement resembles the first, but one is a limitation and the other overcomes it. (D) "Indeed" would reinforce the impossibility just described, yet the next sentence moves the other way.
parts.n: Type: Transitions (concession). Rule or move: when a sentence admits an obstacle and the next one says the goal was reached anyway, the link is still, even so or nevertheless. Trap: (B), because the fix does follow from the flaw in the story, so a cause-and-effect word looks tempting.

mc.stem: Many animals that colonize islands evolve to be much larger or much smaller than their relatives on the mainland, a pattern biologists call the island rule. The extinct dwarf elephants of Sicily and Malta, some barely a meter tall at the shoulder, are a classic example. ______ a survey of fossil elephants from islands around the world by paleontologist Hana Sato and colleagues found that dwarfing happened again and again, independently, on islands from the Mediterranean to Indonesia.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
(A) However,
(B) Instead,
(C) Meanwhile,
(D) Indeed,
parts.a: (D). The first two sentences state the island rule and give one example of it; the sentence after the blank reports a survey showing that the same dwarfing happened repeatedly and independently. That finding reinforces and broadens the rule, which is what "Indeed" signals. (A) "However" would mean the survey challenged the rule or the example, but it supports both. (B) "Instead" would mean the survey offered an alternative to what came before, but it extends it. (C) "Meanwhile" would introduce something happening at the same time elsewhere, but the survey is further evidence for the same point, not a parallel event.
parts.n: Type: Transitions (reinforcement). Rule or move: read what the new study actually found before choosing a contrast word; a study that confirms the previous claim takes indeed or in fact. Trap: (A), because passages so often introduce a new study to overturn an old idea that "However" is the reflex choice.

mc.stem: To test how predators shape lake ecosystems, ecologist Dana Pruitt and colleagues removed most of the bass from one small lake in northern Wisconsin while leaving a neighboring lake untouched. With fewer bass to eat them, minnows multiplied and consumed far more of the tiny animals called zooplankton, which graze on algae. The zooplankton, ______ could no longer keep the algae in check, and by late summer the water in the experimental lake had turned visibly green.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
(A) for example,
(B) nonetheless,
(C) in turn,
(D) in other words,
