parts.a: (C). The passage traces a chain of effects: fewer bass led to more minnows, more minnows led to fewer zooplankton, and fewer zooplankton led to more algae. The sentence with the blank describes the next link, the zooplankton's reduced grazing, which was caused by the previous link and in turn caused the green water. "In turn" marks exactly this kind of step in a sequence. (A) "for example" would make the zooplankton's failure an instance of the minnows' increase, which it is not. (B) "nonetheless" would mean the zooplankton failed despite what came before, when they failed because of it. (D) "in other words" would present the sentence as a restatement, but it adds a new effect rather than rephrasing the minnows' feeding.
parts.n: Type: Transitions (causal sequence). Rule or move: in a chain of cause and effect, "in turn" introduces the link that is caused by the previous one and passes the effect along. Trap: (D), because a reader who sees the zooplankton decline as the same fact as the minnows eating them thinks the sentence restates it.

mc.stem: Botanists sort many flowering plants into groups according to how the length of the night affects their blooming. Spinach, for instance, is a so-called long-day plant: it flowers only when nights fall below a critical length, which is why it tends to bolt, or go to seed, in early summer. ______ chrysanthemums, a short-day plant, flower only once nights exceed a critical length, which is why they bloom in autumn.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
(A) Similarly,
(B) Consequently,
(C) Conversely,
(D) Specifically,
parts.a: (C). Spinach flowers only when nights are shorter than a critical length; chrysanthemums flower only when nights are longer than one. The second case reverses the first, and "Conversely" signals exactly that kind of mirror-image relationship. (A) "Similarly" is the trap: both plants do respond to the night, but the passage is sorting plants into groups, and the sentence's point is that chrysanthemums fall in the opposite group, with the opposite requirement ("short-day" versus "long-day," "exceed" versus "fall below"), and "Similarly" would hide it. (B) "Consequently" would mean chrysanthemums behave as they do because of spinach's behavior. (D) "Specifically" would introduce a detail of the spinach sentence, but the chrysanthemum sentence is a new case.
parts.n: Type: Transitions (contrast of mirror-image cases). Rule or move: name the relationship between the two sentences' main claims, not their shared topic; a reversed condition calls for conversely or by contrast. Trap: (A), because the two plants share a mechanism and "Similarly" fits the topic while contradicting the claim.

mc.stem: Seismologists have long known that the ground can shake very differently in different parts of the same city during a single earthquake. The 1985 earthquake that struck Mexico City is a stark illustration. Its epicenter lay some 350 kilometers away, off the Pacific coast, yet the most severe damage was concentrated in one part of the city. ______ it was concentrated where buildings stood on the soft clay of an ancient lakebed, which amplified the shaking, while buildings on firmer ground nearby suffered far less.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
(A) Specifically,
(B) Nevertheless,
(C) Previously,
(D) As a result,
parts.a: (A). The sentence before the blank says the damage was concentrated in "one part of the city" without saying which part; the sentence after the blank identifies that part precisely (the soft clay of an old lakebed). "Specifically" introduces this more exact version of the same claim. (B) "Nevertheless" would signal something true despite the previous point, but the lakebed detail explains that point rather than resisting it. (C) "Previously" would place the lakebed damage earlier in time than the concentration of damage, but they are the same event. (D) "As a result" would make the lakebed damage a consequence of the damage being concentrated, which is circular.
parts.n: Type: Transitions (specification). Rule or move: when a sentence names something vaguely ("one part," "a factor") and the next pins it down, the link is specifically or in particular. Trap: (D), because the lakebed clay does cause the damage, and the causal language inside the sentence pulls toward a causal transition.

mc.stem: Radiocarbon dating has transformed archaeology. By measuring how much of the unstable isotope carbon-14 remains in bone, charcoal, seeds, or other once-living material, researchers can estimate when an organism died, as far back as about 50,000 years. ______ the method cannot date a stone tool or the clay of a potsherd directly, since neither stone nor clay was ever alive to take in carbon-14; archaeologists instead date organic material found with the objects, such as charcoal from the same layer, and infer that the objects are about as old.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
(A) Accordingly,
(B) Indeed,
(C) For instance,
(D) That said,
parts.a: (D). The first two sentences praise the method; the sentence after the blank concedes a limit on it. "That said" marks a qualification of what came before without taking it back. (A) "Accordingly" would make the limitation a consequence of the method's success. (B) "Indeed" would intensify the praise, but the sentence restricts it. (C) "For instance" would make the stone tool an example of the organic materials the method can date, which is the reverse of the point.
parts.n: Type: Transitions (qualification). Rule or move: when a sentence limits a claim the passage has just praised, use that said, even so or still, not a word that continues the praise. Trap: (C), because the sentence names specific objects (a stone tool, a potsherd), and specifics feel like examples.

mc.stem: In the early 1960s, geologist Harry Hess proposed that new ocean floor forms at mid-ocean ridges and spreads outward from them. If he was right, the seafloor should be youngest at the ridges and grow older with distance from them. Samples drilled from the floor of the South Atlantic in 1968 bore this out. The sediment covering the seafloor was thin near the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and thicker farther away, as expected if sediment had had longer to pile up there. ______ fossils in the lowest layer of sediment, which date the rock just beneath it, were progressively older with distance from the ridge.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
(A) Instead,
(B) Likewise,
(C) Nonetheless,
(D) In short,
parts.a: (B). The passage gives two findings from the same drilling, and both point the same way: sediment thickness increases with distance from the ridge, and so does the age of the oldest fossils. "Likewise" signals that the second finding parallels the first. (A) "Instead" would mean the fossil evidence replaced the sediment evidence or contradicted it. (C) "Nonetheless" would mean the fossils supported Hess despite the sediment evidence, but the sediment evidence also supported him. (D) "In short" would introduce a summary, but the fossil finding is new evidence, not a restatement of the sediment finding.
parts.n: Type: Transitions (parallel evidence). Rule or move: when two findings support the same conclusion in the same way, link them with likewise, similarly or moreover. Trap: (D), because the fossil sentence sounds like a conclusion to the paragraph and "In short" sounds like a wrap-up.

mc.stem: In 1854, physician John Snow mapped the deaths in a cholera outbreak in London's Soho district and traced many of them to a single public water pump on Broad Street; after the pump's handle was removed, the outbreak, already waning, soon ended. ______ most physicians believed that cholera spread through miasma, a poisonous vapor thought to rise from filth and decay, and Snow's argument that the disease spread through contaminated water won few converts for years.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
(A) At the time,
(B) Consequently,
(C) Similarly,
(D) In other words,
parts.a: (A). The sentence after the blank describes what physicians believed while Snow was doing his work, and it sets that belief against his conclusion ("won few converts for years"). "At the time" places the belief in the same period and prepares for that contrast. (B) "Consequently" would make the physicians' belief in miasma a result of Snow's map, when it existed before the map and resisted it. (C) "Similarly" would mean the physicians' view resembled Snow's, but it opposed his. (D) "In other words" would present the miasma belief as a rephrasing of Snow's finding, which it contradicts.
parts.n: Type: Transitions (time and setting). Rule or move: when the next sentence describes the background or prevailing view during the events just narrated, use at the time or then, not a word of cause or likeness. Trap: (B), because Snow's work and the physicians' reaction are connected, and the connection feels causal.

mc.stem: Some astronomers argue that the search for life beyond Earth should focus on Mars rather than on the icy moons of the outer solar system. ______ Mars is far closer and easier to reach, and rovers have been studying its surface for decades. But Jupiter's moon Europa and Saturn's moon Enceladus appear to hold something Mars is not known to have: an ocean of liquid water that extends around each moon beneath its icy shell.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
(A) Therefore,
(B) Instead,
(C) Otherwise,
(D) Granted,
parts.a: (D). The first sentence reports a view the writer goes on to resist ("But Europa and Enceladus..."). The sentence with the blank acknowledges the strength of that view, Mars's nearness and the decades of rover work, before the writer turns against it. "Granted" signals exactly this kind of concession. (A) "Therefore" would present Mars's nearness as a conclusion drawn from the astronomers' argument, when it is a reason for it. (B) "Instead" would introduce an alternative to focusing on Mars, but the sentence supports that focus. (C) "Otherwise" would describe what happens if the first sentence's condition fails, and there is no condition.
parts.n: Type: Transitions (concession before a counterargument). Rule or move: when a sentence grants a point to the other side and a "But" follows, the blank is granted, admittedly or to be sure. Trap: (A), because the sentence gives reasons connected to the argument, and "Therefore" is the reflex word for reasons.

mc.stem:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Astronomers have several ways to detect planets orbiting other stars.
• The transit method watches for a small, regular dip in a star's brightness as a planet passes in front of it.
• The depth of the dip reveals the planet's diameter.
• The radial velocity method measures a star's slight back-and-forth motion caused by an orbiting planet's gravitational tug.
• The size of that motion reveals how massive the planet is.
• Knowing both a planet's diameter and its mass lets astronomers calculate its density and infer whether it is made mostly of rock or mostly of gas.

parts.q:
The student wants to explain why astronomers find it valuable to detect the same planet with both methods. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
(A) The transit method detects a dip in a star's brightness as a planet passes in front of it, while the radial velocity method detects the star's slight back-and-forth motion.
(B) Because the transit method reveals a planet's diameter and the radial velocity method its mass, a planet detected both ways can have its density calculated, showing whether it is mostly rock or gas.
(C) Astronomers can calculate a planet's density and use it to infer whether the planet is made mostly of rock or mostly of gas.
(D) Astronomers have several ways to detect planets orbiting other stars, among them the transit method, which reveals a planet's diameter, and the radial velocity method, which reveals its mass.
parts.a: (B). The goal is a reason for using both methods on one planet. (B) gives it: each method supplies one of the two quantities (diameter from the transit, mass from the radial velocity), and only together do they yield density and so the planet's makeup. (A) describes what each method detects but never says what either reveals or why combining them helps. (C) states the payoff, density and composition, but never connects it to the two methods, so it does not explain why both are needed. (D) comes closest: it pairs each method with what it reveals, but it stops there and never says what knowing both allows, so the value of detecting a planet both ways is left unstated.
parts.n: Type: Rhetorical synthesis (explain a reason). Rule or move: when the goal asks why, the right choice has a because-link that joins the relevant facts to the payoff; facts without the link, or the payoff without the facts, fail. Trap: (D), which lays out the two methods and what each reveals, so the student supplies the missing conclusion without noticing the sentence never states it.

mc.stem:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Hatshepsut ruled ancient Egypt as pharaoh from about 1479 to 1458 BCE.
• She was one of the few women to hold the title of pharaoh.
• She sent a trading expedition to the land of Punt that returned with myrrh trees, ebony, and gold.
• Carved scenes of the expedition still decorate her mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari, near modern Luxor.
• Late in the reign of her successor, Thutmose III, many of her statues were smashed, and her name and images were chiseled from monuments.

parts.q:
The student wants to emphasize that evidence of Hatshepsut's reign survived despite efforts to erase it. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
(A) Hatshepsut, one of the few women to hold the title of pharaoh, ruled ancient Egypt from about 1479 to 1458 BCE.
(B) Late in the reign of Thutmose III, Hatshepsut's successor, many of her statues were smashed, and her name and images were chiseled from monuments.
(C) Though many of Hatshepsut's images were chiseled from monuments late in her successor's reign, carved scenes of her expedition to Punt still decorate her temple at Deir el-Bahari.
(D) Hatshepsut's expedition to Punt returned with myrrh trees, ebony, and gold, a cargo still depicted in carved scenes on her mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari, near modern Luxor.
parts.a: (C). The goal has two parts: something survived, and it survived efforts to erase it. (C) states both and ties them with "Though": the images were chiseled away, yet the carved scenes of the Punt expedition remain. (A) introduces Hatshepsut but mentions neither erasure nor survival. (B) describes only the erasure, so it emphasizes the attempt rather than what outlasted it. (D) shows that the carvings survive ("still depicted") but says nothing about anyone trying to destroy them, so the "despite" half of the goal is missing.
parts.n: Type: Rhetorical synthesis (a two-part goal). Rule or move: split the goal into its parts (here, survival and the attempt to erase) and reject any choice that delivers only one. Trap: (D), which has the word "still" and the surviving carvings, so it seems to answer the goal while dropping the "despite."

mc.stem:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• On May 29, 1919, a total solar eclipse was visible from parts of South America and Africa.
• British astronomers observed it from two sites: Sobral, Brazil, and the island of Príncipe, off the west coast of Africa.
• They photographed stars that appeared near the darkened Sun in order to test a prediction of Albert Einstein's general theory of relativity.
• The theory predicted that the Sun's gravity would bend light from such stars by about 1.75 arcseconds, twice the amount predicted by Newtonian physics.
• The measurements, announced in November 1919, supported Einstein's prediction and made him world-famous.

parts.q:
The student wants to emphasize the purpose of the astronomers' observations. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
(A) Measurements from the 1919 eclipse, announced that November, supported Einstein's general theory of relativity and made him world-famous.
(B) British astronomers observed the total solar eclipse of May 29, 1919, from two sites: Sobral, Brazil, and the island of Príncipe, off the west coast of Africa.
(C) During the 1919 eclipse, British astronomers photographed stars near the darkened Sun to test Einstein's prediction that the Sun's gravity would bend their light.
(D) Einstein's general theory of relativity predicted that the Sun's gravity would bend starlight by about 1.75 arcseconds, twice the amount Newtonian physics predicted.
parts.a: (C). A purpose is what the observers set out to do, and the notes give it: the stars were photographed "in order to test a prediction" of Einstein's theory. (C) states that purpose with an infinitive ("to test Einstein's prediction") and says what the prediction was. (A) reports the outcome, what the measurements showed, not what the astronomers were trying to find out. (B) gives the date and places of the observations but no reason for them. (D) states the prediction itself, without saying that anyone set out to check it, so the astronomers' purpose never appears.
parts.n: Type: Rhetorical synthesis (purpose). Rule or move: purpose is signalled by to + verb, in order to, or aimed to; a result, a method, or the background idea is not a purpose. Trap: (A), because the result reveals what was being tested, and students read the purpose into it.

mc.stem:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Monarch butterflies in eastern North America breed across the United States and southern Canada in spring and summer.
• Several generations are born each summer, and adults of these generations typically live two to six weeks.
• The generation that emerges in late summer does not breed right away.
• Instead, its members fly as far as 4,800 kilometers to forests in central Mexico, where they spend the winter.
• Adults of the late-summer generation can live up to eight months.

parts.q:
The student wants to emphasize how the life span of the late-summer generation differs from that of earlier generations. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
(A) While adult monarchs from the early summer generations typically live two to six weeks, those from the late-summer generation can live up to eight months.
(B) Unlike earlier generations, whose adults breed during the summer, the late-summer generation of monarchs flies as far as 4,800 kilometers to spend the winter in central Mexico.
(C) Adults of the late-summer generation of monarchs, which fly as far as 4,800 kilometers to spend the winter in central Mexico, can live up to eight months.
(D) Monarch butterflies of eastern North America breed across the United States and southern Canada, producing several generations each summer.
parts.a: (A). The goal asks for a difference in life span, which needs both life spans set against each other. (A) gives both (two to six weeks versus up to eight months) and marks the contrast with "While." (B) states a real difference, but in behavior (breeding versus migrating), not in life span. (C) gives only the late-summer generation's life span, with nothing to compare it to. (D) describes the breeding range and the number of generations and mentions no life span at all.
parts.n: Type: Rhetorical synthesis (a comparison on a named dimension). Rule or move: when the goal names what the difference is in (life span, size, cost), the right choice states both sides on that dimension; a difference in something else fails. Trap: (B), which opens with "Unlike earlier generations" and sounds like the comparison the goal wants.

mc.stem:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Shield volcanoes, such as Mauna Loa in Hawaii, are built mostly from basaltic lava.
• Basaltic lava is low in silica and runny, so gas bubbles escape from it readily.
• Shield volcano eruptions therefore tend to be gentle, with lava pouring out in streams.
• Stratovolcanoes, such as Mount St. Helens in Washington State, are built from layers of ash and thick, silica-rich lava.
• Thick lava traps gas bubbles until pressure builds, so stratovolcano eruptions are often explosive.

parts.q:
The student wants to explain why stratovolcano eruptions are often more explosive than shield volcano eruptions. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
(A) Stratovolcanoes, such as Mount St. Helens in Washington State, are built from layers of ash and thick, silica-rich lava, and their eruptions are often explosive.
(B) Shield volcanoes, such as Mauna Loa in Hawaii, are built mostly from basaltic lava, and their eruptions tend to be gentle, with lava pouring out in streams.
(C) Mauna Loa, a shield volcano in Hawaii, and Mount St. Helens, a stratovolcano in Washington State, differ in how explosively they tend to erupt.
(D) Gas escapes readily from the runny basaltic lava of shield volcanoes, but the thick, silica-rich lava of stratovolcanoes traps gas until pressure builds, often causing explosive eruptions.
parts.a: (D). The goal asks why one type is more explosive than the other, so the answer needs the mechanism for both: gas escapes from runny lava but is trapped by thick lava until pressure builds. (D) states that contrast and its result. (A) pairs thick lava with explosive eruptions using only "and," so it describes the stratovolcano without explaining the explosiveness or comparing it with shield volcanoes. (B) describes shield volcanoes alone. (C) states that the two volcanoes differ in explosiveness but gives no reason.
parts.n: Type: Rhetorical synthesis (explain a comparison). Rule or move: a "why is X more ... than Y" goal needs the cause, and the cause must cover both X and Y. Trap: (A), because it names thick, silica-rich lava and explosive eruptions in one sentence, and the reader supplies the causal link that "and" does not state.

mc.stem:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The first transcontinental railroad in the United States was completed on May 10, 1869, at Promontory Summit in Utah Territory.
• The Central Pacific Railroad built eastward from Sacramento, California; the Union Pacific built westward from the Missouri River.
• By the late 1860s, the great majority of the Central Pacific's workers were immigrants from China.
• These workers blasted tunnels through the granite of the Sierra Nevada, often in harsh winter conditions.
• No Chinese workers appear in the best-known photograph of the ceremony marking the railroad's completion.

parts.q:
The student wants to emphasize a contrast between the Chinese workers' contribution to the railroad and the way its completion was commemorated. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
(A) Immigrants from China, who made up the great majority of the Central Pacific's workers by the late 1860s, blasted tunnels through the granite of the Sierra Nevada, often in harsh winter conditions.
(B) Although immigrants from China made up the great majority of the Central Pacific's workers, none appear in the best-known photograph of the ceremony marking the railroad's completion.
(C) The first transcontinental railroad was completed on May 10, 1869, at Promontory Summit in Utah Territory, where the Central Pacific and Union Pacific lines met.
(D) The Central Pacific built eastward from Sacramento and the Union Pacific westward from the Missouri River until their lines met at Promontory Summit in 1869.
parts.a: (B). The goal sets two things against each other: what the Chinese workers contributed and how the completion was commemorated. (B) names both (the great majority of the workforce; absent from the best-known photograph) and joins them with "Although," which makes the contrast explicit. (A) gives the fullest account of the workers' contribution but never mentions the commemoration, so there is nothing to contrast it with. (C) gives the date and place of completion and says nothing about the workers. (D) describes the routes of the two companies and also leaves out both halves of the contrast.
parts.n: Type: Rhetorical synthesis (contrast). Rule or move: a contrast goal needs both sides in the same sentence and a word that sets them against each other (although, while, but). Trap: (A), the longest and most vivid choice, which covers the contribution so fully that the missing second half goes unnoticed.

mc.stem:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• The kākāpō is a large, flightless parrot found only in New Zealand.
• Kākāpō breed only in years when rimu trees produce heavy crops of fruit, which happens every two to four years.
• Ecologist Aroha Tane and colleagues compared records of kākāpō breeding from 1990 to 2020 with counts of rimu fruit made in the same years.
• They found that breeding began in years when the number of unripe fruit on the trees in early summer passed a certain threshold.
• The researchers concluded that early-summer fruit counts could help conservationists predict breeding seasons months in advance.

parts.q:
The student wants to present the study's findings to an audience unfamiliar with the kākāpō. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
(A) In Tane's study, kākāpō began breeding in years when the number of unripe rimu fruit in early summer passed a certain threshold, so fruit counts could help predict breeding seasons.
(B) Tane's team compared records of breeding by the kākāpō, a large, flightless parrot found only in New Zealand, with counts of rimu fruit made from 1990 to 2020.
(C) The kākāpō, a large, flightless parrot found only in New Zealand, breeds only in years when rimu trees produce heavy crops of fruit.
(D) Tane's team found that the kākāpō, a large, flightless parrot found only in New Zealand, began breeding once early-summer counts of unripe rimu fruit passed a threshold.
parts.a: (D). The goal has two requirements: present the findings, and do it for readers who do not know what a kākāpō is. (D) reports the finding (breeding began once early-summer counts of unripe rimu fruit passed a threshold) and explains the bird in an appositive. (A) reports the finding and even the researchers' conclusion, but it never says what a kākāpō is, so the unfamiliar audience would be lost. (B) explains the bird but gives only the method (what was compared), not what was found. (C) explains the bird but gives only background that was known before the study, with no finding from it.
parts.n: Type: Rhetorical synthesis (audience). Rule or move: "an audience unfamiliar with X" means the right choice must say what X is; check for that before judging the rest. Trap: (A), which delivers the finding most completely, so the student forgets the audience half of the goal.

mc.stem:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• In 2006, the International Astronomical Union (IAU) adopted a formal definition of a planet in our solar system.
• Under the definition, a planet must orbit the Sun, have enough mass for its own gravity to pull it into a nearly round shape, and have cleared the neighborhood around its orbit of other objects.
• Pluto orbits the Sun and is nearly round.
• Pluto shares its orbital neighborhood with many other objects in the Kuiper belt.
• The IAU classified Pluto as a "dwarf planet."

parts.q:
The student wants to emphasize that Pluto meets some but not all of the IAU's criteria for a planet. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
(A) Pluto orbits the Sun and is massive enough to be pulled into a nearly round shape, but it has not cleared its orbital neighborhood, which it shares with many Kuiper belt objects.
(B) Under the definition the IAU adopted in 2006, Pluto is classified as a dwarf planet because it shares its orbital neighborhood with many other objects in the Kuiper belt.
(C) Under the IAU's 2006 definition, a planet must orbit the Sun, be massive enough to be nearly round, and have cleared the neighborhood around its orbit of other objects.
(D) Pluto orbits the Sun, and its own gravity is strong enough to pull it into a nearly round shape, two of the requirements in the IAU's 2006 definition of a planet.
parts.a: (A). The goal has two halves: the criteria Pluto meets and the one it does not. (A) names both (it orbits the Sun and is nearly round, but it has not cleared its neighborhood) and sets them against each other with "but." (B) explains why Pluto is a dwarf planet, which covers only the failed criterion; the criteria it meets never appear. (C) lists the criteria without applying any of them to Pluto. (D) is the closest trap: it shows Pluto meeting two requirements and hints that there are others, but it never says Pluto fails any, so the "not all" half is missing.
parts.n: Type: Rhetorical synthesis (a both-sides goal). Rule or move: for "some but not all," the right choice names what is met and what is not, usually joined by but or although. Trap: (D), because "two of the requirements" implies a third, and the student fills in the failure the sentence never states.

mc.stem:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Mount Tambora, on the Indonesian island of Sumbawa, erupted in April 1815.
• It was the largest volcanic eruption in recorded history.
• Particles it released into the upper atmosphere blocked some sunlight and lowered average global temperatures; 1816 became known in Europe and North America as "the Year Without a Summer."
• Krakatoa, a volcanic island between the Indonesian islands of Java and Sumatra, erupted in August 1883.
• Its final explosion was heard some 4,800 kilometers away.
• Particles it released into the upper atmosphere lowered average global temperatures the following year.

parts.q:
The student wants to emphasize a similarity in the effects of the two eruptions. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
(A) Tambora and Krakatoa are both volcanoes in Indonesia, and their famous eruptions occurred within seventy years of each other.
(B) Tambora's 1815 eruption was the largest in recorded history, while the final explosion of Krakatoa in 1883 was heard some 4,800 kilometers away.
(C) The eruptions of Tambora in 1815 and Krakatoa in 1883 both sent particles into the upper atmosphere that lowered average global temperatures.
(D) Particles from Tambora's 1815 eruption lowered average global temperatures, and 1816 became known in Europe and North America as "the Year Without a Summer."
parts.a: (C). The goal is a similarity, and specifically one in the eruptions' effects. (C) names the shared effect, particles in the upper atmosphere that lowered average global temperatures, and marks it as shared with "both." (A) states a similarity, but in location and timing, not in effects. (B) sets two different effects side by side with "while," which is a contrast, not a similarity. (D) describes only Tambora's effect, so there is nothing to compare.
parts.n: Type: Rhetorical synthesis (similarity on a named dimension). Rule or move: check both words of the goal: it must be a similarity, and it must be in the named respect (here, effects). Trap: (A), which is a genuine similarity and says "both," but in the wrong respect.

mc.stem:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• In the 1960s, ecologist Robert Paine began removing the predatory sea star Pisaster ochraceus from a stretch of rocky shore in Washington State.
• The sea star eats mussels, among other prey.
• With the sea star gone, mussels spread across the rocks and crowded out many other species, including limpets, chitons, and several kinds of algae.
• The number of species living on that stretch of shore fell sharply.
• In 1969, Paine introduced the term "keystone species" for a species that has an unusually large effect on the makeup of its community.

parts.q:
The student wants to define the term "keystone species" and illustrate it with an example. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
(A) When Robert Paine removed the sea star Pisaster ochraceus from a stretch of Washington shore in the 1960s, mussels spread across the rocks, and the number of species there fell sharply.
(B) Robert Paine's term "keystone species" names a species with an unusually large effect on its community, such as the sea star Pisaster ochraceus, whose removal let mussels crowd out many other species.
(C) In 1969, ecologist Robert Paine introduced the term "keystone species" for a species that has an unusually large effect on the makeup of its community.
(D) The sea star Pisaster ochraceus eats mussels, and without it, mussels spread across the rocks and crowd out limpets, chitons, and several kinds of algae.
parts.a: (B). The goal asks for a definition and an example. (B) defines the term (a species with an unusually large effect on its community) and illustrates it with the sea star, whose removal let mussels crowd out other species. (A) describes the experiment that illustrates the idea but never names or defines the term. (C) defines the term and dates it but gives no example. (D) describes the sea star's effect but, like (A), never mentions the term, so the reader cannot tell what it exemplifies.
parts.n: Type: Rhetorical synthesis (define and illustrate). Rule or move: for a define-and-illustrate goal, look for the term, its meaning, and a concrete case in the same sentence; an example without the term, or the term without an example, fails. Trap: (C), because it holds the definition word for word from the notes, and students stop there.

mc.stem:
The following text is from George Eliot's 1871–72 novel Middlemarch. Dorothea, recently married to Mr. Casaubon, has been found weeping alone during their wedding journey in Rome.

Nor can I suppose that when Mrs. Casaubon is discovered in a fit of weeping six weeks after her wedding, the situation will be regarded as tragic. Some discouragement, some faintness of heart at the new real future which replaces the imaginary, is not unusual, and we do not expect people to be deeply moved by what is not unusual. That element of tragedy which lies in the very fact of frequency, has not yet wrought itself into the coarse emotion of mankind; and perhaps our frames could hardly bear much of it. If we had a keen vision and feeling of all ordinary human life, it would be like hearing the grass grow and the squirrel's heart beat, and we should die of that roar which lies on the other side of silence. As it is, the quickest of us walk about well wadded with stupidity.

parts.q:
Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
(A) Suffering that is common is not truly tragic, because tragedy depends on events that are rare.
(B) People are seldom moved by commonplace suffering, and fully perceiving it might be more than they could bear.
(C) Only the most perceptive people are able to recognize the suffering that is hidden in ordinary lives.
(D) Mrs. Casaubon's distress is unusual and therefore deserves far more sympathy than it is likely to receive from others.
parts.a: (B). The narrator says that people "do not expect ... to be deeply moved by what is not unusual," that the tragedy in frequent things has not yet entered "the coarse emotion of mankind," and that "perhaps our frames could hardly bear much of it": if we truly felt all ordinary life, "we should die of that roar." Both halves of (B) are in the text. (A) is the trap: the narrator says there is an "element of tragedy which lies in the very fact of frequency," so common suffering is tragic; people simply fail to feel it. (C) is wrong: "the quickest of us," the most perceptive, still "walk about well wadded with stupidity." (D) is wrong: the narrator calls Dorothea's discouragement "not unusual"; that ordinariness is the point.
parts.n: Type: Central ideas (main idea of a literary passage). Rule or move: In a reflective passage, the main idea is the general claim the narrator builds from the particular case; check each choice against the key phrase ("tragedy which lies in the very fact of frequency"). Trap: (A), which confuses "people are not moved by common suffering" with "common suffering is not tragic."

mc.stem:
The following text is from Kate Chopin's 1894 short story "The Story of an Hour." Mrs. Mallard has just learned that her husband has been killed in a railroad accident, and she has gone alone to her room.

There stood, facing the open window, a comfortable, roomy armchair. Into this she sank, pressed down by a physical exhaustion that haunted her body and seemed to reach into her soul.

She could see in the open square before her house the tops of trees that were all aquiver with the new spring life. The delicious breath of rain was in the air. In the street below a peddler was crying his wares. The notes of a distant song which some one was singing reached her faintly, and countless sparrows were twittering in the eaves.

parts.q:
Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
(A) The scene outside Mrs. Mallard's window is full of life and renewal, in contrast to her own exhaustion.
(B) The world outside Mrs. Mallard's window mirrors her grief, with a heavy rain and faint, fading sounds.
(C) Mrs. Mallard is distracted from her grief by the noise and activity of the busy street below her window.
(D) Mrs. Mallard resents the people outside her window for carrying on with their lives as if nothing had happened.
parts.a: (A). The first paragraph shows Mrs. Mallard "pressed down by a physical exhaustion"; the second fills the view from her window with life: trees "aquiver with the new spring life," the "delicious breath of rain," a peddler, a song, "countless sparrows." The text sets a scene of renewal apart from her weariness. (B) is wrong: the rain is only a "delicious breath" in the air, and the lively details work against gloom; the scene does not mirror grief. (C) is wrong: the text lists what she can see and hear, but it never says these things distract her. (D) is wrong: the text reports no feeling of hers toward the people outside, let alone resentment.
parts.n: Type: Central ideas (main idea of a descriptive literary passage). Rule or move: Read what the details actually say rather than what the situation leads you to expect; a grieving character's view need not be gloomy. Trap: (B), which assumes the setting must reflect the character's loss.

mc.stem: In the opening chapter of The Wealth of Nations (1776), Adam Smith describes a small pin factory he had seen, where ten workers divided the making of a pin into about eighteen distinct operations: one drew out the wire, another straightened it, a third cut it, and so on. Together, Smith reports, the ten could make upward of 48,000 pins a day, whereas a worker making whole pins alone could not have made twenty. Smith attributes the difference to three consequences of dividing labor: each worker grows more dexterous at a single task, no time is lost passing from one task to another, and workers who focus on one operation are more likely to devise machines that make it easier.

parts.q:
According to the text, how does Smith account for the difference in output that he describes?
(A) He credits it mainly to machines that the factory's owners had installed before the work was divided.
(B) He explains that the factory's workers worked longer hours each day than a worker making whole pins alone would have.
(C) He argues that the factory hired workers who were more skilled to begin with than the workers employed elsewhere.
(D) He traces it to effects of specialization on the workers' skill, their use of time, and their inventiveness.
parts.a: (D). The last sentence gives Smith's three reasons, all consequences of dividing labor: greater dexterity (skill), no time lost switching tasks (use of time), and a tendency to devise labor-saving machines (inventiveness). (A) is the trap: machines appear in the text, but as something workers devise because they specialize, not as equipment owners installed beforehand. (B) is wrong: the text says nothing about hours worked; the comparison is per day. (C) is wrong: in Smith's account the skill grows from specializing ("grows more dexterous"); it is not something the workers had to begin with.
parts.n: Type: Central ideas and details (detail and its role). Rule or move: When a detail from the passage reappears in a choice, check that its role is the same: here machines are a result of specialization, not its cause. Trap: (A), which reuses the word "machines" in a new causal role.

mc.stem: Economists have long assumed that people value a good according to what it can do for them, not according to what it cost them to obtain. Psychologist Grace Oyelaran and colleagues found an exception. Participants who assembled a plain storage box from a kit offered to pay more to keep it than did participants who were handed the same box already assembled, and the gap grew with the effort the assembly required. When the assembly failed, though, or when participants were stopped before finishing, the gap disappeared. Oyelaran concludes that effort can raise the value people place on a product, but only when the effort pays off.

parts.q:
Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
(A) Economists have been mistaken to assume that people value goods according to what those goods can do for them.
(B) People who fail to finish a task tend to value its product less than people who never attempted the task at all.
(C) Successful effort can raise the value people place on a product, an exception to a common economic assumption.
(D) The more effort people spend on a task, the more they value its product, whatever the outcome of the task.
parts.a: (C). The text sets up an assumption (value depends on usefulness, not cost), reports an exception (assemblers valued the box more), and ends with the conclusion that effort raises value "only when the effort pays off." (C) states that conclusion and its relation to the assumption. (A) is wrong: the text calls the finding "an exception," which limits the assumption rather than showing it is generally mistaken. (B) is wrong: when assembly failed, "the gap disappeared," meaning those participants valued the box about the same as participants who were handed it, not less. (D) is wrong: the gap vanished when the task failed, so the outcome matters.
parts.n: Type: Central ideas (main idea of a research passage). Rule or move: The main idea of a study passage is usually the researcher's final conclusion with its qualifications intact; drop a qualifier and the choice becomes wrong. Trap: (B), which reads "the gap disappeared" as "the value fell below the comparison group."

mc.stem: In Argonauts of the Western Pacific (1922), the anthropologist Bronisław Malinowski described the kula, a system of exchange among the peoples of a ring of islands off the eastern tip of New Guinea. Participants sailed long distances to give and receive two kinds of shell ornaments: necklaces, which traveled around the ring in one direction, and armbands, which traveled in the other. No one kept a kula valuable for long, and the ornaments were seldom worn; a famous piece was prized instead for its history, the renowned men who had held it. Ordinary goods were traded on the same voyages, but Malinowski stressed that the kula itself was a distinct institution, governed by rules of generosity that set it apart from bargaining.

parts.q:
Based on the text, which choice best describes the kula as Malinowski presented it?
(A) A practice set apart from ordinary trade, whose objects were prized for their histories rather than their use
(B) A means of obtaining useful goods that were scarce on some of the islands and plentiful on others
(C) A system in which the most renowned men kept the most valuable ornaments as permanent possessions
(D) A form of trade in which participants bargained hard to make sure that each exchange was exactly equal in value
parts.a: (A). The text says the ornaments were "seldom worn" and "prized instead for [their] history," and that Malinowski "stressed that the kula itself was a distinct institution" set apart from bargaining. (A) combines those two points. (B) is the trap: ordinary goods were traded on the same voyages, but the text separates that trade from the kula itself, whose objects were not valued for use. (C) is wrong: "No one kept a kula valuable for long"; renowned men added to an ornament's history by holding it for a time and passing it on. (D) is wrong: the kula was governed by "rules of generosity that set it apart from bargaining."
parts.n: Type: Central ideas and details (what a source emphasized). Rule or move: When a passage mentions something alongside the main subject ("Ordinary goods were traded on the same voyages, but..."), the word "but" usually marks it as what the subject is not. Trap: (B), which describes the side trade rather than the kula.

mc.stem: "Sonnet 130" is a 1609 poem by William Shakespeare. In the poem, the speaker suggests that the women celebrated in conventional love poetry have been misrepresented by the poets who praise them.

parts.q:
Which quotation from "Sonnet 130" most effectively illustrates the claim?
(A) "My mistress' eyes are nothing like the sun; / Coral is far more red than her lips' red"
(B) "I love to hear her speak, yet well I know / That music hath a far more pleasing sound"
(C) "I grant I never saw a goddess go; / My mistress, when she walks, treads on the ground"
(D) "And yet, by heaven, I think my love as rare / As any she belied with false compare"
parts.a: (D). The claim is about other women, the ones praised in conventional poems, and about their being misrepresented. Only (D) speaks of them: "any she" means any woman, and "belied with false compare" means lied about through false comparisons. The speaker says his love is as rare as any woman whom poets have misrepresented with such comparisons. (A), (B), and (C) all describe the speaker's own mistress in deliberately unflattering, realistic terms (her eyes, her voice, her walk); they show that he refuses the conventional comparisons, but none of them says anything about the women in other poets' work or about those poets misrepresenting them. (A) is the most tempting because it echoes the most famous conventional comparison, but it is still a statement about his mistress only.
parts.n: Type: Command of evidence, textual (quotation that illustrates a claim). Rule or move: Underline the claim's subject and its predicate ("women in conventional poetry" / "misrepresented"); the right quotation must contain both, not just the poem's general attitude. Trap: (A), the famous opening line, which is about the speaker's own mistress.

mc.stem: Many languages require speakers to choose between a familiar and a formal way of addressing one person, as French speakers choose between "tu" and "vous." The choice might depend on how well two speakers know each other, on their relative social status, or on both. Studying speakers of one such language, sociolinguist Amara Nwosu hypothesizes that status matters more than familiarity: speakers, she argues, tend to use the familiar form with people they regard as equals and the formal form with people they regard as superiors, however long they have known them.

parts.q:
Which finding, if true, would most directly support Nwosu's hypothesis?
(A) Speakers used the familiar form more often with close friends than with people they had just met.
(B) Speakers used the familiar form more with newly met coworkers of equal rank than with supervisors they had long known.
(C) Speakers used the formal form when addressing supervisors whom they had met only recently.
(D) Speakers reported that choosing between the two forms was sometimes difficult when they addressed a new acquaintance.
parts.a: (B). To show that status matters more than familiarity, a finding has to set the two against each other. (B) does: new coworkers of equal rank are unfamiliar but equal, and long-known supervisors are familiar but superior. If speakers still used the familiar form with the new equals and the formal form with the old superiors, status won. (A) is wrong: close friends are both familiar and usually equals, so the finding cannot tell which factor mattered, and it looks more like evidence for familiarity. (C) is wrong: recently met supervisors are both unfamiliar and superior, so both factors predict the formal form. (D) is wrong: difficulty in choosing says nothing about which factor drives the choice.
parts.n: Type: Command of evidence, textual (support a hypothesis). Rule or move: When a hypothesis says "A matters more than B," the supporting finding is a case where A and B point in opposite directions and A wins; cases where they agree prove nothing. Trap: (C), which fits the hypothesis but fits the rival explanation just as well.

mc.stem: Retailers often set prices that end in 99 cents, such as $4.99 instead of $5.00. Economist Lucia Ferraz argues that such prices boost sales because shoppers give too much weight to a price's leftmost digit: a shopper glancing at $4.99 registers "four dollars and change" rather than "about five dollars."

parts.q:
Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Ferraz's argument?
(A) Items priced at $4.99 sold more units than the same items priced at $5.00.
(B) Shoppers asked to recall prices after a shopping trip tended to remember prices ending in 99 cents as lower than they were.
(C) Cutting a price from $5.00 to $4.99 raised sales no more than cutting a price from $4.60 to $4.59 did.
(D) Prices ending in 99 cents were more common on inexpensive items than on expensive ones.
parts.a: (C). Ferraz's explanation depends on the leftmost digit changing. Both cuts in (C) are one cent, but only the cut from $5.00 to $4.99 changes the leftmost digit (5 to 4). If her explanation were right, that cut should raise sales more than the cut from $4.60 to $4.59, which leaves the leftmost digit unchanged. Finding no difference undercuts the mechanism she proposes. (A) is wrong: it supports the claim that 99-cent prices boost sales. (B) is wrong: remembering $4.99 as lower than it is fits her idea that shoppers underweight everything after the first digit. (D) is wrong: where such prices are common says nothing about why they affect sales.
parts.n: Type: Command of evidence, textual (weaken an explanation). Rule or move: To weaken a proposed mechanism, find the case where the mechanism predicts a difference and none appears; results that show the effect exists do not test why it exists. Trap: (A), which supports the effect Ferraz is explaining.

mc.stem: "Ozymandias" is an 1818 sonnet by Percy Bysshe Shelley. In the poem, a traveler describes the ruins of a colossal statue of an ancient king in the desert. The poem suggests that the sculptor who made the statue perceived the king's character accurately.

parts.q:
Which quotation from "Ozymandias" most effectively illustrates the claim?
(A) "Two vast and trunkless legs of stone / Stand in the desert"
(B) "Tell that its sculptor well those passions read / Which yet survive, stamped on these lifeless things"
(C) "My name is Ozymandias, King of Kings; / Look on my Works, ye Mighty, and despair!"
(D) "Round the decay / Of that colossal Wreck, boundless and bare / The lone and level sands stretch far away"
parts.a: (B). In (B), the statue's frown and sneer "Tell that its sculptor well those passions read," that is, show that the sculptor read (understood) the king's passions well, and those passions "yet survive" in the stone. That is the claim that the sculptor perceived the king's character accurately. (A) is wrong: it describes what is left of the statue, not the sculptor's insight. (C) is the trap: the inscription reveals the king's pride, but these are the king's own words about himself; they show his character, not that the sculptor perceived it. (D) is wrong: it describes the empty desert around the ruin, which bears on the fate of the king's works, not on the sculptor.
parts.n: Type: Command of evidence, textual (quotation that illustrates a claim). Rule or move: Match the claim's actor: a claim about what the sculptor perceived needs a quotation about the sculptor, not one that merely displays the king's character. Trap: (C), the famous inscription, which shows the king's pride in his own words.

mc.stem: For decades, the painting Harbor at Dusk was attributed to the painter Ilse Brandauer, who died in 1851. Conservator Elif Demir suspects that it was painted instead by Jonas Kerr, Brandauer's former pupil, who went on working in her style for some thirty years after her death.

parts.q:
Which finding, if true, would most directly support Demir's hypothesis?
(A) The original paint contains a pigment first sold several years after Brandauer's death.
(B) The brushwork in the painting closely resembles the brushwork in paintings securely attributed to Brandauer.
(C) Brandauer painted a number of other harbor scenes, most of them in the decade before her death.
(D) An exhibition catalog shows that the painting was displayed under Brandauer's name in 1849.
parts.a: (A). If the original paint contains a pigment that could not be bought until after 1851, the painting was made after Brandauer died, which rules her out and fits Kerr, who kept working in her style for decades. (B) is wrong: because Kerr painted in Brandauer's style, a resemblance to her brushwork cannot tell the two apart. (C) is wrong: it shows only that harbor scenes were a subject of hers, which if anything fits the old attribution. (D) is wrong: a painting shown under her name in 1849 existed during her lifetime, which weakens Demir's hypothesis rather than supporting it.
parts.n: Type: Command of evidence, textual (support a hypothesis). Rule or move: The strongest support for "not X but Y" is evidence that rules out X while leaving Y possible; resemblance evidence fails when the text says Y imitated X. Trap: (B), which ignores that Kerr worked in Brandauer's style.

mc.stem:
Museum researcher Tomás Oliveira measured how long visitors stood in front of four paintings, comparing visitors who used the museum's audio guide with visitors who did not. The guide discusses two of the paintings, Portrait of a Merchant and Still Life with Lemons, at length and mentions the other two only briefly. Oliveira hypothesizes that the guide increases viewing time mainly for the paintings it discusses in detail.

Average viewing time (seconds)
Painting · Without guide · With guide
Portrait of a Merchant · 28 · 61
River Landscape · 19 · 22
Still Life with Lemons · 24 · 57
The Harvest · 31 · 34

parts.q:
Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Oliveira's hypothesis?
(A) Visitors spent more time in front of The Harvest than in front of River Landscape, whether or not they were using the audio guide.
(B) Visitors who used the guide spent more time in front of every one of the four paintings than did visitors who did not use it.
(C) The guide more than doubled viewing time for the two paintings it discusses at length but added only 3 seconds for the other two.
(D) Among visitors without the guide, The Harvest held attention the longest, at an average of 31 seconds.
parts.a: (C). The hypothesis compares the paintings the guide discusses at length with those it barely mentions. (C) makes exactly that comparison: 28 to 61 seconds and 24 to 57 seconds (each more than double) against 19 to 22 and 31 to 34 seconds (3 seconds each). (A) is accurate but compares two briefly mentioned paintings with each other, which says nothing about the guide's detail. (B) is accurate and is the trap: it shows the guide added time everywhere, but not that the gain was concentrated on the two paintings discussed at length. (D) is accurate but describes only visitors without the guide.
parts.n: Type: Command of evidence, quantitative (support a hypothesis). Rule or move: Name the comparison the hypothesis makes (here, detailed versus brief) and choose the data statement that makes that same comparison; true but general statements are the standard trap. Trap: (B), true of every painting and therefore unable to show "mainly."

mc.stem:
Linguist Ravi Menon identified 180 English verbs that had irregular past tense forms in the 1200s (such as "held" rather than "holded") and sorted them into three groups by how often the verbs are used today. He then counted how many in each group still have irregular forms. Menon argues that frequent use protects an irregular form, because speakers hear it often enough to learn it as an exception.

Frequency of use today · Verbs irregular in the 1200s · Verbs still irregular today
High · 40 · 36
Medium · 60 · 27
Low · 80 · 8

parts.q:
Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Menon's argument?
(A) Of the 180 verbs that were irregular in the 1200s, 71 still have irregular forms today.
(B) More of the verbs that were irregular in the 1200s fall into the low-frequency group than into either of the other two groups.
(C) Of the 60 medium-frequency verbs that were irregular in the 1200s, 27, or 45 percent, are still irregular today.
(D) The share still irregular falls from 90 percent of high-frequency verbs to 45 percent of medium and 10 percent of low.
parts.a: (D). Menon's argument predicts that the more often a verb is used, the more likely its irregular form is to survive. Because the groups differ in size, the fair measure is the share that survived: 36 of 40 (90%), 27 of 60 (45%), and 8 of 80 (10%). The shares fall as frequency falls, so (D) supports the argument. (A) is accurate but gives a total for all groups, with no comparison by frequency. (B) is accurate but describes the sizes of the groups, not survival. (C) is accurate and is the trap: it gives the right kind of figure, a share, but for the medium group alone; one group's survival rate, with nothing to compare it to, cannot show that survival depends on how often a verb is used.
parts.n: Type: Command of evidence, quantitative (rates versus counts). Rule or move: When groups differ in size, compare percentages, not raw counts; a bigger group can lose more members while holding on to a larger share of them. Trap: (C), the right kind of figure (a share) for only one group, so no trend across frequency appears.

mc.stem:
An art museum that normally charged $12 for admission tried a pay-what-you-want policy on alternate weeks for a year. Economist Hye-jin Cho compared the weeks under the two policies.

Policy · Average visitors per week · Average payment per visitor
Fixed price ($12) · 1,500 · $12.00
Pay what you want · 3,200 · $6.10

Cho notes that although visitors paid about half as much on average under the pay-what-you-want policy, the museum ______

parts.q:
Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
(A) took in more admission revenue per week, since the rise in attendance more than offset the lower average payment.
(B) took in less admission revenue per week, because the average payment per visitor fell by nearly half.
(C) took in exactly the same admission revenue per week, because the rise in attendance matched the drop in average payment.
(D) attracted fewer visitors per week, because many potential visitors were unsure how much they should pay.
parts.a: (A). Weekly revenue is visitors times average payment: 1,500 × $12.00 = $18,000 under the fixed price and 3,200 × $6.10 = $19,520 under pay-what-you-want. Attendance more than doubled (3,200 is more than twice 1,500) while the average payment fell by slightly less than half, so revenue rose. (B) is the trap: its premise is true (the average payment fell by nearly half), but it ignores attendance, and revenue in fact rose. (C) is wrong: $19,520 is not equal to $18,000. (D) is wrong: attendance rose from 1,500 to 3,200 a week.
parts.n: Type: Command of evidence, quantitative (compute before you choose). Rule or move: When a table gives a count and a per-unit amount, the total is their product; compute it rather than reasoning from one column. Trap: (B), which reasons from the price column alone.

mc.stem:
Psychologist Lena Castell argues that people's tendency to remember the first items in a list and their tendency to remember the last items arise from different mechanisms: early items are rehearsed often enough to be stored in long-term memory, while the last items are still being held in short-term memory when recall begins. To test this, Castell had participants study lists of twelve words and recall them either immediately or after 30 seconds of counting backward, a task that pushes out the contents of short-term memory.

Participants recalling the word (%)
Position in list · Immediate recall · Delayed recall
1 · 72 · 70
2 · 58 · 55
6 · 34 · 33
10 · 49 · 32
11 · 67 · 34
12 · 84 · 35

parts.q:
Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Castell's argument?
(A) Immediate recall was higher than delayed recall at every position shown in the table.
(B) Delay barely changed recall of the first word (72 versus 70 percent) but cut recall of the last word from 84 to 35 percent.
(C) With immediate recall, recall rose at each position shown from the sixth word (34 percent) to the twelfth (84 percent).
(D) With immediate recall, the last word (84 percent) was recalled more often than the first word (72 percent).
parts.a: (B). Castell's argument predicts a split: clearing short-term memory should hurt recall of the last items (held in short-term memory) but not of the first items (already in long-term memory). (B) shows both halves: first word 72% versus 70%, last word 84% versus 35%. (A) is accurate but says only that the delay lowered recall everywhere, which blurs rather than shows the difference between the two ends: it would be just as true if the delay had cut recall of the first and last words equally. (C) is accurate and is the trap: it describes the end-of-list advantage vividly, but only under immediate recall, so it shows that the advantage exists, not that clearing short-term memory removes it while sparing the first items. (D) is accurate but compares the two ends within one condition, which does not bear on whether they depend on different mechanisms.
parts.n: Type: Command of evidence, quantitative (two-part claim). Rule or move: When a claim says two things behave differently, the best data statement shows both: one that changes and one that does not. Trap: (C), which describes the end-of-list effect itself rather than what the delay does to it.

mc.stem:
Sociologist Jun Takeda surveyed residents of four cities about whether they had attended a live concert in the past year. Only City C offers a large program of free public concerts. Takeda hypothesizes that free concerts narrow the gap in concert attendance between lower- and higher-income residents.

Residents who attended a concert in the past year (%)
City · Lowest income group · Highest income group
A · 22 · 61
B · 30 · 58
C · 47 · 63
D · 18 · 55

parts.q:
Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Takeda's hypothesis?
(A) In City C, 63 percent of residents in the highest income group attended a concert, compared with 47 percent of residents in the lowest income group.
(B) In every city, residents in the highest income group were more likely than residents in the lowest income group to have attended a concert.
(C) City C had the highest attendance rate among residents in the highest income group, at 63 percent.
(D) The gap between the highest and lowest income groups was 16 percentage points in City C, smaller than in any other city.
parts.a: (D). The hypothesis is about a gap. The gaps are 61 − 22 = 39 points in A, 58 − 30 = 28 in B, 63 − 47 = 16 in C, and 55 − 18 = 37 in D, so City C, the only city with free concerts, has the smallest gap, as (D) states. (A) is the trap: it gives City C's gap (63 versus 47 percent), but a gap in one city, with no comparison to the other cities, cannot show that the gap is narrower where free concerts are offered; read alone, it shows only that a gap persists. (B) is accurate but true of all four cities, so it cannot distinguish City C. (C) is accurate but concerns only the higher-income group; if anything, higher attendance in that group would widen the gap.
parts.n: Type: Command of evidence, quantitative (a claim about a difference). Rule or move: If the claim is that something narrows a gap, the answer must compare gaps: the gap where the factor is present against the gaps where it is absent. Trap: (A), which states City C's gap but never compares it with the others.

mc.stem: In the seventeenth-century Netherlands, many paintings were sold not on commission but on an open market, through dealers and at fairs, to buyers the painter never met. Some historians argue that this market encouraged painters to specialize: an artist known for winter landscapes, for example, could count on buyers looking for exactly that kind of picture. Art historian Sanne de Wit notes that most of the household inventories from the period that she examined identify each painting by its subject ("a winter scene," "a still life with fish") but not by the name of the painter who made it. If these inventories reflect how buyers thought about the paintings they owned, then ______

parts.q:
Which choice most logically completes the text?
(A) most paintings sold on the open market were made by artists whose names were never recorded anywhere.
(B) painters who specialized in a single subject earned less than painters who worked in many subjects.
(C) buyers may have cared more about a painting's subject than about its painter, which fits the historians' account.
(D) buyers were concerned mainly with the price of a painting and gave little thought to either its subject or its painter.
parts.a: (C). If buyers recorded paintings by subject and not by painter, the natural inference is that subject mattered more to them than authorship. That fits the historians' claim that the market rewarded specialists in particular subjects, since buyers "looking for exactly that kind of picture" were shopping by subject. (A) is wrong: household inventories leaving names out does not show that names went unrecorded everywhere else (for instance, in dealers' records or signatures). (B) is wrong: the text gives no information about earnings, and the inference points the other way. (D) is wrong: the inventories record subjects, which suggests buyers did think about subject; nothing is said about price.
parts.n: Type: Inferences (logical completion). Rule or move: Complete the "if ... then" with the smallest step the premise allows, and check whether the text sets up a claim the step connects to (here, the specialization argument). Trap: (A), which turns "not named in these inventories" into "never recorded anywhere."

mc.stem: Economists have offered two main explanations for why restaurant customers tip: to reward good service, or to avoid the discomfort of appearing stingy in front of the server. At several restaurants, economist Paolo Grieco randomly assigned diners either to pay at the table, with the server present, or to pay through an app after they had left. Tips paid through the app were much smaller on average, even though the two groups rated the quality of their service almost identically. These results suggest that ______

parts.q:
Which choice most logically completes the text?
(A) diners who paid through the app received worse service than diners who paid at the table did.
(B) much of what diners tip at the table reflects the pressure of being observed rather than the quality of service.
(C) diners' tips are determined entirely by the pressure of being observed and not at all by the quality of the service.
(D) diners who prefer to pay through an app are generally less generous than diners who prefer to pay at the table.
parts.a: (B). The two groups rated their service the same, so service quality cannot explain the drop in tips; the difference between the groups was whether the server was present when they paid. The inference is that much of the tip at the table is a response to being observed. (A) is wrong: the two groups rated their service "almost identically." (C) overreaches: tips through the app were smaller, not zero, and the study did not vary service quality, so it cannot show that quality plays no part. (D) is wrong because diners were randomly assigned; they did not choose how to pay, so differences in generosity between people who prefer each method cannot explain the result.
parts.n: Type: Inferences (logical completion from a study design). Rule or move: Random assignment rules out "different kinds of people ended up in each group"; if the groups also agree on everything but one factor, that factor is the explanation. Trap: (C), the right direction pushed to "entirely," which the data cannot support.

mc.stem: Before sound recording, a composer's music reached the public mainly through concerts and printed scores. Musicologist Karin Holm found that between 1880 and 1910, the number of European orchestras performing a given composer's works rose and fell closely with sales of that composer's music in inexpensive editions for amateurs to play at home. Holm argues that the home market drove orchestral programming rather than the reverse: orchestras, she says, chose works their audiences already knew from playing them at home. To support this argument, Holm points out that for most composers in her study, rises in home-edition sales ______

parts.q:
Which choice most logically completes the text?
(A) came several years before the corresponding rises in orchestral performances.
(B) came only after the corresponding rises in orchestral performances had occurred.
(C) were largest for composers whose works were never performed by orchestras.
(D) occurred at about the same time in every European country she studied.
parts.a: (A). Holm has a correlation (performances and home sales rose and fell together) and a claim about its direction (home sales drove performances). Evidence for that direction is that the cause came first: sales rose before performances did. (B) is wrong: sales rising after performances would suggest the reverse, that concerts created demand for home editions. (C) is wrong: it would weaken the close link between sales and performances that her argument starts from. (D) is wrong: timing across countries says nothing about which of the two trends led the other.
parts.n: Type: Inferences (supporting a causal direction). Rule or move: A correlation cannot tell which way the cause runs; the evidence that does is timing, since a cause comes before its effect. Trap: (B), the reversed order, which supports the rival explanation.

mc.stem: In Turkish, a speaker describing a past event must choose between two verb forms: one with a suffix such as -di, used for events the speaker directly witnessed, and one with a suffix such as -miş, used for events the speaker heard about or inferred. Psychologist Deniz Arslan wondered whether a lifetime of making this choice makes Turkish speakers better at remembering how they learned about events. In her study, Turkish-speaking and English-speaking adults were equally accurate at recalling whether they had seen an event themselves or had only been told about it, even though the Turkish speakers used the two verb forms correctly throughout the study. Arslan's results suggest that ______

parts.q:
Which choice most logically completes the text?
(A) the distinction between the two Turkish verb forms is too subtle for most adult speakers to apply consistently.
(B) English speakers mark in their grammar how they learned about an event as regularly as Turkish speakers do.
(C) Turkish speakers are less accurate than English speakers at recalling how they learned about past events.
(D) having to mark how one learned of an event does not necessarily improve one's memory of how one learned of it.
parts.a: (D). Turkish speakers make the grammatical choice constantly (and made it correctly in the study), yet they were no better than English speakers at remembering how they learned of events. So the grammatical habit did not produce a memory advantage, which is what (D) says, with appropriate caution ("not necessarily"). (A) is wrong: the Turkish speakers "used the two verb forms correctly throughout the study." (B) is wrong: the text presents the marking as a feature Turkish requires, and nothing suggests English grammar does the same. (C) is wrong: the two groups were "equally accurate."
parts.n: Type: Inferences (what a null result shows). Rule or move: When a group with a special habit performs no better than a group without it, infer only that the habit does not guarantee the advantage, not that it hurts or that the groups are alike in every way. Trap: (A), which explains away the result with a claim the text directly contradicts.

mc.stem: Many medieval cathedrals took more than a century to build, and historians have often read stylistic differences within a single cathedral (windows in the nave that differ from those in the choir, for example) as records of changing fashions over the decades of construction. Architectural historian Theo Lindqvist examined surviving building accounts for several cathedrals and found cases in which parts built in the same years, by the same workshop, differ in style as much as parts built decades apart. If Lindqvist's findings are representative, then ______

parts.q:
Which choice most logically completes the text?
(A) medieval workshops paid little attention to the changes in architectural fashion taking place around them.
(B) most medieval cathedrals were completed more quickly than historians have believed.
(C) stylistic difference alone cannot show that two parts of a cathedral were built at different times.
(D) the parts of a cathedral that differ most in style were probably built in the same years by a single workshop.
parts.a: (C). Historians have treated stylistic difference as a sign of different dates. Lindqvist found that parts built at the same time, by the same workshop, can differ just as much. If that is typical, style alone cannot date the parts relative to each other, which is (C). (A) is wrong: the findings show that one workshop could vary its style, not that workshops ignored fashion. (B) is wrong: the findings concern how to read style, not how long construction took. (D) is wrong: it overreaches in the other direction; showing that difference is not proof of different dates does not make it evidence of the same dates.
parts.n: Type: Inferences (what a counterexample does). Rule or move: A counterexample to "A signals B" shows that A is not sufficient evidence of B; it does not show that A signals the opposite of B. Trap: (D), which replaces one unreliable inference with its reverse.

parts.q:
If 5(2w − 3) = 4w + 21, what is the value of 3w − 2?
(A) 6
(B) 10
(C) 16
(D) 18
parts.a: (C). Solve for w, then build the quantity the question asks for. 5(2w − 3) = 10w − 15, so 10w − 15 = 4w + 21, 6w = 36 and w = 6. Then 3w − 2 = 18 − 2 = 16. Check by substituting: 5(12 − 3) = 45 and 24 + 21 = 45. Desmos route: graph y = 5(2x − 3) and y = 4x + 21, read the intersection x = 6, then evaluate 3(6) − 2. (A) 6 is w itself: the equation was solved, but the question asks for 3w − 2. (B) 10 comes from distributing 5(2w − 3) as 10w − 3, which gives w = 4 and 3(4) − 2 = 10. (D) 18 is 3w: the − 2 was dropped at the last step.
parts.n: Type: Linear equation in one variable, asking for an expression. Rule or move: Before you answer, reread the last line of the question and compute exactly the expression it names, not the variable you solved for. Trap: (A), the value of w, the number on your scratch paper when you stop one step early.

parts.q:
Membership at a climbing gym increased by 40% from 2022 to 2023 and then decreased by 40% from 2023 to 2024. The gym had 1,050 members in 2024. How many members did the gym have in 2022?
(A) 1,050
(B) 1,218
(C) 1,250
(D) 1,750
parts.a: (C). Each percent is taken of the value at the start of its own year, so chain the multipliers: 2024 membership = (2022 membership) × 1.40 × 0.60 = 0.84 × (2022 membership). So the 2022 membership is 1,050 ÷ 0.84 = 1,250. Check forward: 1,250 × 1.4 = 1,750 in 2023, and 1,750 × 0.6 = 1,050 in 2024. (A) 1,050 assumes a 40% rise and a 40% fall cancel; they don't, because the 40% decrease is taken of a larger base. (B) 1,218 finds the net 16% decrease but undoes it by adding 16% of 1,050 (1,050 × 1.16); the 16% was a percent of the 2022 value, so the change must be undone by dividing by 0.84. (D) 1,750 is the 2023 membership: it undoes only the decrease (1,050 ÷ 0.6) and stops a year short.
parts.n: Type: Successive percent changes, worked backward. Rule or move: Turn each percent change into a multiplier, multiply the multipliers, and undo a change by dividing by its multiplier, never by applying the opposite percent. Trap: (A) or (B), treating +40% and −40% as canceling, or undoing a net 16% decrease with a 16% increase.

parts.q:
The circumference of a circular rug is 144π inches. What is the area of the rug, in square feet? (1 foot = 12 inches)
(A) 12π
(B) 36π
(C) 432π
(D) 5,184π
parts.a: (B). Convert the length first, then square it. C = 2πr = 144π gives r = 72 inches, which is 6 feet, so the area is π(6)² = 36π square feet. (Converting after squaring also works, but then you divide by 12² = 144: 5,184π ÷ 144 = 36π.) (A) 12π is the circumference in feet (144π ÷ 12): the right conversion applied to the wrong quantity. (C) 432π divides the area in square inches by 12 instead of by 144, converting a square unit as if it were a length. (D) 5,184π is π(72)², the area in square inches: the conversion to feet was skipped.
parts.n: Type: Circle measurement with a change of units. Rule or move: Convert lengths before you square them; a square foot is 144 square inches, not 12. Trap: (C), dividing square inches by 12.

parts.q:
3x − ky = 8
6x + 10y = c
In the given system of equations, k and c are constants. If the system has no solution, which of the following must be true?
(A) k = −5 and c ≠ 16
(B) k = −5 and c = 16
(C) k = 5 and c ≠ 16
(D) k = 5 and c = 16
parts.a: (A). No solution means parallel, distinct lines: the x- and y-coefficients are proportional but the constants are not. Doubling the first equation gives 6x − 2ky = 16. Matching the second equation's y-coefficient, −2k = 10, so k = −5. With k = −5 the left sides are identical, so the lines are distinct only if c ≠ 16. (B) k = −5 and c = 16 makes the two equations the same line, which gives infinitely many solutions, the opposite case. (C) drops the minus sign in −ky and sets 2k = 10: with k = 5 the first line is 3x − 5y = 8, with slope 3/5, while the second has slope −3/5, so the lines cross once. (D) makes the same sign slip and also matches the constants.
