Rule or move: an opening -ing phrase must be followed immediately by the noun that performs the action; passive versions that tuck the doer into a "by" or "of" phrase fail. Trap: (B), because it contains the right people ("by researchers") and the right facts, just not as the subject.

mc.stem: HMS Beagle sailed from Plymouth, England, in December 1831 on a surveying voyage that would last nearly five years, with a young Charles Darwin aboard as a gentleman naturalist. The ship's ______ Robert FitzRoy, was only twenty-six years old, just four years older than Darwin himself.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
(A) captain—
(B) captain
(C) captain;
(D) captain,
parts.a: (D). A ship has only one captain, so "The ship's captain" already identifies the person; the name "Robert FitzRoy" adds information that could be removed, and it is set off with a pair of commas. The comma after "FitzRoy" is the second of the pair, so a comma is needed after "captain" to open it. (A) opens the interruption with a dash that the comma after "FitzRoy" cannot close. (B) leaves only the comma after "FitzRoy," which then separates the subject from its verb, "was." (C) puts a semicolon between the subject and the rest of the sentence; "The ship's captain" is not an independent clause.
parts.n: Type: Boundaries (nonessential appositive). Rule or move: when the noun before a name already picks out one person (the ship's captain, her husband, the author of the book), the name is extra and takes a pair of commas; a bare title before a name (astronomer Galileo Galilei) takes none. Trap: (B), for students who have learned that a title before a name takes no comma.

mc.stem: Great Basin bristlecone pines grow slowly in the cold, dry air of California's White Mountains, and in a harsh year a tree may add a growth ring only a fraction of a millimeter thick. Counting the rings in thin cores drilled from living trees without harming them ______ that some of these pines are more than 4,000 years old.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
(A) have shown
(B) are showing
(C) has shown
(D) show
parts.a: (C). The subject of the second sentence is the gerund phrase "Counting the rings in thin cores drilled from living trees without harming them." A gerund phrase names one activity, counting, so it is singular and takes the singular verb "has shown." (A), (B), and (D) are plural ("have shown," "are showing," "show"); they agree with "rings," "cores," or "trees," plural nouns inside the phrase that are not the subject.
parts.n: Type: Form, structure, and sense (subject-verb agreement). Rule or move: a subject that begins with an -ing word (counting, measuring, studying) is one activity and takes a singular verb, however many plural nouns follow it. Trap: (A), which agrees with "trees," the nearest plural noun before the blank.

mc.stem: The French effort to build a canal across Panama, begun in 1881 under Ferdinand de Lesseps, collapsed before the decade was out. Yellow fever and malaria killed thousands of workers, and the company's finances crumbled under mounting costs. ______ the French had set out to dig a sea-level canal, a design that required removing vastly more earth and rock than the system of locks the United States chose after taking over the project in 1904.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
(A) However,
(B) Moreover,
(C) Consequently,
(D) Nonetheless,
parts.a: (B). The second sentence gives causes of the French failure (disease and money), and the third adds another: the sea-level design demanded far more excavation. "Moreover" adds a further point of the same kind. (A) "However" would set the sea-level design against the causes just listed, but it is one more of them; the contrast with the United States' locks lies inside the sentence ("than"), not between the sentences. (C) "Consequently" would make the choice of design a result of the deaths and the money troubles, when it was a separate decision. (D) "Nonetheless" would mean the French chose the design despite the disease and debts, a relationship the text does not suggest.
parts.n: Type: Transitions (addition). Rule or move: decide what the new sentence does in relation to the one before (here, adds another cause), and ignore contrasts that live inside the sentence. Trap: (A), because the sentence contrasts the French design with the American one and "However" seems to announce it.

mc.stem: A lichen can look like a single organism, a crust of gray or orange on a rock or a tuft hanging from a branch. In fact, it is a partnership between a fungus and a photosynthetic partner, usually an alga or a cyanobacterium, and the two live so closely intertwined that together they form a body neither could form alone. ______ a lichen is less an individual than a small, self-contained community.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
(A) For example,
(B) Nevertheless,
(C) Previously,
(D) In other words,
parts.a: (D). The last sentence restates the point of the one before it in more general terms: a partnership of two organisms forming one body is, put another way, a community rather than an individual. "In other words" introduces that restatement. (A) "For example" would make the last sentence an instance of the partnership, but it is a summary of it. (B) "Nevertheless" would mean the lichen is a community despite being a partnership, when it is a community because it is one. (C) "Previously" would place the last sentence earlier in time, but both sentences describe what a lichen is now.
parts.n: Type: Transitions (restatement). Rule or move: if the new sentence says the same thing more generally or more simply, the link is in other words or that is. Trap: (B), because the text contrasts appearance (a single organism) with reality, and a contrast word lingers from the second sentence's "In fact."

mc.stem: Unlike iron, copper, and most other metals, gold does not react with oxygen or water under ordinary conditions. ______ gold objects recovered from shipwrecks and ancient tombs often gleam almost as brightly as they did the day they were made, while iron objects from the same sites may have rusted away entirely.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
(A) For this reason,
(B) In contrast,
(C) Nevertheless,
(D) Meanwhile,
parts.a: (A). The first sentence states a property of gold (it does not react with oxygen or water), and the second gives its consequence (gold objects still gleam while iron ones rust away). "For this reason" signals that cause-and-effect link. (B) "In contrast" is the trap: the second sentence does contain a contrast, between gold and iron, but that contrast sits inside the sentence ("while"), and the sentence as a whole follows from the first rather than opposing it. (C) "Nevertheless" would mean the gold gleams despite its resistance to corrosion. (D) "Meanwhile" would mark events happening at the same time, but the sentences are a property and its result.
parts.n: Type: Transitions (cause and effect). Rule or move: compare the main claim of each sentence, not a contrast tucked inside one of them. Trap: (B), because "while iron objects ... may have rusted away" makes the second sentence look like a contrast.

mc.stem:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• In 1901, sponge divers recovered corroded lumps of bronze from an ancient shipwreck off the Greek island of Antikythera.
• The lumps turned out to be fragments of a hand-cranked device built in the second or first century BCE.
• The device used interlocking bronze gears to predict the positions of the Sun and Moon and the timing of eclipses.
• Because the fragments are fused and fragile, they cannot be taken apart.
• Researchers have used X-ray imaging to see gears and read inscriptions hidden inside the fragments.

parts.q:
The student wants to emphasize how researchers have learned about the device's inner workings despite its condition. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
(A) Built in the second or first century BCE, the Antikythera mechanism used interlocking bronze gears to predict the positions of the Sun and Moon and the timing of eclipses.
(B) In 1901, sponge divers recovered corroded lumps of bronze from a shipwreck off Antikythera, and the lumps turned out to be fragments of an ancient hand-cranked device.
(C) Although the fused, fragile fragments of the Antikythera mechanism cannot be taken apart, X-ray imaging has let researchers see the gears and inscriptions hidden inside.
(D) Researchers have used X-ray imaging to study the Antikythera mechanism, an ancient device that predicted the positions of the Sun and Moon and the timing of eclipses.
parts.a: (C). The goal has three pieces: how researchers learned (X-ray imaging), what they learned about (the inner workings, the hidden gears and inscriptions), and the obstacle (fragments too fused and fragile to take apart). (C) gives all three, and "Although" marks the "despite." (A) describes what the device did but not how anyone learned it or what condition it is in. (B) describes the recovery and the corrosion but not how researchers studied the fragments. (D) names the method but leaves out the device's condition, so the "despite" half of the goal is missing.
parts.n: Type: Rhetorical synthesis (a goal with a built-in obstacle). Rule or move: when a goal says "despite" or "although," the right choice names the obstacle as well as the achievement. Trap: (D), which names the right method and sounds complete but never mentions the condition it overcame.

mc.stem:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Many animals appear to sense Earth's magnetic field and use it to navigate.
• Loggerhead sea turtles that hatch on Florida beaches use the field to stay within the warm currents of the North Atlantic during their first migration.
• Sockeye salmon appear to use the field to find their way from the open ocean back to the river where they hatched.
• Homing pigeons carrying small magnets on their heads have more trouble finding their way home on overcast days.

parts.q:
The student wants to make a generalization about the animals in the notes. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
(A) Loggerhead sea turtles that hatch on Florida beaches use Earth's magnetic field to stay within the warm currents of the North Atlantic during their first migration.
(B) Animals as different as sea turtles, salmon, and pigeons appear to use Earth's magnetic field to find their way.
(C) Homing pigeons carrying small magnets on their heads have more trouble finding their way home on overcast days, suggesting that the magnets interfere with their navigation.
(D) Like loggerhead sea turtles, sockeye salmon use Earth's magnetic field to navigate during long journeys through the ocean.
parts.a: (B). A generalization makes a broad claim that covers the cases; (B) draws one claim, magnetic navigation, from all three animals in the notes and stresses their range ("as different as"). (A) describes one species only. (C) describes one experiment with one species and the inference it supports. (D) is the closest trap: it goes beyond a single species, but it only compares two of them and leaves out the pigeons, so it is a comparison rather than a generalization about the animals in the notes.
parts.n: Type: Rhetorical synthesis (generalization). Rule or move: a generalization states what the cases have in common, usually naming or gesturing at all of them; a single case, or a pairing of two, is not one. Trap: (D), because "Like X, Y" sounds like a pattern, though it only compares two cases.

mc.stem:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Seismologist Dara Quinn studied swarms of small earthquakes beneath Mount Hood, a volcano in Oregon.
• She wanted to know whether the earthquakes were caused by magma moving underground or by rock slipping along faults.
• She analyzed vibrations recorded by twelve seismometers placed around the mountain.
• The vibrations matched the pattern produced when rock slips along a fault rather than the pattern produced by moving magma.
• She concluded that the swarms did not signal an approaching eruption.

parts.q:
The student wants to present Quinn's research question and the answer her study provided. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
(A) Quinn asked whether the small earthquakes beneath Mount Hood came from moving magma or from rock slipping along faults, and the vibrations pointed to slipping rock.
(B) Quinn analyzed the vibrations from swarms of small earthquakes beneath Mount Hood, recorded by twelve seismometers placed around the mountain.
(C) Quinn concluded that the swarms of small earthquakes beneath Mount Hood, a volcano in Oregon, did not signal that an eruption was approaching.
(D) To learn what was causing the swarms of small earthquakes beneath Mount Hood, Quinn analyzed the vibrations recorded by twelve seismometers around the mountain.
parts.a: (A). The goal pairs a question with its answer. (A) states the question (moving magma or slipping rock?) and the answer the data gave (slipping rock). (B) gives only the method. (C) gives Quinn's broader conclusion about eruptions but not the question the study was designed to answer or what the vibrations showed. (D) states the purpose and the method, so it poses the question, but it stops before the answer.
parts.n: Type: Rhetorical synthesis (question and answer). Rule or move: map each part of the goal to a note (question: note 2; answer: note 4), then pick the only choice that uses both. Trap: (D), which opens with "To learn what was causing" and so seems to cover the question, but never reports what the study found.

mc.stem:
The following text is from Henry David Thoreau's 1854 book Walden.

I went to the woods because I wished to live deliberately, to front only the essential facts of life, and see if I could not learn what it had to teach, and not, when I came to die, discover that I had not lived.

parts.q:
As used in the text, what does the word "front" most nearly mean?
(A) lead
(B) confront
(C) conceal
(D) come before
parts.a: (B). Thoreau went to the woods to "front only the essential facts of life," that is, to face or confront them directly, and to learn what they had to teach. (A) is wrong: "front" can mean to lead (as in fronting a band), but Thoreau is not leading the facts of life anywhere. (C) is wrong: "conceal" draws on "a front" in the sense of a false appearance, but hiding the essential facts would contradict his wish to learn from them. (D) is wrong: "come before" draws on "in front of," but the sentence is not about coming before the facts in order or time.
parts.n: Type: Words in context (uncommon sense of a common word). Rule or move: Test each dictionary sense of the word against the purpose the sentence states; "to learn what it had to teach" requires meeting the facts head on. Trap: (C) conceal, suggested by the noun "a front" (a false appearance).

mc.stem: John Cage's 4′33″ (1952) instructs its performers not to play for the length of the piece, so that its "music" consists of whatever sounds happen to occur in the hall. Critics who dismiss the work as a mere stunt, musicologist Aiko Mori argues, overlook how ______ it is: the score divides the silence into three separately timed movements, and at the premiere the pianist marked the start and end of each by closing and opening the keyboard lid.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
(A) spontaneous
(B) derivative
(C) ephemeral
(D) meticulous
parts.a: (D). Mori answers the charge that the piece is a stunt by pointing, after the colon, to its careful construction: separately timed movements, each formally marked in performance. "Meticulous" (showing great care over detail) is the word that evidence supports. (A) is the trap: the sounds heard during the piece are spontaneous, but the colon's evidence is about how carefully the piece itself is organized. (B) is wrong: "derivative" (imitative of earlier work) is a criticism, and the evidence says nothing about borrowing. (C) is wrong: every performance may be fleeting, but timing and marking the movements shows planning, not transience.
parts.n: Type: Words in context (precise word, colon evidence). Rule or move: Ask what the evidence after the colon proves, then pick the word for that; a true description of something else in the passage is a trap. Trap: (A) spontaneous, which describes the ambient sounds, not the composition.

mc.stem: Native speakers of English reliably say "a big red ball" rather than "a red big ball," and they keep size before color across countless other phrases. Yet few speakers could state the rule they are following, or even say that there is one. Their knowledge of adjective order is thus ______: it shapes what they say without ever being put into words.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
(A) tacit
(B) rudimentary
(C) dubious
(D) communal
parts.a: (A). "Tacit" means understood or applied without being stated. The colon defines exactly that: the knowledge "shapes what they say without ever being put into words." (B) is the trap: speakers cannot state the rule, but they apply it "reliably" across countless phrases, so their knowledge is not basic or undeveloped; it is simply unspoken. (C) is wrong: nothing in the text casts doubt on the knowledge; speakers use it correctly. (D) is wrong: the knowledge is shared by native speakers, but "communal" does not match the colon's point, which is about the knowledge never being put into words.
parts.n: Type: Words in context (precise sophisticated word). Rule or move: When a colon follows the blank, treat what comes after as a definition of the missing word. Trap: (B) rudimentary, which confuses "cannot explain it" with "does not know it well."

mc.stem: Economists generally expect that when the price of a good rises, people will buy less of it. In The Theory of the Leisure Class (1899), Thorstein Veblen described an apparent exception: goods bought partly to display wealth, whose appeal can grow as their price rises, since a high price is precisely what makes them a display. Economists still debate how common such "Veblen goods" are: for many luxury items, studies find, higher prices still reduce the number sold.

parts.q:
Which choice best describes the function of the third sentence in the text as a whole?
(A) It presents evidence showing that Veblen's account of buying goods to display wealth was simply mistaken.
(B) It explains why the appeal of certain goods can increase as their prices rise.
(C) It suggests that the exception described in the second sentence may be narrower than it first appears.
(D) It introduces a second exception to the general expectation described in the first sentence.
parts.a: (C). The third sentence says economists "debate how common" Veblen goods are and that, for "many luxury items," higher prices still reduce sales. That limits the reach of Veblen's exception without denying it: the exception may apply to fewer goods than it seems to. (A) overstates: evidence about many luxury items shows that not all luxury goods behave as Veblen goods, not that Veblen was wrong about goods bought for display; the text calls the matter a continuing debate. (B) is wrong: the explanation of rising appeal (a high price is what makes the display) is in the second sentence. (D) is wrong: luxury items whose sales fall as prices rise follow the general expectation; they are not a new exception to it.
parts.n: Type: Text structure (function of a sentence). Rule or move: "Debate how common" and "many" (not "all") signal a limit on a claim's scope, not a refutation; match the choice's strength to the sentence's. Trap: (A), which turns a question of scope into a verdict that Veblen was mistaken.

mc.stem:
The following text is adapted from Mark Twain's 1883 memoir Life on the Mississippi. The narrator has spent years learning to pilot steamboats on the Mississippi River.

Now when I had mastered the language of this water and had come to know every trifling feature that bordered the great river as familiarly as I knew the letters of the alphabet, I had made a valuable acquisition. But I had lost something, too. I had lost something which could never be restored to me while I lived. All the grace, the beauty, the poetry had gone out of the majestic river!

parts.q:
Which choice best describes the function of the phrase "as familiarly as I knew the letters of the alphabet" in the text?
(A) It extends the comparison of the river to a language that the narrator has learned to read.
(B) It suggests that the narrator's knowledge of the river is as elementary as a child's grasp of the alphabet.
(C) It emphasizes that learning to pilot the river was as easy for the narrator as learning to read had been.
(D) It introduces the sense of loss that the narrator goes on to describe in the rest of the text.
parts.a: (A). The sentence opens with the narrator having "mastered the language of this water"; knowing the river's features as he knows "the letters of the alphabet" carries that image forward, treating the river as a text he can now read fluently. (B) is wrong: the alphabet is elementary, but the comparison is about how thoroughly he knows the river ("mastered," "every trifling feature"), not how little. (C) is wrong: "familiarly" describes how well he knows the river, not how easily he learned it; the text says he spent years at it. (D) is wrong: the loss is introduced by the next sentence, "But I had lost something, too"; the phrase belongs to the account of what he gained.
parts.n: Type: Text structure (function of a phrase). Rule or move: Read a comparison for the quality it transfers (here, thorough familiarity) and for the larger image it continues (the river as language). Trap: (B), which transfers the wrong quality of the alphabet (simplicity) instead of the right one (familiarity).

mc.stem:
Text 1
Why do people enjoy music that sounds sad? Philosopher Nora Feld argues that listeners do not actually feel sad when they hear such music; rather, they recognize sadness in it, much as a person can recognize grief in a mourner's posture without grieving. On this view, the pleasure of a sad song is the pleasure of perceiving an emotion skillfully expressed, not of undergoing a painful one.

Text 2
In surveys conducted by music psychologist Tariq Aziz, many listeners reported that sad music does make them feel sad, sometimes intensely, yet they described the experience as enjoyable, often mentioning feelings of comfort or of being understood. Aziz suggests that sadness evoked by music, which is detached from any real loss in the listener's life, can be pleasurable in its own right.

parts.q:
Based on the texts, how would Aziz (Text 2) most likely respond to Feld's argument in Text 1?
(A) He would agree that listeners only recognize sadness in music but add that this recognition brings them comfort.
(B) He would argue that her account does not fit listeners who report actually feeling sad while enjoying sad music.
(C) He would argue that sad music gives pleasure only to listeners who are coping with a real loss of their own.
(D) He would argue that listeners who report feeling sad while hearing sad music are mistaken about their own experience.
parts.a: (B). Feld's argument rests on the claim that listeners "do not actually feel sad." Aziz's surveys found listeners who say they do feel sad, "sometimes intensely," and enjoy it anyway, and he proposes that such sadness can itself be pleasurable. He would say her account does not fit those listeners. (A) is wrong: Aziz's evidence is that listeners feel sadness, not merely recognize it. (C) is wrong: Aziz stresses that musical sadness is "detached from any real loss." (D) reverses the positions: doubting listeners' reports of feeling sad is the move Feld's view would require, not Aziz's; his argument takes those reports at face value.
parts.n: Type: Cross-text connections (response to an argument). Rule or move: Find the premise Text 1 depends on (listeners do not feel sad) and ask whether Text 2's evidence contradicts it. Trap: (D), which gives Aziz the reply that Feld would make to him.

mc.stem:
Text 1
The 1964 Venice Charter, a founding document of modern architectural conservation, holds that new work added to repair a historic building must be distinguishable from the original, so that the building remains an honest record of its past. Conservator Stefano Ferri defends the principle: a repair disguised as original material, he argues, falsifies the historical evidence that a building contains.

Text 2
At the Ise Grand Shrine in Japan, the main sanctuaries are rebuilt from new timber every twenty years, on a site beside the previous buildings and to the same design, a practice that has continued, with interruptions, for more than a thousand years. Historian Keiko Hayashi observes that the shrine's builders locate its authenticity not in any original material, none of which survives, but in the faithful handing down of its form and of the carpenters' skills from one generation to the next.

parts.q:
Based on the texts, how would Hayashi (Text 2) most likely respond to Ferri's view that a repair disguised as original material falsifies a building's historical evidence?
(A) She would argue that the rebuilding at Ise is itself a kind of falsification, since none of the shrine's original material survives.
(B) She would agree with his view and argue that the shrine at Ise should be preserved rather than rebuilt every twenty years.
(C) She would argue that his principle should apply only to buildings whose original material has been entirely lost.
(D) She would point out that his view locates authenticity in original material, which the builders at Ise do not do.
parts.a: (D). Ferri's objection to disguised repairs makes sense only if what a building preserves, and what must not be falsified, is its original material. Hayashi reports a tradition that locates authenticity elsewhere: in form and in inherited skill, with no original material left at all. She would note that his view rests on an assumption the Ise builders do not share. (A) is wrong: Hayashi describes the Ise rebuilding as the builders' way of preserving authenticity, not as falsification. (B) is wrong: nothing in Text 2 suggests Hayashi thinks the shrine should stop being rebuilt; she explains the practice on its own terms. (C) is wrong: neither text proposes limiting Ferri's principle to such buildings, and Hayashi's point is about the assumption behind the principle, not its range.
parts.n: Type: Cross-text connections (exposing an assumption). Rule or move: When Text 2 describes a practice that works on different premises, the likely response is "your view assumes X, which not everyone assumes," not agreement or outright attack. Trap: (A), which judges Ise by Ferri's standard instead of Hayashi's.

mc.stem:
The following text is from Willa Cather's 1918 novel My Ántonia. The narrator, a young boy, is being driven at night across the Nebraska prairie to his grandparents' farm.

Cautiously I slipped from under the buffalo hide, got up on my knees and peered over the side of the wagon. There seemed to be nothing to see; no fences, no creeks or trees, no hills or fields. If there was a road, I could not make it out in the faint starlight. There was nothing but land: not a country at all, but the material out of which countries are made.

parts.q:
Based on the text, what is the narrator's impression of the land?
(A) It seems threatening, because the darkness hides the road that the wagon must follow.
(B) It seems familiar, since it resembles the fields and hills that he had known back home.
(C) It seems raw and unshaped by people, more a substance to be formed than a settled place.
(D) It seems crowded with features that he cannot quite make out in the dim starlight.
parts.a: (C). The narrator sees "no fences, no creeks or trees, no hills or fields," and concludes that this is "not a country at all, but the material out of which countries are made": raw material not yet shaped into a place. (A) is wrong: he cannot make out a road, but the text expresses no fear; his emphasis is on emptiness. (B) is wrong: the absence of "hills or fields" is exactly what strikes him; nothing suggests he has seen land like this before. (D) is wrong: the problem is not features he cannot see clearly but that "there seemed to be nothing to see."
parts.n: Type: Central ideas and details (a narrator's impression). Rule or move: Build the answer from the passage's strongest image (here, "the material out of which countries are made") and reject choices that add a feeling the text never names. Trap: (A), which invents fear from the darkness.

mc.stem: The Dutch "tulip mania" of the 1630s, when single tulip bulbs briefly sold for more than a skilled craftsman's yearly income, is often told as the story of a whole society ruined by speculation. Historian Pieter Lans, examining notarial and court records from the period, found few bankruptcies linked to the crash of 1637 and little sign of wider economic harm; most of the trading had been confined to a fairly small circle of merchants and artisans. The legend of general ruin, Lans suggests, owes more to moralizing pamphlets published after the crash than to the crash itself.

parts.q:
Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
(A) A historian's research suggests that the familiar account of the tulip mania greatly exaggerates its effects.
(B) A historian argues that the tulip mania was driven by moralizing pamphlets rather than by speculation.
(C) A historian shows that the crash of 1637 harmed merchants and artisans more than it harmed the rest of Dutch society.
(D) A historian explains how single tulip bulbs came to sell for more than a skilled craftsman's yearly income.
parts.a: (A). The text sets the usual story (a whole society ruined) against Lans's findings (few bankruptcies, little wider harm, trading confined to a small circle) and ends with his explanation of where the exaggerated story came from. The main idea is that the familiar account overstates the mania's effects. (B) is wrong: the pamphlets explain the legend of general ruin, not the mania itself. (C) is wrong: the text implies that trading, and so any losses, stayed within a small circle, but Lans's point is how little harm the crash did overall; (C) turns that background detail into a comparison of harm between groups that the text never measures, and it drops the contrast with the legend of general ruin. (D) is wrong: the high prices are mentioned only as background; the text does not explain how they arose.
parts.n: Type: Central ideas (main idea of a revisionist passage). Rule or move: When a text sets a familiar story against new evidence, the main idea is the correction, stated no more strongly than the evidence allows. Trap: (B), which moves the pamphlets from causing the legend to causing the event.

mc.stem: Many listeners report feeling "chills," a tingling sensation sometimes accompanied by goosebumps, at particular moments in a piece of music. Music psychologist Elena Petrova hypothesizes that chills are triggered mainly by sudden, unexpected changes in the music, such as an abrupt shift in harmony or loudness, rather than by the music's overall emotional character.

parts.q:
Which finding, if true, would most directly support Petrova's hypothesis?
(A) Listeners reported chills more often while hearing sad pieces than while hearing cheerful ones.
(B) Listeners reported chills at abrupt changes in both sad and cheerful pieces but seldom during unchanging stretches.
(C) Listeners who reported chills during a piece rated that piece as more enjoyable than did listeners who reported none.
(D) Listeners reported chills more often during pieces they already knew well than during pieces they had never heard.
parts.a: (B). Petrova sets two possible triggers against each other: abrupt change versus overall emotional character. (B) holds emotional character constant in each direction (sad and cheerful pieces both produced chills) and varies change (chills at abrupt changes, seldom when the music changed little), so it points to change as the trigger. (A) is wrong: a link between chills and sad pieces points to emotional character, the rival explanation. (C) is wrong: enjoyment says nothing about what triggers chills. (D) is wrong: well-known pieces hold fewer surprises for a listener, so more chills during familiar pieces would, if anything, cut against a hypothesis about unexpected changes.
parts.n: Type: Command of evidence, textual (support a hypothesis against a rival). Rule or move: The best support for "A rather than B" varies A while holding B fixed and shows the effect following A. Trap: (D), which sounds like it concerns expectation but actually points the wrong way.

mc.stem:
Linguist Camila Reyes recorded conversations among bilingual Spanish-English speakers in three settings and counted how often speakers switched languages within a single sentence, a practice known as code-switching. Reyes concluded that setting influences code-switching more strongly among younger speakers than among older speakers.

Code-switches per 100 sentences
Setting · Speakers under 30 · Speakers 30 and older
Family meals · 18 · 11
Conversations with friends · 27 · 14
Workplace meetings · 6 · 5

parts.q:
Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Reyes's conclusion?
(A) Speakers under 30 switched languages more often than speakers 30 and older did in every one of the three settings.
(B) Speakers in both age groups switched languages least often in workplace meetings, at 6 and 5 switches per 100 sentences.
(C) Speakers 30 and older switched more often at family meals (11 per 100 sentences) than younger speakers did in workplace meetings (6).
(D) For speakers under 30, the rate ranged from 6 per 100 sentences to 27 across settings; for older speakers, only from 5 to 14.
parts.a: (D). "Setting influences code-switching more strongly among younger speakers" means their rate should vary more from setting to setting. (D) shows this: a spread of 21 (6 to 27) for younger speakers against 9 (5 to 14) for older speakers. (A) is accurate and is the trap: it shows that younger speakers switch more overall, a difference by age, not a difference in how much setting matters. (B) is accurate but shows a pattern the two groups share. (C) is accurate but compares different groups in different settings, which cannot show how strongly setting affects either group.
parts.n: Type: Command of evidence, quantitative (effect of one factor within groups). Rule or move: "X affects group 1 more than group 2" is a claim about spread within each group, so compare the ranges, not the group averages. Trap: (A), a true difference between the groups that does not involve setting.

mc.stem:
Economist Ana Lima offered two groups of concertgoers a choice of season subscriptions. Group 1 chose between a full-season balcony subscription ($90) and a full-season orchestra subscription ($150). Group 2 had the same two options plus a third: a weekdays-only orchestra subscription, also priced at $150.

Participants choosing each option (%)
Option · Group 1 · Group 2
Balcony, full season ($90) · 62 · 31
Orchestra, weekdays only ($150) · not offered · 3
Orchestra, full season ($150) · 38 · 66

Lima found that an option almost no one chose nonetheless changed how participants chose between the other two: ______

parts.q:
Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
(A) the full-season orchestra subscription was the single most popular option in each of the two groups.
(B) a majority of participants in Group 2 chose the balcony subscription, the least expensive option.
(C) the share choosing the full-season orchestra subscription rose from 38% in Group 1 to 66% in Group 2.
(D) the weekdays-only subscription was chosen by fewer participants than any other option offered in either group.
parts.a: (C). The statement needs evidence that adding the weekdays-only option changed choices between the balcony and full-season orchestra subscriptions. (C) supplies it: the full-season orchestra share jumped from 38% to 66% once the third option was added. (A) is wrong: in Group 1 the balcony subscription (62%) was the most popular. (B) is wrong: only 31% of Group 2 chose the balcony. (D) is accurate (3%) but merely restates that almost no one chose the new option; it does not show any change in how the other two were chosen, which is what the colon promises.
parts.n: Type: Command of evidence, quantitative (complete a claim). Rule or move: Read what the colon promises (here, a change in the other two choices) and choose the data that delivers it rather than data that repeats the setup. Trap: (D), true but a restatement of "an option almost no one chose."

mc.stem: Anthropologist Ruth Okafor studied two fishing villages on the same stretch of coast, where boats, gear, and fishing grounds are much alike. In one village, each day's catch is pooled and divided among all households, whatever each boat has caught; in the other, each household keeps its own catch. Okafor found that fishers in the pooling village were more willing to take chances, such as heading for distant, uncertain fishing grounds on days when nearer waters were yielding little. She attributes the difference to the pooling arrangement itself, reasoning that ______

parts.q:
Which choice most logically completes the text?
(A) when catches are shared, a household whose boat comes back empty still receives a portion, so a failed gamble costs it far less.
(B) fishers in the pooling village are more skilled than fishers in the other village and therefore less likely to return empty-handed.
(C) distant fishing grounds reliably yield larger catches than nearer waters do, so taking chances is always the more profitable strategy.
(D) households that keep their own catches must fish close to home every day, which leaves them no time to travel to distant grounds.
parts.a: (A). Okafor explains the difference by the pooling arrangement "itself," so the completion must show how pooling makes risk-taking more attractive. (A) does: pooling cushions a household against a bad day, so a gamble that fails is much less costly. (B) is wrong: it explains the difference by skill, not by the arrangement, and the text stresses how alike the villages are. (C) is wrong: the text calls the distant grounds "uncertain," and even if they paid off reliably, fishers in both villages would benefit, so this would not explain the difference between them. (D) is wrong: nothing in the text says households that keep their catch must fish close to home; that is an invented constraint.
parts.n: Type: Inferences (complete a researcher's reasoning). Rule or move: When the text says what the explanation must rest on ("the pooling arrangement itself"), eliminate every choice that explains the result by something else. Trap: (C), which ignores "uncertain" and would apply equally to both villages.

mc.stem: Louis Daguerre's 1838 photograph of the Boulevard du Temple, a busy street in Paris, shows the boulevard as almost deserted. The only clearly visible people are a man standing with one foot raised while his boots are being polished and the person polishing them. The exposure for the photograph lasted several minutes, so ______

parts.q:
Which choice most logically completes the text?
(A) the photograph must have been taken at an hour when the boulevard was actually empty of traffic.
(B) people and carriages that kept moving left no clear trace, but the two figures stood still long enough to register.
(C) Daguerre must have asked the two figures to hold perfectly still so that they would appear in the finished photograph.
(D) the buildings along the boulevard appear blurred, while the people who passed by appear sharp.
parts.a: (B). A long exposure records only what stays in place long enough; anything that keeps moving is spread too thin across the plate to register. That explains both facts: the busy street looks empty, and the only visible people are two who stood still for a boot polish. (A) is wrong: the text calls the boulevard "a busy street," and the long exposure explains its empty look without assuming it was empty. (C) is wrong: the figures may simply have stood still because of what they were doing; nothing in the text shows Daguerre posed them. (D) is wrong: it reverses the effect of a long exposure; the stationary buildings would be sharp and moving people blurred or invisible.
parts.n: Type: Inferences (cause and effect). Rule or move: Let the stated cause (a long exposure) explain every fact in the text; a completion that needs an extra assumption ("must have asked") is weaker than one that follows from the cause alone. Trap: (A), which explains the empty street by contradicting "a busy street."

mc.stem: Zora Neale Hurston studied anthropology with Franz Boas and collected folklore in Florida and the Caribbean, and this fieldwork shaped her ______ the dialogue in her 1937 novel Their Eyes Were Watching God draws on speech she had carefully recorded in Florida.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
(A) fiction, for example,
(B) fiction for example,
(C) fiction, for example;
(D) fiction; for example,
parts.a: (D). Two independent clauses meet here: "... this fieldwork shaped her fiction" and "the dialogue ... draws on speech she had carefully recorded in Florida." The second is the example, so "for example" belongs to it: a semicolon ends the first clause and a comma follows the introductory "for example." (A) is a comma splice: commas alone cannot join the two independent clauses. (B) fuses the clauses with no punctuation before "for example." (C) attaches "for example" to the first clause, which makes the general claim the example, and leaves the example clause without its signal.
parts.n: Type: Boundaries (conjunctive adverb between independent clauses). Rule or move: With "for example," "however," or "therefore" between two independent clauses, put the semicolon before the word if it introduces the second clause and after it if it belongs to the first; commas alone make a splice. Trap: (C), grammatical in form but pinning the example on the wrong clause.

mc.stem: In the 1940s, Frances Glessner Lee built a series of dollhouse-scale dioramas that reproduce, in minute detail, scenes based on real cases of unexplained death. The tiny, meticulously furnished rooms that Lee built to train homicide ______ are still used in training seminars today.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
(A) investigators,
(B) investigators—
(C) investigators
(D) investigators;
parts.a: (C). The subject of the sentence is the long noun phrase "The tiny, meticulously furnished rooms that Lee built to train homicide investigators," and its verb is "are still used." No punctuation belongs between a subject and its verb, however long the subject. (A) and (B) wrongly separate subject from verb with a single comma or dash (neither is one of a pair setting off an interrupting element). (D) is wrong: a semicolon must join two independent clauses, but "are still used in training seminars today" has no subject of its own.
parts.n: Type: Boundaries (subject and verb). Rule or move: Find the main verb, then cover everything between the subject's head noun and the verb; if no pair of commas or dashes sets off an interrupter, no punctuation goes before the verb. Trap: (A), the comma a reader wants to insert to "breathe" after a long subject.

mc.stem: Florence Price's Symphony in E Minor—which the Chicago Symphony Orchestra premiered in ______ was the first symphony by a Black woman to be performed by a major American orchestra.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
(A) 1933—
(B) 1933,
(C) 1933;
(D) 1933
parts.a: (A). A dash opens the nonessential clause "which the Chicago Symphony Orchestra premiered in 1933," so a matching dash must close it before the main verb "was." (B) is wrong: a comma cannot close an element opened with a dash; the marks must match. (C) is wrong: a semicolon would separate the subject ("Florence Price's Symphony in E Minor") from its verb. (D) is wrong: without a closing mark, the interrupting clause runs into the main clause and the sentence becomes unreadable ("premiered in 1933 was the first symphony").
parts.n: Type: Boundaries (paired punctuation around a nonessential element). Rule or move: A nonessential element is set off by a matching pair: two commas, two dashes, or two parentheses; look back for the opening mark and match it. Trap: (B), because a comma usually closes a "which" clause, but not one opened with a dash.

mc.stem: When Walter Gropius founded the Bauhaus school of art and design in Weimar, Germany, in 1919, he stated its central aim in a founding ______ architects, sculptors, and painters must all return to the crafts.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
(A) manifesto,
(B) manifesto:
(C) manifesto
(D) manifesto, which
parts.a: (B). The first part of the sentence is an independent clause that announces "its central aim," and the second part, also an independent clause, states that aim. A colon is the mark for an independent clause followed by an explanation or elaboration of it. (A) is a comma splice, joining two independent clauses with a comma alone. (C) fuses the two clauses with no punctuation, and the reader first takes "architects" as part of the phrase about the manifesto. (D) makes the second part a relative clause that does not make sense: "which architects, sculptors, and painters must all return to the crafts" has no role for "which" to play.
parts.n: Type: Boundaries (colon after an independent clause). Rule or move: A colon needs a complete sentence before it; what follows can be a list, a phrase, or another sentence that explains or specifies the first ("its central aim" sets up exactly what the colon delivers). Trap: (A), the comma splice that reads naturally aloud.

mc.stem: Lina Bo Bardi's design for the São Paulo Museum of Art, which lifts the galleries above the ground on four massive pillars in order to leave an open public plaza beneath, ______ as a gathering place for the city as much as a home for the museum's collection.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
(A) conceived
(B) being conceived
(C) was conceived
(D) having been conceived
parts.a: (C). The sentence's subject is "Lina Bo Bardi's design," and everything from "which" to "beneath" is a nonessential clause set off by commas. The sentence still needs a main verb, and only "was conceived" is a finite verb that can serve. (A) is wrong: "conceived" without "was" reads as a participle modifying "design," leaving the sentence without a main verb. (B) and (D) are also participles ("being conceived," "having been conceived"), not finite verbs, so they too leave the sentence a fragment.
parts.n: Type: Form, structure, and sense (finite verb). Rule or move: Strip out the nonessential clause and read the skeleton ("Bo Bardi's design ______ as a gathering place"); if it has no finite verb, the blank must supply one. Trap: (A), which sounds complete because "conceived" can be a past-tense verb, but here it needs "was."

mc.stem: Before she studied architecture in London, Zaha Hadid earned a degree in mathematics in Beirut. Drawn to geometry throughout her career, ______

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
(A) the sweeping, fluid curves of her buildings are often traced back by critics to that early training.
(B) her buildings' sweeping, fluid curves are often traced to that early training.
(C) that early training is often seen by critics in the sweeping, fluid curves of her many buildings.
(D) Hadid designed buildings whose sweeping, fluid curves are often traced to that early training.
parts.a: (D). "Drawn to geometry throughout her career" describes a person, so the noun that immediately follows the comma must be the person it describes: Hadid. Only (D) begins with "Hadid." (A) makes "the sweeping, fluid curves" the ones drawn to geometry. (B) makes "her buildings' ... curves" the subject; the possessive "her" is not the subject, so the modifier still attaches to the curves. (C) makes "that early training" the thing drawn to geometry throughout her career.
parts.n: Type: Form, structure, and sense (dangling modifier). Rule or move: An introductory modifier describes the grammatical subject that comes right after the comma; ask "who was drawn to geometry?" and demand that noun. Trap: (B), where a possessive ("her") seems to supply the person but is not the subject.

mc.stem: Among the most celebrated features of the Alhambra, the palace complex built by the Nasrid rulers of Granada, ______ the domed ceilings of the Hall of the Two Sisters and the Hall of the Abencerrajes, whose thousands of small, honeycomb-like cells, known as muqarnas, seem to dissolve the ceilings into light.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
(A) is
(B) are
(C) was
(D) being
parts.a: (B). The sentence is inverted: the subject comes after the verb. The subject is "the domed ceilings," which is plural, and the ceilings still exist, so the present-tense plural "are" is correct ("the domed ceilings ... are among the most celebrated features"). (A) and (C) are singular, probably chosen to agree with "the Alhambra" or "complex," which sit inside the opening prepositional phrase and cannot be the subject; (C) is also in the wrong tense for features that exist today. (D) is wrong: "being" is not a finite verb, so it leaves the sentence without a main verb.
parts.n: Type: Form, structure, and sense (agreement in an inverted sentence). Rule or move: When a sentence opens with "Among ..." or "Here is/are ...," flip it around to find the real subject after the verb. Trap: (A), which agrees with a nearby singular noun inside the opening phrase.

mc.stem: The English word "nice" has changed its meaning repeatedly. Borrowed from Old French around 1300, it first meant "foolish," reflecting its origin in the Latin nescius, "ignorant." By the 1500s it had come to mean "precise" or "fussy," a sense that survives in the phrase "a nice distinction." ______ its most familiar modern sense, "pleasant," did not appear until the 1700s.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
(A) Later still,
(B) Meanwhile,
(C) Consequently,
(D) In other words,
parts.a: (A). The text traces the word's meanings in time order (around 1300, the 1500s), and the final sentence adds the latest stage (the 1700s). "Later still" continues that sequence. (B) is wrong: "meanwhile" means at the same time, but the 1700s sense came two centuries after the 1500s one. (C) is wrong: the text does not say the "precise" sense caused the "pleasant" sense. (D) is wrong: the final sentence adds a new meaning; it does not restate the previous one.
parts.n: Type: Transitions (sequence). Rule or move: When a passage is organized by dates, choose the transition that fits the time relation between the two sentences; "meanwhile" means simultaneous, not next. Trap: (B), which sounds like narrative sequence but means "at the same time."

mc.stem: Early in his career, the jazz pianist Thelonious Monk was often dismissed as a player of limited technique; critics pointed to his angular melodies and jarring, dissonant chords as evidence that he simply could not play "correctly." ______ Monk had taken classical piano lessons as a boy, and his dissonances were deliberate choices rather than errors.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
(A) Admittedly,
(B) Similarly,
(C) In reality,
(D) As a result,
parts.a: (C). The second sentence corrects the critics' belief with facts: Monk had classical training, and his dissonances were chosen, not mistakes. "In reality" introduces the truth that the preceding view got wrong. (A) is wrong: "admittedly" concedes a point that cuts against the writer's own position, but the writer has not yet taken a position, and the sentence does not concede anything to the critics; it refutes them. (B) is wrong: the sentence does not describe something similar to the critics' view. (D) is wrong: Monk's training was not a result of the critics' dismissal; it came long before.
parts.n: Type: Transitions (correction). Rule or move: When a sentence reports what people believed and the next sentence gives facts that overturn it, use a correcting transition ("in reality," "in fact"), not a concession. Trap: (A), which sounds contrastive but concedes rather than corrects.

mc.stem: Kintsugi, the Japanese practice of mending broken ceramics with lacquer dusted with powdered gold, makes the history of an object's damage visible rather than concealing it. A bowl repaired in this way is, strictly speaking, less intact than it was before it broke. ______ collectors often value such a bowl more highly than an undamaged one, prizing the golden seams as part of its story.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
(A) Therefore,
(B) Likewise,
(C) In other words,
(D) Even so,
parts.a: (D). The second sentence notes a drawback (the bowl is less intact), and the third reports an outcome that runs against what the drawback would lead one to expect (collectors value it more). "Even so" signals that the outcome holds despite the preceding point. (A) is wrong: being less intact is not a reason to value the bowl more; the relationship is contrast, not cause. (B) is wrong: collectors' esteem is not similar to the bowl's being less intact. (C) is wrong: the third sentence does not restate the second; it says something opposed to what the second implies.
parts.n: Type: Transitions (concession then contrast). Rule or move: Read the sentence before the blank, not just the paragraph's theme; here the immediately preceding sentence is a drawback, so the next sentence's positive outcome needs a contrast. Trap: (A), which fits the paragraph's overall praise of kintsugi but not the sentence it follows.

mc.stem:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Katsushika Hokusai (1760–1849) was a Japanese printmaker and painter.
• Around 1831 he published the woodblock print Under the Wave off Kanagawa, often called The Great Wave.
• The print belongs to his series Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji.
• In the print, Mount Fuji appears small in the distance, framed by the curling crest of an enormous wave.
• The print's deep blues come from Prussian blue, a synthetic pigment first made in Europe.

parts.q:
The student wants to introduce The Great Wave to an audience unfamiliar with Hokusai, emphasizing how the print treats the subject of the series to which it belongs. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish these goals?
(A) Katsushika Hokusai (1760–1849), a Japanese printmaker and painter, used Prussian blue, a synthetic pigment first made in Europe, in The Great Wave.
(B) In The Great Wave (c. 1831), from Japanese printmaker Katsushika Hokusai's series Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji, the mountain appears small in the distance, framed by a huge wave.
(C) In The Great Wave, Mount Fuji appears small in the distance, framed by the curling crest of an enormous wave.
(D) Hokusai's The Great Wave belongs to his series Thirty-Six Views of Mount Fuji, published around 1831.
parts.a: (B). The goals have three parts: identify Hokusai for readers who do not know him, name the series (whose subject is Mount Fuji), and show how the print treats that subject. (B) does all three: it calls Hokusai a Japanese printmaker, names the series, and notes that the mountain appears small, framed by the wave. (A) introduces Hokusai but discusses the pigment, not the treatment of Mount Fuji. (C) describes the treatment but never identifies Hokusai or the series, so an unfamiliar reader would not know that Mount Fuji is the series' subject. (D) names the series but says nothing about how the print treats the mountain and does not explain who Hokusai is.
parts.n: Type: Rhetorical synthesis (multi-part goal). Rule or move: Break the goal into its parts (audience, emphasis, context) and check every choice against each part; "audience unfamiliar with X" means X must be identified. Trap: (C), which nails the emphasis but skips the introduction the audience needs.

mc.stem:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Economists Amal Nasser and Pierre Laurent studied the effect of a waiting period on purchases.
• Participants could buy concert tickets either immediately or only after a mandatory 24-hour wait.
• 64% of participants who could buy immediately bought tickets; 41% of those who had to wait did.
• 17% of immediate buyers later asked for a refund; 5% of buyers who had waited did.

parts.q:
The student wants to present both a cost and a benefit of the waiting period from the sellers' point of view. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
(A) The 24-hour wait lowered the share of participants who bought tickets from 64% to 41%, but it also lowered the share of buyers seeking refunds from 17% to 5%.
(B) The 24-hour wait cut the share of buyers who later asked for a refund from 17% to 5%, a clear sign that the waiting period benefited sellers.
(C) The 24-hour wait reduced ticket purchases from 64% of participants to 41%, a drop that would cost sellers a substantial share of their sales.
(D) Nasser and Laurent compared participants who could buy concert tickets immediately with participants who had to wait 24 hours before buying.
parts.a: (A). For a seller, fewer sales are a cost and fewer refund requests are a benefit. (A) presents both, with the numbers: purchases fell from 64% to 41%, and refund requests fell from 17% to 5%. (B) gives only the benefit. (C) gives only the cost. (D) describes the study's design and reports neither a cost nor a benefit.
parts.n: Type: Rhetorical synthesis (two-part goal). Rule or move: When the goal says "both," eliminate every choice that delivers only one half, however well written. Trap: (C), which frames the cost vividly from the sellers' side but omits the benefit.

mc.stem:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Silbo Gomero is a whistled form of Spanish used on La Gomera, one of the Canary Islands.
• Kuş dili ("bird language") is a whistled form of Turkish used around the village of Kuşköy in northeastern Turkey.
• Both developed in rugged terrain, where whistles carry across deep valleys farther than shouted speech.
• Silbo Gomero has been a required subject in La Gomera's schools since 1999.
• In 2017, UNESCO added Kuş dili to its list of cultural heritage in need of urgent safeguarding.

parts.q:
The student wants to contrast the present-day status of the two whistled languages. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
(A) Both Silbo Gomero and Kuş dili developed in rugged terrain, where whistles carry across deep valleys farther than shouted speech.
(B) Silbo Gomero, a whistled form of Spanish, is used on La Gomera, while Kuş dili, a whistled form of Turkish, is used around Kuşköy.
(C) Silbo Gomero has been a required school subject on La Gomera since 1999, while Kuş dili was placed on UNESCO's urgent-safeguarding list in 2017.
(D) In 2017, UNESCO added Kuş dili, a whistled form of Turkish used around Kuşköy, to its list of heritage in need of urgent safeguarding.
parts.a: (C). "Present-day status" concerns how each language is faring now: Silbo Gomero is taught as a required subject, while Kuş dili is listed as heritage in need of urgent safeguarding. (C) sets those two facts side by side with "while." (A) states a similarity, not a contrast. (B) is the trap: it is a contrast, but of place and base language, not of status. (D) gives the status of only one language, so it cannot contrast the two.
parts.n: Type: Rhetorical synthesis (contrast on a named dimension). Rule or move: When the goal names both a relationship (contrast) and a dimension (present-day status), a choice must match both; a contrast on the wrong dimension fails. Trap: (B), a well-formed contrast about location and language rather than status.

mc.stem: When physicist Heike Kamerlingh Onnes cooled a sample of mercury with liquid helium in 1911, its electrical resistance fell gradually at first and then, at about 4.2 kelvins, dropped abruptly to a value too small for his instruments to detect. Physicists had debated whether a metal's resistance would fade smoothly to zero at absolute zero, level off at some small value, or instead rise as its electrons became fixed in place, but none of these views ______ a sudden collapse at a temperature above absolute zero. The result therefore demanded an explanation that no existing theory could supply.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
(A) precluded
(B) contested
(C) obscured
(D) accommodated
parts.a: (D). 'Accommodated' means 'made room for.' None of the competing views had a place for a sudden drop to zero at a temperature above absolute zero, which is exactly why, as the last sentence says, the result 'demanded an explanation that no existing theory could supply.' (A) is wrong because 'none of these views precluded' a collapse would mean that every view allowed it; a result that all the theories permitted would not have demanded a new explanation, so the phrase says the opposite of what the text needs. (B) is wrong for the same reason: if none of the views 'contested' a sudden collapse, all of them accepted it. (C) is wrong because a theory does not 'obscure' an outcome it fails to predict; the word does not describe any relationship between a theory and a result.
parts.n: Type: Words in context. Rule or move: When the blank follows 'none,' 'neither,' 'not' or 'no,' read the negation into each choice before judging it; the whole phrase, not the word alone, must say what the rest of the text says. Trap: (A) 'precluded' feels right because the theories could not handle the result, but 'none of these views precluded it' means every view allowed it.

mc.stem: A popular claim holds that glass is really a liquid that flows too slowly to notice, which is supposedly why the panes in some centuries-old windows are thicker at the bottom than at the top. Materials scientists regard the claim as ______: calculations based on the viscosity of old window glass indicate that at room temperature it would need far longer than the age of the universe to sag visibly, and the uneven panes are better explained by older glassmaking methods, which produced sheets of uneven thickness that were often installed with the thicker edge down.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
(A) untenable
(B) incomplete
(C) premature
(D) unfalsifiable
parts.a: (A). 'Untenable' means 'impossible to defend.' The colon introduces two reasons the claim fails outright: the glass could not have flowed noticeably in the time available, and a different cause accounts for the thick bottoms. (B) is wrong because 'incomplete' implies that the claim is partly right and needs something added, but the calculations say the proposed flow does not happen at all on any relevant timescale. (C) is wrong because 'premature' implies that the evidence is not yet in; the text presents a calculation and an alternative explanation that already settle the matter. (D) is wrong because 'unfalsifiable' means the claim cannot be tested, yet the text describes exactly such a test: the viscosity calculation checks the claim against evidence and finds it wanting.
parts.n: Type: Words in context. Rule or move: Let the evidence after the colon set the strength of the word; evidence that refutes a claim calls for a word of refutation, not a word of limitation or delay. Trap: (D) 'unfalsifiable' sounds scientific, but a claim that a calculation can refute is by definition falsifiable.

mc.stem:
The following text is adapted from Arthur Conan Doyle's 1887 novel A Study in Scarlet. Sherlock Holmes explains to Dr. Watson why he does not bother to remember facts that are unrelated to his work.
"I consider that a man's brain originally is like a little empty attic, and you have to stock it with such furniture as you choose. A fool takes in all the lumber of every sort that he comes across, so that the knowledge which might be useful to him gets crowded out, or at best is jumbled up with a lot of other things so that he has a difficulty in laying his hands upon it."

parts.q:
As used in the text, what does the word "lumber" most nearly mean?
(A) Heavy material used for building
(B) Miscellaneous clutter
(C) Clumsy or awkward movement
(D) Carefully chosen supplies
parts.a: (B). The fool 'takes in all the lumber of every sort that he comes across,' and this lumber crowds out or buries 'the knowledge which might be useful to him.' Holmes is using the older sense of the word: odds and ends that are stored away but serve no purpose, that is, clutter. (A) is wrong because, although the attic-and-furniture image might suggest building material, nothing is built from this lumber; it only takes up space. (C) is wrong because it is the sense of the verb 'to lumber' (to move heavily), while here the word is a noun, something the fool 'takes in.' (D) is wrong because it reverses Holmes's point: the fool takes in things 'of every sort,' without choosing, and careful choosing is what Holmes recommends instead.
parts.n: Type: Words in context (meaning of a word as used). Rule or move: For a familiar word in an older text, set aside the everyday meaning and define the word by what it does in the sentence; here, the lumber crowds out useful knowledge. Trap: (A), the everyday sense of 'wood for building,' which the attic-and-furniture metaphor makes feel natural.

mc.stem: Historians have long credited the Erie Canal, completed in 1825, with making New York City the dominant port in the United States. In a recent study, economic historian Ruth Adair ______ that account: she agrees that the canal greatly strengthened the city's position, but she argues that New York had already pulled ahead of rivals such as Philadelphia and Boston in the decade before the canal opened, thanks largely to its auction system for imported goods and to the regularly scheduled transatlantic packet ships that began sailing from its harbor in 1818.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
(A) reiterates
(B) repudiates
(C) qualifies
(D) corroborates
parts.a: (C). To 'qualify' a claim is to accept it only in a limited form. Adair accepts that the canal 'greatly strengthened the city's position' but denies that it explains how New York became dominant, since the city 'had already pulled ahead' before the canal opened; she limits the account rather than accepting or rejecting it whole. (A) is wrong because 'reiterates' would mean she simply repeats the account, but she offers a competing explanation for the city's lead. (B) is wrong because 'repudiates' would mean she rejects the account outright, yet she 'agrees that the canal greatly strengthened the city's position.' (D) is wrong because 'corroborates' would mean she supplies evidence confirming the account; her evidence, the auction system and the packet ships of the 1810s, points to causes other than the canal.
parts.n: Type: Words in context. Rule or move: 'Agrees that ... but argues that ...' after a colon is the signature of 'qualify,' a common word in its less common sense of 'limit' or 'modify.' Trap: (D) 'corroborates,' chosen by students who notice only that Adair agrees the canal mattered.

mc.stem:
The following text is adapted from George Eliot's 1871–72 novel Middlemarch.
Miss Brooke had that kind of beauty which seems to be thrown into relief by poor dress. Her hand and wrist were so finely formed that she could wear sleeves not less bare of style than those in which the Blessed Virgin appeared to Italian painters; and her profile as well as her stature and bearing seemed to gain the more dignity from her plain garments, which by the side of provincial fashion gave her the impressiveness of a fine quotation from the Bible,—or from one of our elder poets,—in a paragraph of to-day's newspaper. She was usually spoken of as being remarkably clever, but with the addition that her sister Celia had more common-sense.

parts.q:
Which choice best describes the function of the final sentence in the text as a whole?
(A) It suggests that Miss Brooke's preference for plain clothing stems from an intelligence that others in her community have failed to recognize.
(B) It reveals that the admiration the narrator expresses for Miss Brooke's appearance is not shared by the people who know her.
(C) It shifts attention from Miss Brooke to Celia, indicating that Celia's practical judgment will matter more to the story than her sister's cleverness.
(D) It reports how Miss Brooke is generally regarded, pairing praise of her intellect with a reservation that favors her sister in one respect.
parts.a: (D). The first two sentences are the narrator's own description of Miss Brooke's looks. The final sentence turns to how 'she was usually spoken of': as 'remarkably clever,' but always 'with the addition that her sister Celia had more common-sense.' It reports common opinion, and that opinion attaches a reservation to its praise, one in which Celia comes out ahead on a single point. (A) is wrong because the sentence draws no link between Miss Brooke's dress and her intelligence, and others do recognize her cleverness: they call her 'remarkably clever.' (B) is wrong because the final sentence concerns her intellect and common sense, not her appearance, so it says nothing about whether others share the narrator's view of her looks. (C) is wrong because Celia appears only as a point of comparison; nothing in the text predicts her importance to the story.
parts.n: Type: Text structure and purpose (function of a sentence). Rule or move: Ask what the sentence does that the ones before it did not; here it moves from the narrator's view to public opinion, and from praise to a qualified judgment. Trap: (A), which invents a cause-and-effect link between the plain dress of the first sentences and the cleverness of the last.

mc.stem: During the Crimean War (1853–1856), Florence Nightingale compiled records showing that far more British soldiers died in army hospitals from infectious diseases than from wounds received in battle. Doubting that columns of figures alone would move the officials and the public she hoped to persuade, she published the data in 1858 as circular diagrams divided into wedges, one for each month. The area of each wedge was proportional to the number of deaths that month, and shading distinguished the causes. The areas representing deaths from preventable disease dwarfed those representing deaths from wounds, so that even a reader with no patience for statistics could not miss the pattern.

parts.q:
Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
(A) To argue that Nightingale's diagrams conveyed the death figures more accurately than tables of the same figures could have
(B) To explain how Nightingale presented her data in a form meant to overcome an obstacle she expected in persuading her audience
(C) To describe how the causes of death among British soldiers during the Crimean War changed from one month to the next
(D) To show that Nightingale's diagrams convinced the government to adopt reforms that ended deaths from disease in army hospitals
parts.a: (B). The text names an obstacle Nightingale expected (her audience would not be moved by 'columns of figures alone'), describes the form she chose to get around it (wedges whose areas show deaths by cause), and says why that form worked ('even a reader with no patience for statistics could not miss the pattern'). (A) is wrong because the text never claims the diagrams were more accurate; they present the same data in a more persuasive form. (C) is wrong because, although each wedge stands for a month, the text says nothing about how the causes of death changed over time; the months are mentioned only as part of how the diagrams were built. (D) is wrong because the text does not mention any reforms, so it cannot show that the diagrams produced them.
parts.n: Type: Text structure and purpose (main purpose). Rule or move: A main-purpose answer must cover the whole text; a choice that describes one detail, or that claims an outcome the text never reaches, fails. Trap: (D), because students who know the history read the diagrams' later influence into a text that stops before any result.

mc.stem:
Text 1
Polylactic acid (PLA), a plastic made from sugars in plants such as corn, is increasingly used for cups, cutlery, and food packaging. Because microorganisms can break PLA down into water and carbon dioxide, packaging engineer Dana Whitlock argues that PLA packaging, unlike conventional plastic packaging, which can persist for centuries, would disappear within months of being thrown away.

Text 2
Chemist Omar Reyes notes that PLA breaks down reliably only under the conditions found in industrial composting facilities, where temperatures near 58°C soften the plastic enough for microbes to attack it. In soil or seawater at ordinary temperatures, PLA can remain largely intact for years. Reyes regards PLA as a genuine improvement where industrial composting is available, but he cautions that its benefits depend less on the material itself than on the waste systems that receive it.

parts.q:
Based on the texts, how would Reyes (Text 2) most likely respond to Whitlock's argument in Text 1?
(A) By rejecting it, on the grounds that PLA persists in soil and seawater for as long as conventional plastics do
(B) By endorsing it, while adding that PLA breaks down even more quickly in seawater than in industrial composting facilities
(C) By accepting it in part, while noting that it holds only if discarded PLA reaches conditions that not all disposal routes provide
(D) By challenging it, on the grounds that it ignores the environmental costs of growing the crops from which PLA is made
parts.a: (C). Reyes calls PLA 'a genuine improvement where industrial composting is available,' so he accepts part of Whitlock's argument, but he points out that PLA breaks down reliably 'only' in such facilities and 'can remain largely intact for years' in soil or seawater. Whitlock's promise that PLA packaging 'would disappear within months' therefore holds only if the packaging reaches an industrial composter, which is why Reyes says its benefits depend on 'the waste systems that receive it.' (A) is wrong because Reyes does not reject the argument outright, and he says PLA can last 'for years,' not as long as conventional plastics, which Text 1 says can persist 'for centuries.' (B) is wrong because Text 2 says the opposite: PLA stays largely intact in seawater. (D) is wrong because Text 2 says nothing about growing crops; Reyes's reservation concerns disposal.
parts.n: Type: Cross-text connections. Rule or move: When Text 2 says a claim holds 'where' or 'only if' something is true, its response is conditional agreement: it accepts the claim but names the unstated assumption the claim depends on. Trap: (A), the flat-disagreement choice, which stretches Reyes's 'for years' into 'as long as conventional plastics.'

mc.stem:
Text 1
In September 1928, bacteriologist Alexander Fleming noticed that a mold contaminating one of his culture plates had killed the bacteria growing near it. Popular histories often treat this observation as the moment the antibiotic era began: a single flash of insight that, once it occurred, set medicine on a new course.

Text 2
Fleming's observation was indispensable, and he published it in 1929. But he could not purify the unstable substance he called penicillin, and he largely turned to other work. Only in 1940 did a team at the University of Oxford, led by Howard Florey and Ernst Chain, produce enough of it to show that it could cure infections in mice, and only with the large-scale production methods developed during the Second World War did penicillin become widely available. The antibiotic era, on this view, was not discovered in 1928 so much as built over the following fifteen years.

parts.q:
Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely characterize the account described in Text 1?
(A) As right about the importance of Fleming's observation but misleading in implying that the observation was enough, by itself, to transform medicine
(B) As wrong to present Fleming's observation as a product of chance rather than of a deliberate search for substances that kill bacteria
(C) As exaggerating Fleming's contribution, since the Oxford team would probably have discovered penicillin's effects even without his published observation
(D) As essentially accurate, since the later work at Oxford and during the war merely applied what Fleming's observation had already established
parts.a: (A). The author of Text 2 calls Fleming's observation 'indispensable,' agreeing with Text 1 that it mattered, but rejects the idea that it began the antibiotic era by itself: purification, the Oxford experiments of 1940, and wartime mass production were all still needed, so the era 'was not discovered in 1928 so much as built over the following fifteen years.' That challenges Text 1's picture of 'a single flash of insight' that 'set medicine on a new course.' (B) is wrong because Text 2 never discusses whether Fleming's observation was accidental or planned. (C) is wrong because calling the observation 'indispensable' means the later work depended on it; Text 2 does not suggest the Oxford team could have done without it. (D) is wrong because Text 2 presents the later work as essential steps that Fleming himself could not accomplish, not as a mere application of something already established.
parts.n: Type: Cross-text connections. Rule or move: Separate what Text 2 grants ('indispensable') from what it denies (that the observation was sufficient); the right answer names both halves. Trap: (C), which turns Text 2's point that later work was necessary into a claim that Fleming's work was unnecessary.

mc.stem:
The following text is adapted from Jack London's 1908 short story "To Build a Fire." A man is traveling alone on foot through the Yukon Territory on an extremely cold day.
The trouble with him was that he was without imagination. He was quick and alert in the things of life, but only in the things, and not in the significances.
