Fifty degrees below zero meant eighty odd degrees of frost. Such fact impressed him as being cold and uncomfortable, and that was all. It did not lead him to meditate upon his frailty as a creature of temperature, and upon man's frailty in general, able only to live within certain narrow limits of heat and cold; and from there on it did not lead him to the conjectural field of immortality and man's place in the universe.

parts.q:
Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
(A) The man misjudges the temperature, believing the cold to be less severe than it actually is.
(B) The man regards the cold as a practical discomfort without considering what it reveals about human vulnerability.
(C) The man is too preoccupied with questions about humanity's place in the universe to prepare properly for the cold.
(D) The man understands that the cold could kill him but decides that the risk of traveling is worth taking.
parts.a: (B). The narrator says the man is alert to 'the things of life' but not to 'the significances.' The fact of fifty below 'impressed him as being cold and uncomfortable, and that was all'; it 'did not lead him to meditate upon his frailty as a creature of temperature,' or upon humans' ability to live only 'within certain narrow limits of heat and cold.' (A) is wrong because nothing in the text suggests that the man misjudges how cold it is; the narrator faults him not for underestimating the cold but for grasping it only as 'cold and uncomfortable,' so his failure is one of interpretation, not measurement. (C) is wrong because it reverses the text: the cold 'did not lead him' to questions about 'man's place in the universe.' (D) is wrong because the cold struck him as merely 'cold and uncomfortable, and that was all,' so he never saw a deadly risk to weigh and accept.
parts.n: Type: Central ideas and details. Rule or move: In a character sketch, find the narrator's diagnosis (here, 'without imagination ... not in the significances') and choose the answer that restates it, not one that names a different flaw. Trap: (A), which confuses not grasping what the cold means with not knowing how cold it is.

mc.stem: Nickel-titanium alloys can be bent and then return to their original shape, a property that makes them useful in medical stents and eyeglass frames. With repeated bending, however, the alloys gradually lose some of this ability. Materials scientist Ines Okafor and colleagues hypothesize that the decline is caused mainly not by the buildup of microscopic cracks, as is often assumed, but by small regions of the alloy that become stuck in the crystal structure the metal adopts when it is deformed and never change back.

parts.q:
Which finding, if true, would most directly support Okafor and colleagues' hypothesis?
(A) Samples that had been bent many thousands of times contained both more microscopic cracks and more stuck regions than did samples that had been bent only a few times.
(B) Samples that had been bent many thousands of times recovered their original shape less completely than samples that had been bent only a few times.
(C) Samples that were bent under heavy loads developed microscopic cracks sooner than samples that were bent under light loads did.
(D) Heating heavily used samples enough to return stuck regions to their original structure, without repairing any cracks, restored most of their lost shape recovery.
parts.a: (D). The hypothesis says stuck regions, not cracks, mainly cause the decline. A treatment that undoes the stuck regions while leaving the cracks in place isolates that cause: if it restores most of the lost ability, the stuck regions were responsible for most of the loss. (A) is wrong because it shows cracks and stuck regions increasing together, which fits the crack explanation just as well; it cannot tell the two explanations apart. (B) is wrong because it merely restates the decline the researchers are trying to explain, without bearing on its cause. (C) is wrong because it concerns how quickly cracks form under different loads, not whether cracks or stuck regions are responsible for the lost shape recovery.
parts.n: Type: Command of evidence (textual: support a hypothesis). Rule or move: When a hypothesis says 'caused by X rather than Y,' the strongest support changes X while holding Y fixed; evidence in which X and Y rise together cannot decide between them. Trap: (A), which mentions the stuck regions but cannot rule out the cracks.

mc.stem: In Mary Shelley's 1818 novel Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus, Victor Frankenstein's scientific ambition is bound up with a desire to be honored: he imagines his success chiefly in terms of what those who would benefit from it would owe him.

parts.q:
Which quotation from Frankenstein most effectively illustrates the claim?
(A) "Life and death appeared to me ideal bounds, which I should first break through, and pour a torrent of light into our dark world."
(B) "I had worked hard for nearly two years, for the sole purpose of infusing life into an inanimate body. For this I had deprived myself of rest and health."
(C) "A new species would bless me as its creator and source; many happy and excellent natures would owe their being to me. No father could claim the gratitude of his child so completely as I should deserve theirs."
(D) "Learn from me, if not by my precepts, at least by my example, how dangerous is the acquirement of knowledge, and how much happier that man is who believes his native town to be the world, than he who aspires to become greater than his nature will allow."
parts.a: (C). The claim has two parts: Victor pictures his success in terms of what its beneficiaries would owe him, and this reflects a wish to be honored. In this quotation the new species 'would bless me,' natures 'would owe their being to me,' and he 'should deserve' more gratitude than any father; the success is described entirely as a debt owed to Victor. (A) is wrong because, although it shows his ambition, it pictures his success as a gift to the world ('a torrent of light into our dark world'), not as something owed to him. (B) is wrong because it shows his dedication and what the work cost him, not what he expected others to owe him. (D) is wrong because it is a warning against ambition, spoken in hindsight; it says nothing about the honor he once hoped for.
parts.n: Type: Command of evidence (textual: illustrate a claim with a quotation). Rule or move: Mark the specific part of the claim (here, what the beneficiaries 'would owe him') and pick the quotation that shows that part; a quotation that fits the topic but not the specific claim is wrong. Trap: (A), which shows ambition, the claim's topic, but pictures the reward as light for the world rather than a debt to Victor.

mc.stem:
Anode capacity before and after 500 charge-discharge cycles
Anode · Initial capacity (mAh/g) · Capacity after 500 cycles (mAh/g) · Capacity retained (%)
Graphite only · 350 · 322 · 92
Graphite + 5% silicon · 450 · 396 · 88
Graphite + 10% silicon · 540 · 432 · 80
Graphite + 20% silicon · 700 · 406 · 58

Adding silicon to the graphite anodes of lithium-ion batteries raises the amount of charge the anodes can store, but silicon swells and cracks as a battery charges and discharges, so silicon-rich anodes lose capacity faster over repeated cycles. Battery engineer Tomás Varga argues that the usual way of reporting this loss, as a percentage of initial capacity, understates the practical value of silicon: in his team's tests, even the anode that lost the largest share of its initial capacity still outperformed the graphite-only anode after 500 cycles.

parts.q:
Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Varga's claim?
(A) After 500 cycles, the 20% silicon anode, despite retaining only 58% of its initial capacity, stored 406 mAh/g, versus 322 mAh/g for graphite alone.
(B) The 20% silicon anode retained only 58% of its initial capacity after 500 cycles, the lowest share of any anode tested, whereas the graphite-only anode retained 92%.
(C) The 20% silicon anode had an initial capacity of 700 mAh/g, twice the initial capacity of 350 mAh/g recorded for the graphite-only anode in the tests.
(D) After 500 cycles, the 10% silicon anode stored 432 mAh/g, which was more than the 406 mAh/g stored after 500 cycles by the 20% silicon anode.
parts.a: (A). Varga's claim is that the anode that lost 'the largest share' of its capacity, the 20% silicon anode at 58% retained, 'still outperformed the graphite-only anode after 500 cycles.' Only this choice pairs that anode's low percentage with its actual capacity after cycling, 406 mAh/g, and compares it with graphite's 322 mAh/g. (B) is wrong because, although accurate, it reports only percentages, the very measure Varga says understates silicon's value; on its own it makes the silicon anode look worse. (C) is wrong because it compares capacities before any cycling, while the claim concerns performance after 500 cycles. (D) is wrong because it compares two silicon anodes with each other; the claim is about the 20% silicon anode's performance relative to graphite.
parts.n: Type: Command of evidence (quantitative). Rule or move: When every choice is true of the table, pick the one that matches each element of the claim: which item, compared with what, measured when, and in which units. Trap: (B), which is accurate and prominent in the table but uses the percentage measure the claim calls misleading.

mc.stem:
Patients whose monthly migraine days fell by at least half (%)
Group · After 4 weeks · After 12 weeks
Placebo · 11 · 19
Low dose · 24 · 51
High dose · 45 · 53

Neurologist Priya Anand and colleagues tested two doses of an experimental drug for preventing migraines. For each group, they recorded the percentage of patients whose number of monthly migraine days fell by at least half, a common threshold for a meaningful response. Anand concluded that the higher dose mainly makes the drug work sooner rather than making it work better: ______

parts.q:
Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
(A) at both 4 weeks and 12 weeks, the percentage of patients meeting the threshold was higher in the high-dose group than in the placebo group.
(B) the percentage of patients meeting the threshold rose between 4 weeks and 12 weeks in all three groups, including the placebo group.
(C) after 12 weeks, the percentage of patients meeting the threshold in the low-dose group was more than twice that in the placebo group.
(D) the high-dose group's advantage over the low-dose group was 21 percentage points after 4 weeks but only 2 percentage points after 12 weeks.
parts.a: (D). The conclusion compares the two doses over time: if the higher dose makes the drug work 'sooner' but not 'better,' it should lead the low dose early and the two should end up close together. The table shows exactly that: 45% versus 24% after 4 weeks (21 points apart) but 53% versus 51% after 12 weeks (2 points apart). (A) is wrong because it compares the high dose with placebo, which shows that the drug works but says nothing about how the two doses differ. (B) is wrong because a rise in every group, placebo included, says nothing about the difference between the doses. (C) is wrong because it compares the low dose with placebo; like (A), it shows the drug is effective but not how the higher dose differs from the lower one.
parts.n: Type: Command of evidence (quantitative). Rule or move: Identify the exact comparison the claim makes (high dose versus low dose, early versus late) and discard true statements that compare anything else, such as drug versus placebo. Trap: (A), which is true and flattering to the high dose, but a comparison with placebo cannot show whether the higher dose works better or only sooner than the lower one.

mc.stem: In 1969, pharmacologist Tu Youyou joined a Chinese government project to find new treatments for malaria. Her team tested hundreds of extracts of herbs used in traditional medicine. Extracts of sweet wormwood (Artemisia annua) sometimes suppressed the malaria parasite in mice but often failed to, whether the team had prepared them with hot water, as most herbal remedies are prepared, or with other heated solvents. Tu then noticed that a fourth-century medical text by Ge Hong told readers to soak a handful of sweet wormwood in water, wring out the juice, and drink it, a preparation that called for no heating at all. Tu's interest in this instruction suggests that she suspected ______

parts.q:
Which choice most logically completes the text?
(A) the active compound dissolves more readily in water than in the other solvents her team had used.
(B) the heat used in her team's extraction methods could be damaging the herb's active compound.
(C) the sweet wormwood available to Ge Hong contained more of the active compound than modern plants do.
(D) the malaria parasites of Ge Hong's time were more vulnerable to the herb than modern parasites are.
parts.a: (B). The text sets up a single contrast between the team's method and Ge Hong's: the team prepared its extracts 'with hot water' or 'with other heated solvents,' while Ge Hong's preparation 'called for no heating at all.' The team's extracts worked only sometimes, so an instruction that avoids heat would catch Tu's attention if she suspected that heat was destroying some of the active substance. (A) is wrong because the team's hot-water extracts were as unreliable as the others, so water itself cannot be what distinguishes Ge Hong's method. (C) and (D) are wrong because the text gives no information about differences between ancient and modern plants or parasites, and neither possibility would explain why Tu focused on how the herb was soaked.
parts.n: Type: Inferences. Rule or move: Find the one variable that separates the method that worked from the one that did not (here temperature, since both methods used water) and complete the text with that variable. Trap: (A), which fixes on 'water' in Ge Hong's instruction without noticing that the team also used water, only heated.

mc.stem: When a drop of coffee dries on a countertop, it leaves a dark ring at its edge. The drop's edge stays pinned in place as the liquid evaporates, and because evaporation is fastest at the edge, liquid flows outward from the center to replace what is lost there, carrying suspended particles with it. Researchers have found that drops of certain other liquids also evaporate fastest at their pinned edges, but in those drops a second flow runs along the drop's surface from the edge back toward the center, and the particles end up spread fairly evenly. These findings suggest that a ring forms ______

parts.q:
Which choice most logically completes the text?
(A) whenever evaporation is faster at a drop's edge than at its center, regardless of what other flows occur in the drop.
(B) only in drops that contain more suspended particles than drops of the other liquids do.
(C) when the particles carried outward toward the edge are not carried back by a flow toward the center.
(D) because the edges of coffee drops evaporate faster than the edges of drops of the other liquids do.
parts.a: (C). In both kinds of drops, evaporation is fastest at the pinned edge and liquid flows outward, carrying particles with it, yet only the drops without a return flow leave a ring. The outward flow alone therefore does not guarantee a ring; a ring forms when nothing carries the particles back toward the center. (A) is wrong because the other liquids also evaporate fastest at their edges and still leave no ring, so faster evaporation at the edge is not enough. (B) is wrong because the text never compares how many particles the drops contain; the difference it identifies is the second flow. (D) is wrong because the text gives no comparison of evaporation rates between liquids; it says only that both kinds of drops evaporate fastest at their edges.
parts.n: Type: Inferences. Rule or move: When two cases share a factor but differ in outcome, the shared factor is not sufficient; the inference must name the factor that differs. Trap: (A), which treats the outward flow, a condition both kinds of drops share, as enough to produce a ring.

mc.stem: In May 1952, Rosalind Franklin's Photo 51—an X-ray diffraction image of DNA made at King's College London by Raymond Gosling, a doctoral student working under Franklin's supervision______ showed the X-shaped pattern that indicates a helical structure. The image later helped James Watson and Francis Crick build their model of the molecule.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
(A) supervision,
(B) supervision—
(C) supervision;
(D) supervision
parts.a: (B). The dash after 'Photo 51' opens a long nonessential element that identifies the photograph, and an element opened with a dash must be closed with a dash before the sentence resumes with its verb, 'showed.' That dash also ends the shorter phrase about Gosling nested inside the element. (A) is wrong because a comma would close only the inner phrase ('a doctoral student ...') and leave the element opened by the dash unclosed; the two marks that set off one element must match. (C) is wrong because a semicolon joins independent clauses, and here it would separate the subject, 'Photo 51,' from its verb, 'showed.' (D) is wrong because with no punctuation the nonessential element runs straight into the main verb and the dash is never closed.
parts.n: Type: Boundaries (nonessential elements). Rule or move: Find the mark that opened the element (dash, comma or parenthesis) and close with the same mark, however long or nested the element is. Trap: (A), because the nearest opening mark is the comma before 'a doctoral student,' and students close that one instead of the dash.

mc.stem: Physicists studying radioactive substances around 1900 found that the radiation those substances gave off was not all of one kind. By the early 1900s, they had distinguished three types: alpha rays, which could be stopped by a sheet of paper______ beta rays, which could pass through thin sheets of aluminum; and gamma rays, which were far more penetrating than either.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
(A) paper;
(B) paper,
(C) paper:
(D) paper—
parts.a: (A). The colon introduces a list of three items, and each item contains its own comma ('alpha rays, which ...'). When list items contain internal commas, semicolons separate the items so the reader can tell where each one ends, and the text already uses a semicolon between the second and third items. (B) is wrong because a comma here would look like the commas inside the items, blurring where the first item ends and breaking the pattern the later semicolon sets. (C) is wrong because the list has already been introduced by a colon; a second colon would wrongly signal that what follows explains 'a sheet of paper.' (D) is wrong because a single dash would set off the rest of the sentence as an interruption or explanation of the first item instead of continuing the series.
parts.n: Type: Boundaries (lists with internal commas). Rule or move: If any item in a series contains a comma, separate all the items with semicolons, and make the missing separator match the ones the text already uses. Trap: (B), the comma, which is how a simple list is punctuated.

mc.stem: Alice Ball, a chemist at the College of Hawaii who found a way to make oil from the seeds of the chaulmoogra tree injectable, and therefore far more useful in treating Hansen's disease______ did not live to see her method widely adopted. She died in 1916, at the age of twenty-four, and for years afterward the technique was credited to a colleague who continued her work.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
(A) disease—
(B) disease;
(C) disease,
(D) disease
parts.a: (C). The comma after 'Alice Ball' opens a long nonessential element identifying her, and that element must be closed with a matching comma before the verb 'did not live.' The comma before 'and therefore far more useful' opens a second interrupting phrase that ends at the same point, so one comma closes both. (A) is wrong because a dash cannot close an element that was opened with a comma; the marks must match. (B) is wrong because a semicolon would separate the subject, 'Alice Ball,' from its verb, and the words before it do not form an independent clause. (D) is wrong because with no punctuation the long element runs into 'did not live' and is never closed.
parts.n: Type: Boundaries (nonessential elements). Rule or move: When a long interruption separates a subject from its verb, strip it out ('Alice Ball ... did not live') and close it with the mark that opened it. Trap: (D), because after so many commas students hesitate to add another and forget that the element opened after 'Ball' still needs closing.

mc.stem: Having spent nearly three decades refining a series of marine timekeepers, the fourth of which lost only about five seconds during a voyage from England to Jamaica______ John Harrison still had to appeal to King George III before Parliament granted him a substantial further reward in 1773. The delay reflected, in part, the preference of some officials for an astronomical method of finding longitude at sea.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
(A) Jamaica;
(B) Jamaica:
(C) Jamaica.
(D) Jamaica,
parts.a: (D). Everything before the blank is an introductory phrase ('Having spent ...') with a nonessential clause ('the fourth of which ...') nested inside it. None of it is an independent clause, because 'having spent' is not a main verb. The phrase describes John Harrison, so a comma separates it from the main clause that begins with his name. (A) is wrong because a semicolon must join two independent clauses, and the words before it are only a phrase. (B) is wrong because a colon must follow an independent clause. (C) is wrong because a period would leave the opening phrase as a sentence fragment.
parts.n: Type: Boundaries (introductory phrases). Rule or move: Before choosing a semicolon, colon or period, check that the words before the blank could stand alone as a sentence; a long '-ing' phrase cannot, however complete it feels. Trap: (A), because the phrase is long and contains its own 'which' clause, so it feels like a complete clause.

mc.stem: The first transatlantic telegraph cable, completed in 1858, stopped working within weeks. Among the changes that allowed a cable laid in 1866 to succeed where the earlier one had failed ______ a thicker copper conductor, heavier insulation, and the use of a single ship, the Great Eastern, large enough to carry the entire length of cable.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
(A) was
(B) has been
(C) were
(D) is
parts.a: (C). The sentence is inverted: the phrase 'Among the changes ... had failed' comes first, and the subject follows the verb. That subject is a compound, 'a thicker copper conductor, heavier insulation, and the use of a single ship,' so it takes the plural verb 'were,' and the past tense fits events completed in 1866. (A) is wrong because 'was' is singular; it would agree with only one item in the series, such as 'a thicker copper conductor.' (B) is wrong because 'has been' is singular and also shifts to the present perfect for events long finished. (D) is wrong because 'is' is singular.
parts.n: Type: Form, structure, and sense (subject-verb agreement). Rule or move: In a sentence that opens with 'Among ...,' 'Here ...' or 'There ...,' the subject comes after the verb; find it and count it. Trap: (A) 'was,' chosen by students who match the verb to 'the earlier one' or to the first singular noun after the blank.

mc.stem: In the early 1950s, polio paralyzed thousands of children in the United States each year, and a vaccine was urgently sought. Tested in 1954 in a field trial involving more than a million schoolchildren, ______

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
(A) the vaccine developed by Jonas Salk was declared safe and effective in April 1955.
(B) Jonas Salk learned in April 1955 that his vaccine had been declared safe and effective.
(C) researchers announced in April 1955 that Jonas Salk's vaccine was safe and effective.
(D) April 1955 brought the announcement that Jonas Salk's vaccine was safe and effective.
parts.a: (A). An introductory modifier describes whatever noun immediately follows it. The thing 'tested in 1954 in a field trial' was the vaccine, so the main clause must begin with 'the vaccine developed by Jonas Salk.' (B) is wrong because it makes Jonas Salk the thing that was tested. (C) is wrong because it says the researchers were tested in the trial. (D) is wrong because it says April 1955 was tested; the vaccine appears only later in the clause.
parts.n: Type: Form, structure, and sense (modifier placement). Rule or move: Ask 'who or what was tested?' (or whatever the modifier says) and choose the answer whose first noun is that thing. Trap: (C), which reads like natural news reporting but puts 'researchers' where the vaccine must go.

mc.stem: Wilhelm Röntgen announced his discovery of X-rays in December 1895, and within weeks physicians in Europe and North America were using the rays to locate bullets and examine broken bones. By the time Röntgen received the first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901, X-ray machines ______ fixtures in many large hospitals.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
(A) have become
(B) had become
(C) become
(D) will have become
parts.a: (B). 'By the time' followed by a past event ('received ... in 1901') calls for the past perfect: the machines' becoming fixtures in those hospitals was complete before that past moment, so 'had become' is correct. (A) is wrong because the present perfect 'have become' connects an action to the present, not to a moment in 1901. (C) is wrong because the present tense 'become' clashes with the past-tense frame of the sentence. (D) is wrong because the future perfect 'will have become' describes something completed before a future moment, and 1901 is in the past.
parts.n: Type: Form, structure, and sense (verb tense). Rule or move: 'By the time' plus a past-tense event signals the past perfect (had + past participle) for the earlier action. Trap: (A) 'have become,' which sounds natural but ties the action to the present rather than to 1901.

mc.stem: Nuclear fusion, the process that powers the Sun, has long been promoted as a potential source of abundant energy. In December 2022, researchers at the National Ignition Facility in California reported the first controlled fusion experiment to release more energy than the laser light delivered to its target. ______ the lasers themselves drew far more energy from the electrical grid than the reaction released, so the result was a scientific milestone rather than a demonstration of a practical power source.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
(A) Moreover,
(B) For this reason,
(C) In other words,
(D) Still,
parts.a: (D). The second sentence reports an achievement; the third sets a limiting fact against it (the lasers used far more energy from the grid than the reaction produced) and concludes that the result, though a milestone, is not yet a practical power source. 'Still' introduces a point that pushes back against what came before without denying it. (A) is wrong because 'Moreover' adds a point in the same direction, but the grid energy undercuts the achievement rather than adding to it. (B) is wrong because the achievement did not cause the lasers to draw so much energy; there is no cause-and-effect relationship. (C) is wrong because the third sentence does not restate the second; it introduces a different comparison, energy drawn from the grid rather than laser energy delivered to the target.
parts.n: Type: Transitions. Rule or move: Before looking at the choices, decide whether the new sentence supports, restates, results from or pushes back against the one before it. Trap: (C) 'In other words,' because both sentences compare energy in with energy out, but they measure the energy going in at different points.

mc.stem: Some bacteria survive antibiotic treatment without being genetically resistant to the drug: if the survivors are allowed to multiply, their descendants are killed by it as readily as ever. ______ these so-called persister cells enter a dormant state in which the processes that most antibiotics attack, such as building cell walls and making proteins, slow nearly to a halt, leaving the drugs little to act on.

parts.q:
Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
(A) Specifically,
(B) As a result,
(C) Nevertheless,
(D) By contrast,
parts.a: (A). The first sentence says that some bacteria survive without being resistant; the second explains how they manage it, by going dormant so that antibiotics have nothing to act on. 'Specifically' introduces a more precise account of a claim just made. (B) is wrong because it reverses cause and effect: the cells do not become dormant as a result of surviving; they survive as a result of becoming dormant. (C) is wrong because 'Nevertheless' signals a concession or contrast, but the second sentence explains the first rather than working against it. (D) is wrong because 'By contrast' would set the persister cells against the bacteria just described, and they are the same bacteria.
parts.n: Type: Transitions. Rule or move: Test a cause-and-effect transition by reading it as 'because of what the first sentence says, what the second says happened'; if the causation runs the other way, look for an elaborating transition such as 'Specifically.' Trap: (B) 'As a result,' which senses a causal link but points it in the wrong direction.

mc.stem:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• In 1869, Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev published a periodic table that left gaps for elements not yet discovered.
• He predicted the properties of one missing element, which he called eka-aluminum, including a density of about 5.9 grams per cubic centimeter (g/cm³).
• In 1875, French chemist Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran discovered gallium, which occupied eka-aluminum's place in the table.
• Lecoq de Boisbaudran first reported gallium's density as 4.7 g/cm³.
• Mendeleev suggested that the sample had been impure; a measurement of a purified sample gave about 5.9 g/cm³.

parts.q:
The student wants to emphasize how strongly Mendeleev trusted the predictions of his periodic table. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
(A) In 1875, Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran discovered gallium, an element that filled one of the gaps in the periodic table Mendeleev had published in 1869.
(B) Mendeleev predicted that eka-aluminum would have a density of about 5.9 g/cm³, and a purified sample of gallium was eventually measured at about that density.
(C) When gallium's discoverer reported a density of 4.7 g/cm³ instead of the 5.9 g/cm³ Mendeleev had predicted, Mendeleev suggested that the sample was impure.
(D) Mendeleev's 1869 periodic table left gaps for elements not yet discovered, including one that he called eka-aluminum and whose properties he predicted.
parts.a: (C). Mendeleev's trust in his table shows most clearly at the moment a measurement contradicted it: rather than revising his prediction, he proposed that the sample was impure. (B) is wrong because it shows that his prediction turned out to be accurate, which speaks to the table's success, not to how firmly he trusted it before that success was confirmed. (A) is wrong because it reports the discovery of gallium without showing Mendeleev's attitude toward his predictions at all. (D) is wrong because leaving gaps and predicting an element's properties show that he made predictions, not that he held to them against contrary evidence.
parts.n: Type: Rhetorical synthesis. Rule or move: Match the goal's key word (here 'trusted') to the note that shows it in action; a note showing that a prediction came true is different from one showing how strongly someone believed it. Trap: (B), which describes the prediction's vindication and feels like the triumphant choice, but shows accuracy rather than trust.

While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Charles Drew (1904–1950) was an American surgeon and medical researcher.
• In 1940, he completed a doctoral thesis at Columbia University on the preservation of blood.
• At the time, whole blood could be stored for only a limited time before its red blood cells broke down.
• Plasma, the liquid portion of blood with the cells removed, could be stored far longer and could be given to patients without matching blood types.
• In 1940, Drew led Blood for Britain, a program that shipped plasma from the United States to treat wounded soldiers and civilians in Britain.

parts.q:
The student wants to explain why the Blood for Britain program shipped plasma rather than whole blood. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
(A) Charles Drew, who completed a doctoral thesis on the preservation of blood at Columbia University in 1940, led the Blood for Britain program that same year.
(B) Because plasma could be stored far longer than whole blood and did not require matching blood types, Blood for Britain shipped plasma instead.
(C) Whole blood could be stored for only a limited time, and the Blood for Britain program shipped plasma to treat wounded soldiers and civilians in Britain.
(D) Plasma is the liquid portion of blood with the cells removed, and in 1940 the Blood for Britain program shipped it from the United States to Britain.
parts.a: (B). The goal is to explain why the program chose plasma over whole blood, and this choice gives both reasons from the notes, plasma's longer storage life and its not requiring matching blood types, in a sentence built on 'because.' (A) is wrong because it presents Drew's credentials and role, not a reason for choosing plasma. (C) is wrong because it states whole blood's short storage life but never says that plasma lasted longer, so the comparison, and with it the explanation, is left incomplete. (D) is wrong because it defines plasma and reports the shipments without giving any reason for choosing plasma.
parts.n: Type: Rhetorical synthesis. Rule or move: A 'why' goal needs a reason stated as a reason, and a 'rather than' goal needs both sides of the comparison. Trap: (C), which uses the note about whole blood and so sounds like an explanation, but never says what plasma offered instead.

While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• In 1942, film actress Hedy Lamarr and composer George Antheil received a US patent for a "secret communication system."
• The system was designed to guide torpedoes by radio without the signal being jammed by an enemy.
• It used frequency hopping: the transmitter and receiver switched together among 88 radio frequencies in a sequence known only to them.
• To keep the transmitter and receiver synchronized, the inventors adapted a mechanism like the paper rolls that drive player pianos.
• The US Navy did not adopt the system during World War II, but frequency hopping later became part of technologies such as Bluetooth.

parts.q:
The student wants to explain how the system was designed to protect its signal from jamming. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
(A) Lamarr and Antheil's 1942 patent described a system that would guide torpedoes by radio and that was designed to keep an enemy from jamming the signal.
(B) Lamarr and Antheil kept their system's transmitter and receiver in step by adapting a mechanism like the paper rolls that drive player pianos.
(C) Although the US Navy did not adopt the system during World War II, frequency hopping later became part of technologies such as Bluetooth.
(D) The system was meant to defeat jamming by having its transmitter and receiver switch together among 88 frequencies in a sequence known only to them.
parts.a: (D). The goal is to explain how the system was meant to prevent jamming, and this choice gives the method: the signal kept moving among 88 frequencies in a sequence shared only by the transmitter and receiver, so an enemy would not know which frequency to jam. (A) is wrong because it states that the system was designed to prevent jamming, which is its purpose, but not how it would do so. (B) is wrong because it explains how the transmitter and receiver stayed synchronized, a supporting detail, without saying how switching frequencies defeated jamming. (C) is wrong because it concerns the system's later history, not how it worked.
parts.n: Type: Rhetorical synthesis. Rule or move: Distinguish a goal's 'how' from its 'what' or 'why'; a choice that restates the purpose does not explain the method. Trap: (A), which repeats the goal's word 'jamming' but gives only the purpose.
